comments.title: Comment Submitted by Saurav Dahal
comments.commentText:
In 1685, King Louis XIV of France revoked the Edict of Nantes, forcing thousands of skilled Huguenots to flee religious persecution. England, the Netherlands, and Brandenburg-Prussia welcomed many of these refugees, gaining craftsmen, merchants, technical knowledge, and industrial expertise. France lost valuable human capital while competing economies benefited.

More than two centuries later, history repeated itself under far more tragic circumstances.

In the early twentieth century, Germany was one of the world’s greatest scientific powers, leading in physics, chemistry, mathematics, and engineering. Then came 1933. The Nazi regime expelled and persecuted Jewish scholars and political opponents. Albert Einstein, Hans Bethe, and numerous other brilliant scientists left Germany, many ultimately contributing to American and British research. Some played important roles in the Manhattan Project, while others transformed universities and scientific institutions.

Germany lost scientific talent. America gained scientific strength.

The circumstances of historical persecution are fundamentally different from today’s immigration policies. Nevertheless, the economic lesson remains: when countries drive away knowledge and talent, other nations can benefit.

America’s own technological rise offers further evidence.

In 1957, Andrew Grove arrived in America as a Hungarian refugee. He later helped build Intel into a semiconductor powerhouse, contributing to the computing revolution.

Sergey Brin immigrated to America as a child after his family left the Soviet Union. He later co-founded Google, helping transform the global technology economy.

Imagine the American technology industry without the contributions of immigrants like these.

Now consider 2026.

We are entering perhaps the most consequential technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution. Artificial intelligence is advancing at extraordinary speed, reshaping medicine, computing, robotics, scientific discovery, and economic productivity.

China and other nations are investing heavily in research infrastructure and competing to attract scientific talent.

Yet at this precise moment, America is proposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations.

Have we learned nothing from history?

The United States attracts exceptional international students, trains them at world-leading universities, and benefits from their research. Then, just as these graduates prepare to contribute to American industry, the government proposes extraordinary financial barriers on the institutions supporting their employment authorization.

What happens when these researchers decide to leave?

They do not stop innovating. They innovate elsewhere.

They join laboratories in competing nations, establish startups, develop intellectual property, mentor future scientists, and help build industries that may eventually compete with America.

And what happens when American companies cannot efficiently recruit specialized talent? They may expand research and development overseas. Investment, future employment opportunities, and technological capabilities can follow.

This could ultimately hurt American workers rather than protect them.

The consequences are especially serious in artificial intelligence, where years of lost progress could reshape global technological competition. Unlike previous industrial revolutions, today’s scientific landscape can change dramatically within a remarkably short period.

There is a dangerous assumption that America will always remain the world’s technological leader simply because it has dominated for decades.

History offers no such guarantee.

France lost skilled people who strengthened its competitors. Germany’s persecution of scientists contributed to the growth of scientific institutions abroad. America became stronger partly because it welcomed people whom other countries had driven away.

Will historians look back at 2026 and ask why America chose to discourage global scientific talent at the very beginning of the AI revolution?

Immigration enforcement and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives. But effective policy requires understanding long-term consequences, not simply creating enormous financial barriers.

A great nation should not confuse restricting talent with strengthening its economy.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and seriously examine its consequences for American innovation, employment, and scientific competitiveness.

History will not remember how much money America tried to collect from international graduates. It will remember which countries enabled the next great technological revolution and which countries allowed that opportunity to slip away.
comments.reason: Argues that driving away skilled talent through restrictive immigration policies harms American economic and scientific strength.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I ask the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. Section 214(a)(1) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) authorizes DHS to prescribe the time and conditions of a nonimmigrant’s admission. DHS reads that provision to authorize a $70,000 initial payment and a $30,000 subsequent payment by a separate party, the educational institution. The proposal does not explain why that is the best reading of the statute.
The question is who can be made to pay and under what authority
In Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), the court upheld DHS’s authority to permit practical training as part of the terms of F-1 admission. That decision supports DHS’s authority to prescribe substantive terms for training, including the role of a school recommendation. The power to recognize or require a school’s academic judgment does not by itself establish the power to charge the school for exercising that judgment. Nor does DHS’s authority to regulate SEVP-certified schools resolve which monetary exactions Congress authorized.
Congress has expressly prescribed immigration charges elsewhere in the INA. For example, 8 U.S.C. § 1184(c)(12) identifies liable parties and sets amounts for specified fraud prevention and detection fees. Congress separately provided for a charge supporting the foreign-student information collection program in 8 U.S.C. § 1372(e), with provisions governing the payer, calculation, and disposition of the proceeds. Those statutes illustrate the detail Congress used when it authorized payments in related settings. Section 1372(e) need not govern the proposed levy for that contrast to matter. Under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), a reviewing court independently determines the scope of the delegation.
DHS also has a reasoned decision-making problem
Even assuming DHS can impose some financial condition, the proposal does not adequately explain why a mandatory payment by the school before its recommendation is the appropriate instrument. DHS attributes potential fraud to students, employers, and schools, yet it attaches liability to every covered recommendation without distinguishing which party can detect or prevent the conduct. A school can assess whether training relates to the degree, but it may have limited ability to verify that an outside employer actually provides the promised supervision. DHS should explain why the recommending institution is the appropriate payer across those different circumstances and compare that choice with enforcing substantive duties on the actors who control the relevant conduct.
Finalizing this proposal would raise a statutory-authority objection under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(C). Independently, failing to explain the choice of payer and its relationship to the stated problem would make the rule arbitrary and capricious under § 706(2)(A). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ II, IV.C, V.A. 8 U.S.C. §§ 1184(a)(1), 1184(c)(12), 1372(e). Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2022/10/21-5028-1967339.pdf. Loper Bright, https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/22-451_7m58.pdf.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS proposes to collect $70,000 for an initial recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation. The proposal justifies these amounts in substantial part by their deterrent effect and by reference to H-1B charges. It does not adequately identify what the school would receive for the payment or explain why these amounts are appropriate.
The purpose and design of the charge matter
DHS says the proceeds would go to Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. § 3302, and ICE could not retain them under the authority cited for the rule. Section 3302 governs the handling of money received by the government. It supplies no independent authority to impose the charge. Deposit in the Treasury is compatible with a valid fee, but here it is significant alongside DHS’s position that the charge would work even if Congress never appropriated the proceeds to support enforcement. The intended mechanism is the pressure the assessment places on participation.
In National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340–42 (1974), the Supreme Court distinguished charges for particular benefits from assessments imposed to advance broader public policies. That case interpreted the predecessor to 31 U.S.C. § 9701. Its reasoning is instructive by analogy here because DHS invokes general regulatory language to impose a large assessment that it expressly designs to deter conduct. DHS should identify the federal service or particular benefit conferred on the school, distinguish it from USCIS’s adjudication of the student’s separate employment authorization application, and explain how it values that benefit. If the assessment instead serves as a public-policy levy, DHS should identify the congressional delegation that authorizes it.
DHS needs to justify both prices
Even if DHS has authority to charge for a particular benefit, the proposal needs an explanation for $70,000 and $30,000. H-1B and OPT have different payers, eligibility rules, and functions. A comparison with H-1B charges does not establish the value of an OPT recommendation or the price needed to deter abuse. DHS should identify the data connecting each amount to the expected response of legitimate and fraudulent participants. It should also explain why the first recommendation warrants the higher amount when the fee can purchase access to training periods of very different lengths, and why two recommendations covering portions of the ordinary OPT period should produce a greater charge than one covering the entire period.
On this record, adopting the proposal would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) because the agency has not connected either price to the benefit or deterrent effect it invokes. The absence of an adequate statutory basis for a deterrent levy also raises a separate objection under § 706(2)(C). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ IV.C, V.A, VII.A.5.d. 31 U.S.C. §§ 3302, 9701. National Cable Television, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-415/pdf/USREPORTS-415-336.pdf.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The transition fails to account for schools’ reliance on existing OPT rules

DHS should withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. The proposed transition generally turns on the date a designated school official recommends a student for OPT. That date may be administratively convenient, but it is a poor proxy for when schools, students, and employers made commitments in reliance on the existing framework.
Schools make commitments years before the recommendation
An institution can recruit an entering class, set tuition and aid, hire staff for career advising, and commit resources to employer partnerships well before any member of that class is eligible for a recommendation. A school may develop a multi-year degree program around a sequence of classroom instruction and training opportunities, even though a particular placement remains contingent on federal approval. An employer may budget for supervision and extend an offer before the recommendation date. The proposed cutoff can protect one recommendation while exposing a planned STEM extension for the same student to a $70,000 charge if the extension is the first recommendation subject to the fee.
DHS discusses reliance in § VI, states that the public interest outweighs it, and emphasizes prospective application. That answers when DHS would collect money. It leaves open what investments become difficult to recover and whether DHS could preserve them while addressing current risks. A student’s ability to depart the country or seek a different status does not address an institution’s staffing commitments, approved budgets, or agreements with training partners. Likewise, evidence of fraud in some placements does not establish how much enforcement benefit DHS would give up by adopting temporary protection for defined, existing cohorts.
DHS should evaluate alternatives tied to actual reliance
DHS should identify how many already-enrolled students and current OPT participants would be affected, using enrollment cohorts and SEVIS records where feasible. It should solicit information on existing institutional budgets, recruiting commitments, and training agreements, then compare the 60-day cutoff with at least three alternatives. Those include grandfathering students enrolled by a defined date through completion of their current program and associated OPT, protecting STEM extensions for students already on initial OPT, and delaying implementation until schools have completed a full budget and admissions cycle. DHS should estimate each alternative’s duration, scope, and effect on enforcement. Existing fraud and eligibility controls could continue to apply to protected cohorts.
DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1, 30–33 (2020), requires an agency changing policy to consider serious reliance interests and weigh them against competing concerns. A federal benefit can remain contingent while institutions reasonably rely on the existing process when making investments. Finalizing the proposal without grappling with those interests and plausible ways to accommodate them would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ V.C, VI, and proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(3). Regents, https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/19pdf/18-587_5ifl.pdf.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed fee triggers leave schools unable to determine the amount due.

DHS should reconsider the proposed fees and withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. The proposed regulatory text does not reliably tell a school which amount it must pay before recommending a student. This ambiguity concerns the central legal obligation and the data used to estimate the proposal’s effects.
The proposed paragraphs produce different answers on their face
Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(1) describes a one-time $70,000 payment for the first recommendation. Paragraph (i)(2) requires $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation if the student previously participated in OPT and paid the initial fee. Paragraph (i)(3) first appears to require $70,000 for any recommendation on or after the effective date, then provides for the subsequent $30,000 charge once the initial fee has been paid. The preamble suggests that DHS intends to collect $70,000 for the first recommendation subject to the rule and $30,000 for qualifying later recommendations. The text should implement that result explicitly, including which provision governs when the first recommendation preceded the effective date. It should also consistently identify the school as the payer rather than conditioning the later amount on wording that refers to payment by the student.
Three cases illustrate the practical problem. First, a student is already on initial OPT when the rule takes effect and then requests a STEM extension. Second, a student had a pre-effective-date recommendation, but the designated school official must issue a replacement recommendation after the cutoff. Third, a school previously paid $70,000, but a different school later recommends the student after a higher degree. The second case also requires DHS to distinguish a clerical correction from a new recommendation. In the third case, the later school needs an authoritative way to establish payment history before deciding whether to commit funds. The difference between fee tiers is $40,000 per recommendation.
The public needs an opportunity to evaluate the actual obligation
DHS should publish a decision table showing the fee and payer for each case, identify the precise triggering event, and specify how the school can verify the result before payment. It should reconcile the operative text with its participation, cost, and revenue estimates. A website instruction issued after finalization would leave the public without an opportunity to comment on any material changes to the triggering events. If DHS pursues a revised rule, it should publish corrected text and updated estimates for comment under 5 U.S.C. § 553.
Finalizing the proposed text without resolving these issues would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). DHS cannot rationally assess the consequences of a two-tier charge while leaving schools uncertain about which tier governs common transitions. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ V.A, V.C, VI, VII.A, and proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(1)–(3). 5 U.S.C. §§ 553, 706.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.
Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (requiring a reasoned explanation connecting the record to the agency’s decision), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-463/pdf/USREPORTS-463-29.pdf

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
5. The OPT fee could deter legitimate training more effectively than fraud
Public comment on Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
91 Fed. Reg. 64,566 (Oct. 8, 2026)
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS predicts that a large fee will discourage abuse and give schools a greater stake in screening recommendations. That prediction depends on who bears the fee and how legitimate and fraudulent participants respond. The proposal does not adequately test either link.
DHS should evaluate who leaves and who stays
A school or employer offering a genuine placement weighs the fee against the value of supervised training. That value can be substantial even when the placement brings in little revenue. An organized scheme could have different incentives. A broker might raise the price it charges students, pool financing, or concentrate its business in placements where it can recover the cost. The fee could make some schemes uneconomic. The record needs to explain which schemes would exit, which could adapt, and how those responses compare with the expected exit of legitimate programs.
For example, assume a program starts with 1,000 legitimate placements and 20 fraudulent ones. If a fee deters 500 legitimate placements and five fraudulent ones, the number of fraudulent placements falls, but their share rises from about 2 percent to about 3 percent. This illustration is not a forecast. It shows why total participation, fraud prevalence, and the number of violations prevented are different measures. DHS should assess all three and explain how their movement would affect investigative workload and the likelihood of identifying violations.
Pass-through also changes the screening incentive
The preamble predicts schools will screen more carefully because they bear a financial stake. The economic analysis also anticipates that schools may shift the charge to students or employers. A school that collects the full amount before it recommends a student still faces administrative and compliance risks, but it does not bear the same financial exposure as a school paying from its own budget. DHS should separately analyze school-funded, employer-funded, and student-funded recommendations and explain how each arrangement affects screening. It should compare the fee with controls directed at facts a broker cannot establish merely by producing payment, such as whether a worksite exists and whether it provides the training it claims to offer.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), finalizing the proposal would be arbitrary and capricious if DHS continues to assume that a smaller pool is a better-screened pool without examining these countervailing incentives. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ IV.A, IV.C, VII.A. Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983).
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.
Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (requiring a reasoned explanation connecting the record to the agency’s decision), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-463/pdf/USREPORTS-463-29.pdf

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
6. Employer financing of OPT fees could restrict worker mobility and reporting
Public comment on Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
91 Fed. Reg. 64,566 (Oct. 8, 2026)
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS treats employer financing as a way schools might absorb the charge. The agency should also examine what happens when an employer agrees to fund a recommendation only if the student accepts conditions that make leaving or reporting abuse expensive.
Repayment terms could undermine the rule’s objectives
An employer that advances money might require a trainee to repay part or all of it upon resignation, through a contract, payroll deductions, or an arrangement with a staffing intermediary. For example, a trainee who discovers that promised supervision is absent might have to choose between continuing the placement and incurring a five-figure debt. Such a clause could also deter a worker from reporting inaccurate training records or wage violations. The proposal does not itself create a debt to an employer. The concern is the private arrangements that its financing model makes possible.
This issue directly concerns DHS’s stated goals. A rule intended to improve training integrity should consider whether workers will still report that their training is fictitious or has changed. A rule intended to protect U.S. workers should consider whether large repayment obligations could give employers extra bargaining power over OPT workers and affect working conditions for comparable employees. DHS’s STEM OPT rules already require commensurate terms and a non-displacement attestation. DHS should explain how it would assess those assurances where a worker’s effective compensation or ability to leave depends on a fee repayment agreement.
Congress addressed an analogous problem in the H-1B program by prohibiting early-cessation penalties and reimbursement of a specified statutory fee. See 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(2)(C)(vi). Those provisions apply to H-1B and offer a model for evaluating comparable risks in OPT. DHS should seek evidence on proposed financing terms and, if it pursues a replacement rule, evaluate prohibiting fee-related payroll deductions, repayment triggered by departure, and retaliation for reporting violations. It should address coverage of staffing intermediaries and explain how trainees could report violations confidentially.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), finalizing the proposed fee would be arbitrary and capricious if DHS relies on employer financing to support its participation assumptions while disregarding foreseeable terms of that financing that could frustrate its own labor and anti-fraud objectives. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ III.D, IV.B, VII.A. 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C). 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(2)(C)(vi), https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/laws-and-regulations/laws/ina/h1b.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
. DHS should assess substitution from pre-completion OPT into curricular training
Public comment on Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
91 Fed. Reg. 64,566 (Oct. 8, 2026)
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS anticipates that some participants will shift from pre-completion OPT to post-completion OPT. It should also examine a different response. Schools and employers may try to preserve in-degree placements by shifting eligible training into Curricular Practical Training (CPT), which the proposed fee does not cover.
The price difference can change how schools structure academic programs
Consider a school with an existing internship elective and an employer offering a supervised summer placement before graduation. If the placement meets current CPT requirements through the school’s curriculum, a school may seek to use CPT in place of pre-completion OPT. Other schools may consider revising course offerings, academic calendars, or internship requirements so future placements qualify. CPT has its own eligibility and authorization rules, and many placements cannot move into it. That variation is precisely what DHS should study. The same proposed charge may redirect training at one institution and eliminate a comparable opportunity at another.
Schools have reliance interests here. Programs may have allocated faculty time, developed advising and employer relationships, or committed to specific sequencing of in-class and work-based training. A school may be unable to revise that sequence in one semester because it must obtain curricular approvals or honor commitments to existing students. DHS should distinguish near-term losses of placements from later changes that schools could make after an academic planning cycle.
A shift in authorization category is a separate regulatory outcome
DHS should use SEVIS data to identify the schools and fields that use both CPT and pre-completion OPT, then test realistic low- and high-substitution scenarios. It should estimate how many placements would move into CPT, how many would move after graduation, and how many would disappear. If similar placements persist under CPT, DHS should assess what changes in oversight and whether that shift advances its fraud-prevention objective. It should compare the proposed charge with alternatives that target deficient placements across the existing authorization categories or that protect existing pre-completion training sequences during a transition.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), finalizing a large price difference between training pathways would be arbitrary and capricious if DHS failed to examine a foreseeable shift that could change its forecasts of costs, benefits, and compliance. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ III.D, VII.A.5.d. 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10), including the applicable CPT requirements. State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS’s federalism finding does not account for direct costs to state universities
Public comment on Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
91 Fed. Reg. 64,566 (Oct. 8, 2026)
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. Section VII.F concludes that the proposal is unlikely to impose substantial direct compliance costs on state or local governments. Elsewhere, DHS estimates that 1,044 public institutions were among the institutions with at least one OPT recommendation in its historical analysis and treats these public institutions as state-run for its small-entity analysis. DHS should reconcile those findings before it imposes a federal payment obligation on public institutions that continue to recommend students.
State budget decisions matter even when payment is conditional
The proposal places the charge on the recommending school. A state university that makes 50 initial recommendations and 20 subsequent recommendations in a year would owe $4.1 million at the proposed rates. That calculation illustrates the scale for one hypothetical institution. DHS should estimate actual exposure using its recommendation data, then explain who pays at state-run campuses and systems and what limits apply to the use of appropriations, tuition, grants, or other restricted funds. Potential reimbursement may reduce net costs in some cases, but it does not remove the school’s payment obligation or establish that public institutions can advance the money.
A public institution could avoid payments by curtailing recommendations. DHS should examine that scenario separately. It has different consequences for state decisions about educational programming, existing training partnerships, and allocations already approved for multi-year cohorts. A state budget cycle may also prevent a university from adjusting its appropriations on 60 days’ notice. Those are concrete institutional reliance and implementation concerns that an estimate of aggregate national transfers cannot resolve.
DHS should revisit its finding and consult state officials
Executive Order 13132 § 6 calls for an accountable process for timely state and local input on policies with federalism implications and provides additional requirements in specified circumstances. DHS states in § VII.D that it did not consult elected representatives of affected state, local, and tribal governments. I ask DHS to address § 6 directly, consult relevant officials, and explain whether a federalism summary impact statement is warranted. This request is separate from the APA objection. The APA issue is the inconsistency between the agency’s assessment of which institutions it regulates and its treatment of the direct costs and implementation constraints for those institutions.
Finalizing the rule without resolving that inconsistency would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ V.C, VI, VII.B.3, VII.D, VII.F. Executive Order 13132 §§ 1, 6, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1999-08-10/pdf/99-20729.pdf.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.
Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (requiring a reasoned explanation connecting the record to the agency’s decision), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-463/pdf/USREPORTS-463-29.pdf
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees rule due to uncounted costs on state universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed fee would make school budget decisions determine access to OPT
Public comment on Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
91 Fed. Reg. 64,566 (Oct. 8, 2026)
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. The proposal prevents a designated school official from recommending a student until the school pays. DHS expects this to make schools more selective. It does not adequately explain how schools will allocate scarce funds or why those allocation decisions would identify the students whose training best meets federal requirements.
A school’s financial decision is separate from its assessment of eligibility
Under the current framework, a school already has a substantive role in recommending training. The proposal adds a separate decision over whether to commit institutional funds. Two students may present equally sound training plans, yet one department may have an employer partner willing to pay and another may have exhausted its discretionary funds. A campus might allocate a fixed number of recommendations at the start of the year, leaving a later graduating cohort without access despite equally strong qualifications. Those outcomes would follow from funding and timing even if school officials assess the quality of the training correctly.
The effect on access cannot be measured only by aggregate participation. DHS should assess which offices would control payment, how approvals would interact with federal filing deadlines, and what would happen when a finance office denies a request or makes a processing error. Because the payment comes before the recommendation, the student may lose the opportunity to have USCIS consider the application at all. Schools also may have recruited and advised current cohorts under existing practices. A short transition may leave them little time to develop consistent procedures or communicate material changes to students approaching graduation.
DHS should assess the allocation system it is creating
DHS should seek information on how schools would ration funds, including whether decisions would vary by department, graduating term, or availability of outside financing. It should compare that system with existing substantive eligibility and oversight tools. If it pursues a replacement proposal with an institutional payment, DHS should address published allocation criteria, timely written reasons for adverse decisions, and a means to correct payment or allocation errors before filing deadlines expire. It should distinguish an academic recommendation decision from a school’s decision about whether to finance it.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), it would be arbitrary and capricious for DHS to rely on greater school selectivity as a program-integrity benefit while leaving the actual financial criteria, decision process, and consequences for eligible students unexplored. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM §§ IV.C, VI, and proposed 8 C.F.R. §§ 214.2(f)(11), 214.13(i). State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.
Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (requiring a reasoned explanation connecting the record to the agency’s decision), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-463/pdf/USREPORTS-463-29.pdf
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees rule due to negative impacts on school budgets and student access.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Existing foreign funding disclosures cannot establish the source of individual OPT fees
Public comment on Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
91 Fed. Reg. 64,566 (Oct. 8, 2026)
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. In § IV.C, DHS suggests that existing disclosures of foreign gifts and contracts could help enforcement authorities identify foreign adversaries financing participation. DHS should show how the reporting system would reveal that link before crediting the proposed fee with this national-security benefit.
The existing disclosure system has a different unit of reporting
Section 117 of the Higher Education Act, 20 U.S.C. § 1011f, covers institutions that meet its statutory definition. Its gift and contract reporting trigger generally looks to $250,000 in transactions with a foreign source in a calendar year, and the statute also addresses foreign ownership or control. Many disclosures are reported in aggregate, with additional detail for specified restricted or conditional arrangements. A reported institutional gift can reveal a funding relationship. The report does not ordinarily establish that a particular dollar amount funded an OPT recommendation for a particular trainee.
For example, a $210,000 contribution would cover three initial fees. If it were the only qualifying transaction with that source in the calendar year and there were no foreign ownership or control, it would fall below the general gift and contract reporting trigger. At the other end, a reportable general-purpose gift could be fully disclosed while offering little evidence about whether it paid for any recommendation. DHS should distinguish institutional accounting records, reports to the Department of Education, and the payment records ICE would receive. The proposal should identify what information each system provides and what lawful data linkage would be needed to trace a payment.
DHS should test the mechanism against the baseline
Existing disclosure obligations operate without the new fees. DHS should explain what additional evidence the proposal would produce, how many affected institutions are subject to the statute, and which funding channels would remain difficult to trace. It should also examine the possibility that requiring large payments would encourage institutions to seek new external financing. Any benefit estimate should distinguish legitimate financing from risk indicators and compare the proposed fee with targeted financial inquiries or coordination under existing authorities where there is evidence of suspicious activity.
If DHS finalizes the proposal on the theory that existing disclosures will expose covert financing without demonstrating the link between the proposed payment and information the government can actually obtain, it would rely on a mechanism the record does not support. That would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
Authorities
NPRM § IV.C. 20 U.S.C. § 1011f(a)–(c), (h), https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title20-section1011f. State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.
Proposed rule, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm
Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title5-section706.
Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (requiring a reasoned explanation connecting the record to the agency’s decision), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-463/pdf/USREPORTS-463-29.pdf

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee rule because it would directly hurt America's economy and global competitiveness.

First, the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations would make it impossible for American employers to hire international graduates. The rule would effectively drive international talent out of the American workforce, depriving American businesses of skilled workers, researchers, and entrepreneurs. This would hurt not only international students but also American businesses and workers who benefit from the jobs and economic opportunities they help create.

Second, the rule would weaken America's position in the global technology race, especially in artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies. At a time when the United States is competing with countries like China and India, it makes little sense to attract and educate talented students from around the world only to force them to take their skills and knowledge elsewhere. America would invest in educating these students while its competitors benefit from their work.

The proposed rule would not stop international students from contributing to technological development. It would simply push their talent, research, innovation, and the jobs they could create to other countries. If the goal is to protect American workers and businesses, driving away people who could help them grow would achieve the opposite. America's ability to attract talent from around the world has long been one of its greatest strengths. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm the economy, prevent hiring international talent, and weaken global competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on the schools this fee would hit hardest — not the wealthy private universities, but the community colleges, regional public universities, and minority-serving institutions that educate the students with the fewest alternatives.

A flat fee is a regressive tax, and the arithmetic makes that plain. A community college with forty international graduates a year would owe $2.8 million in OPT fees — a sum larger than many community colleges' entire international-office budgets, and a figure no state appropriation covers. These are institutions that run on thin margins, answer to legislatures that have cut funding for years, and cannot raise tuition on a whim. There is no endowment to draw on and no wealthy alumni base to absorb the cost. The only realistic response is to stop recommending OPT, which means the international students who chose that college — often because it was the affordable option — lose the very training authorization that made the degree worth pursuing.

What disappears next matters to American students, too. At regional and minority-serving schools, international students paying full tuition are often the cross-subsidy that keeps programs open: the nursing cohort, the teacher-preparation track, the small graduate program that serves a rural county. Lose those students, and the programs close for everyone — including the first-generation American students who enrolled precisely because the school was close to home and affordable. The domestic student who loses a scholarship, a lab placement, or a degree program is a casualty of this rule just as surely as the international graduate who loses OPT.

DHS applies the fee uniformly, as though uniformity were fairness. It is not. A charge that a rich campus absorbs as an inconvenience and a modest campus cannot pay at all sorts opportunity by wealth, and it sorts it against the schools doing the hardest work in American higher education — the ones that open doors rather than guard them. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are regressive, financially ruinous for smaller schools, and harms students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: ICEB– 2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

To Whom It May Concern,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees. I am a Designated School Official at an institution of higher education. I have worked in the international education field for many years. I strongly oppose the proposed rule of imposing such astronomical fees and urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I understand that there may be concerns of potential fraud but implementing such a fee structure is not the solution. This would be a huge detriment to the global talent that this country has reaped over many years. In general, the majority of international students who come to the U.S. come with a targeted purpose. They are here to pursue their academic programs and appreciate the opportunity to use the skills learned during their programs after graduation in the U.S. As OPT is only for a limited time, these students would only use OPT for 1 year to possibly 3 years at the most. In the end, there is a final date to their time in that F-1 status.

The contributions from this population is immeasurable. The talent ,skills and perspectives are what adds to the richness of this country. They contribute not only economically by bringing in billions of dollars to the local economy and to the country as a whole, but have also helped shape the U.S. workforce and country to lead on the global stage in innovation and research.

I would like to raise concerns regarding the following:

Proposed rule creates unfair access to OPT

By imposing such a fee, it will create unfair access to this immigration benefit. All institutions do not have the same resources nor do all international students. Such an action would lead to inequity amongst this population and universities where OPT has been a benefit to all those eligible in this status for decades. Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10), students may access this benefit before or after their program of study. It is in the regulations and should be accessible for all those pursuing a full-time program of study.

Weakening of U.S. position on the world stage

International students will be deterred from pursuing their education in the U.S. if such a rule were implemented. The potential decline in admission to higher educational institutions would not only hurt the institutions itself, but the rippling effects would be damaging to domestic students, the local economy and the country as a whole. A majority of these students pursue majors in STEM fields and make up a large part of the graduate programs across the country. If other countries are more welcoming to this population, we will lose our competitive edge and the results would be detrimental to the country.

Better options to monitor potential fraud

The majority of students who decide to come to the U.S. for their academic studies come with a specific purpose. This country attracts the best and brightest from all over the world and we should be proud of what our institutions can offer students in their academic pursuits. If there are a few who may not follow the rules, they are in the minority. I believe there are better ways to address these matters through targeted enforcement and oversight and not through excessive financial impediments. It is unclear how imposing such fees will directly reduce perceived fraud. There are many layers of security and enforcement already in place throughout a student’s journey in the U.S. The SEVIS database already tracks and monitors all international students and USCIS reviews and adjudicates each OPT request. There is no need to impose such exorbitant fees for the sake of reducing fraud. There is no connection and it does not make sense. The rule itself lacks clarity regarding implementation, particularly with respect to the logistical procedures for collecting the proposed fee.

In the end, if we want the U.S. to remain the global leader it is, we must remember that the contributions of the international student community add an immense value to this country. U. S. Companies benefit from their knowledge, expertise and global perspectives. Placing barriers on potential student contributions would only weaken the strength of the U.S. in its competitiveness and global leadership. This proposed fee is not the answer and I urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the astronomical OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed increase in fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT). My concern is not only the additional financial burden on current students, but also the message this sends to prospective international students considering an education in the United States.
Choosing to study abroad is a major financial and personal commitment. Prospective students must weigh tuition, living expenses, and the opportunity to gain relevant professional experience after graduation. Raising OPT-related fees could make the United States a less attractive option, particularly for qualified students with limited financial resources. Students may instead choose countries where the overall cost and pathway from education to practical training seem more affordable and predictable.
I urge the agency to consider the broader consequences if fewer international students choose American universities. The potential effects extend beyond individual applications: universities could lose talented applicants, research programs could miss out on future contributors, and local communities could lose spending from students who would otherwise live and study there. Employers could also have fewer opportunities to recruit graduates trained at U.S. institutions.
The agency should not assume that prospective students will continue choosing the United States regardless of rising costs. Even if an individual fee seems modest in isolation, it adds to the total financial burden and may influence where a student decides to enroll.
I respectfully request that the agency withdraw the proposed OPT fee increases and assess their potential effects on international student enrollment, university research, and the United States’ ability to attract global talent before moving forward
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fee increases, arguing they harm students, universities, and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Harry G
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 and $30,000. International students already contribute significantly to the U.S. economy through tuition, research, innovation, and skilled work. These excessive fees would unfairly punish legitimate students, make opportunities dependent on wealth rather than merit, and discourage global talent from studying and working in the United States. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As an international student, I chose to study in the United States because of its academic excellence, opportunities for innovation, and the ability to connect classroom knowledge with real-world professional experience. OPT is an important part of that educational experience. It allows students to apply what they have learned, develop practical skills, and contribute to the American economy.

First, the proposed fees would create unreasonable financial barriers. International students already make substantial financial commitments through tuition, housing, insurance, and living expenses. Even though the proposed fees would formally be paid by educational institutions, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb such extraordinary costs. As a result, many qualified students could lose access to practical training opportunities regardless of their academic achievements, skills, or potential contributions.

Second, the proposal undermines the expectations of students who have already invested in American higher education. Many international students made their educational decisions with the understanding that OPT would provide a legitimate opportunity to gain professional experience related to their studies. Introducing such substantial financial barriers after students have committed years of effort and significant resources creates uncertainty and damages confidence in the U.S. education system.

Third, these fees could weaken America’s ability to attract and retain global talent. International students contribute diverse perspectives, technical knowledge, research, and innovation to American universities and industries. Restricting their access to practical training may discourage future students from choosing the United States and reduce the country’s long-term competitiveness, particularly in science, technology, and emerging industries.

I understand the government’s interest in preventing fraud and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs. However, imposing extraordinarily high fees on educational institutions is not a proportionate or equitable solution. More targeted enforcement, stronger oversight, and improved verification processes would better address these concerns without penalizing legitimate students.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and consider alternatives that protect program integrity while preserving accessible, merit-based opportunities for international students.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

An International Student in the United States
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create unreasonable financial barriers that harm international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. These excessive fees are disproportionate, economically unjustified, and fundamentally inconsistent with the educational purpose of OPT. Although DHS identifies fraud prevention and the protection of American workers as its objectives, the proposal fails to demonstrate why such extraordinary financial barriers are necessary or how they would effectively address misconduct. Rather than targeting fraudulent activities, the rule would penalize legitimate international students who have complied with immigration regulations and invested substantial financial resources in obtaining an American education. OPT is an essential bridge between academic training and professional experience, not merely an alternative employment visa program. Requiring universities to pay tens of thousands of dollars for each OPT recommendation would place an unreasonable burden on American higher education institutions, particularly public universities and smaller colleges with limited budgets. These costs would inevitably risk being passed on to students or employers, making professional opportunities increasingly dependent on financial resources rather than academic qualifications, professional skills, or merit. Furthermore, the proposal would undermine the international competitiveness of American universities by discouraging talented students from pursuing education in the United States. International students contribute tuition revenue, support local economies, participate in research, and enrich American classrooms and communities. Creating financial barriers to practical training would weaken the attractiveness of American higher education and potentially drive talented students toward competing countries. American employers would also suffer, particularly universities, research institutions, nonprofit organizations, and small businesses that rely on access to qualified graduates. Many employers simply cannot afford these additional costs, regardless of a candidate's qualifications or potential contributions. The proposal also fails to account for the realities of the labor market, particularly for graduates entering education, journalism, communication, public service, and other professions where starting salaries are relatively modest. A $70,000 fee could exceed an individual's annual salary, making the requirement economically unreasonable. Moreover, reducing access to OPT does not necessarily prevent fraud or protect American workers; it may instead reduce legitimate economic participation and limit access to skilled talent. If DHS seeks to improve program integrity, targeted investigations, stronger institutional oversight, and enforcement against actual violations would be more proportionate approaches. I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to withdraw this proposed rule. The United States should not undermine its own educational competitiveness, restrict opportunities for qualified graduates, or impose unnecessary financial burdens on American institutions and employers without clear and compelling evidence of corresponding benefits.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessive, economically unjustified, and create unreasonable financial barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees and request withdrawal. I am an economist trained in applied empirical analysis, commenting in my personal capacity. Program integrity and protection of American workers are legitimate objectives, but DHS must show that this payment mechanism advances them and is authorized by Congress.

1. Authority for the payment.
Authority to regulate practical training does not itself establish authority to impose a payment of this magnitude. DHS should identify the statutory language authorizing this particular exaction and explain its limiting principle. Calling the payment a regulatory deterrent does not answer whether Congress authorized it. Nor does showing that it exceeds processing costs alone resolve the issue; DHS must justify the mechanism and amount under the statute it invokes.

2. Ability to pay is not evidence of compliance.
A compliant student with limited resources may be excluded while a well-financed fraudulent participant pays. If a student or employer funds the charge, payment also does not establish that a school independently assessed the training as worth its own expenditure. DHS should provide evidence that payment improves verification, rather than merely reducing participation, and estimate erroneous exclusion by financial resources, field, institution, and employer size. A smaller program is not necessarily a cleaner program.

3. Participation estimates require credible behavioral assumptions.
Historical STEM participation does not identify willingness or ability to pay a new, exceptionally large upfront charge. Averaging high and low scenarios is a modeling choice, not an estimated demand response. Future earnings cannot automatically finance a payment due before work begins. DHS should test substantial participation declines, distinguish initial OPT from extensions and current students from future entrants, and account for financing costs, job-search risk, and training periods shorter than the maximum authorization.

4. Evaluate economic effects beyond fee receipts.
Payments to government are transfers, but behavioral responses can destroy mutually beneficial training and production. DHS should separately assess real compliance costs, lost output, institutional effects, and distributional burdens, avoiding double counting. An administratively chosen fee is not, without supporting analysis, a measure of forgone tuition or educational surplus. Tuition, wages, hiring, and research budgets may adjust, shifting costs to American students and workers.

An international graduate's departure does not establish that an American worker fills the same job. Employers may cancel projects, automate, or expand abroad. Glennon's research on H-1B restrictions identifies offshoring as a relevant adjustment margin; its numerical estimates should not be mechanically applied to OPT. DHS should assess domestic substitution alongside complementary employment, innovation, and retention of U.S.-trained talent, including differences across startups, universities, and multinational firms.

5. The payroll-tax rationale requires proportionality.
The F-1 payroll-tax exemption depends on tax residency and qualifying employment; it does not apply uniformly to OPT participants. DHS should measure actual exempt years and affected workers, distinguish employer savings from employee tax treatment, and explain how those differences support the proposed amount. A statutory tax exemption is not evidence of misconduct.

6. Reliance and alternatives require substantive comparison.
Prospective application can still disrupt prior enrollment, tuition, research, and hiring commitments. Preserving current authorization may not protect an enrolled student's expected STEM extension. Under DHS v. Regents, significant reliance interests must be assessed and weighed, although they do not prevent policy change.

DHS should compare protection for enrolled students and pending applications, staged implementation, risk-based audits, employer verification, sanctions for proven misconduct, and lower fees tied to lawful administrative purposes. If receipts go to the Treasury, speculative future appropriations should not be counted as funded enforcement improvements. Alternatives and the proposed payment should face the same standards for effectiveness, cost, and erroneous exclusion.

Please withdraw the proposal. If DHS proceeds, disclose the supporting data, calculations, and assumptions; explain why targeted enforcement is inadequate; and allow meaningful comment on material revisions. A threat to discontinue OPT does not establish the legality or merits of this particular fee.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and requests withdrawal of the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Annie S
comments.commentText:
**Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Economic Consequences of Proposed OPT Fees**

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under Section V.A. The Department should withdraw these fees and conduct a more comprehensive analysis of their economic consequences.

International students are not merely participants in the U.S. labor market. They are consumers, taxpayers, researchers, and contributors to local economies. According to NAFSA's 2025 economic analysis, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year.

The economic risks are already visible. NAFSA's August 2026 analysis projected that a decline of approximately 111,000 international students could cost the United States $3.4 billion in economic contributions and nearly 40,000 jobs. These figures are not estimates of this proposed rule's effects, but they demonstrate how sensitive American employment and economic activity are to international enrollment.

A $70,000 fee for temporary practical training would make American education substantially less attractive. Students considering U.S. universities would reasonably question why they should invest hundreds of thousands of dollars in tuition and living expenses when their institutions might later be unable or unwilling to support their OPT applications.

The resulting losses would extend beyond international students. Universities, landlords, restaurants, retailers, transportation providers, and other local businesses depend on international student spending. Reductions in enrollment would threaten jobs held by American workers in these sectors.

Furthermore, OPT participants who obtain paid employment generally contribute to federal and state tax revenues. Their temporary immigration status does not mean their economic contributions are temporary or insignificant.

Protecting American workers is a legitimate policy objective. However, DHS should demonstrate that the proposed fees would produce measurable employment benefits exceeding the foreseeable losses in tuition revenue, consumer spending, research activity, and tax receipts.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and publish a rigorous economic impact assessment incorporating enrollment elasticity, local employment effects, and the potential diversion of international talent to competing countries.

Source: NAFSA, International Student Economic Value (2025); NAFSA, Fall 2026 International Student Enrollment Outlook & Economic Impact (August 2026).
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees harm students and the U.S. economy, urging DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by John Q
comments.commentText:
**Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Financial Burdens on Universities and Students**

I oppose the proposed OPT fees under Sections V.A and VI because they impose extraordinary financial obligations on educational institutions without adequately addressing who will ultimately bear those costs.

Under the proposed rule, universities must pay $70,000 before recommending a student for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. Consider a university with 500 students seeking initial OPT in a year. The institution would face $35 million in fees for those students alone. This is a hypothetical illustration, not an estimate for a particular institution, but it demonstrates the scale of the proposal.

Where would this money come from?

Universities operate under budget constraints. They could reduce academic programs, research funding, financial aid, student services, or faculty hiring. Alternatively, institutions might attempt to recover the expense through higher tuition or other charges, where legally permitted. Some schools may simply stop recommending otherwise eligible students for OPT.

International students already pay substantial tuition and living expenses. Many are ineligible for federal student aid, and access to institutional financial assistance varies significantly. A student who has completed an expensive American degree should not lose the opportunity to obtain practical training because their university cannot afford an additional $70,000.

This proposal could also harm domestic students. International tuition revenue helps support university operations, while international enrollment sustains campus employment and surrounding businesses.

According to the American Council on Education's discussion of the Fall 2025 international enrollment survey, 92% of responding institutions indicated that many international students would choose other countries without OPT opportunities. DHS should therefore examine whether the proposed fees would reduce future enrollment and undermine the financial stability of American universities.

The proposal also raises serious distributional concerns. Wealthy institutions may have greater capacity to absorb these fees, while smaller universities, public institutions, and financially constrained schools may not. Access to practical training would increasingly depend on institutional wealth rather than academic achievement or compliance with immigration requirements.

DHS should withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate their effects on institutional budgets, tuition, financial aid, and educational access before pursuing any alternative.

Source: American Council on Education, International Student Enrollment Slows as Concerns About the Visa Application Process Rise (2025).
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees because they create excessive financial burdens for universities and students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Cynthia C
comments.commentText:
**Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Fee Justification, Proportionality, and Less Restrictive Alternatives**

I respectfully oppose the proposed fees in Section V.A and question whether DHS has adequately justified their magnitude and necessity.

I recognize the Department's legitimate interest in preventing OPT fraud, protecting American workers, and strengthening immigration compliance. However, a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee require particularly strong justification.

DHS should explain precisely how these amounts were determined. What portion represents the actual administrative cost of OPT oversight? What portion is intended to deter participation? How much additional revenue would be collected, and how would it be allocated? Would any revenue support immigration enforcement or administrative activities unrelated to OPT?

These distinctions matter. A fee designed to recover administrative costs is fundamentally different from a financial barrier intended to discourage participation. DHS should identify the statutory authority supporting each component and explain how the amounts are proportionate to the stated objectives.

The proposal also risks penalizing compliant institutions and students for misconduct committed by others. Fraud involving particular schools, employers, or students should justify targeted investigations and sanctions, not an indiscriminate financial burden on every legitimate OPT recommendation.

There are more proportionate alternatives: risk-based institutional audits, stronger employer verification, enhanced SEVIS reporting, closer cooperation with designated school officials, targeted inspections of suspicious employment arrangements, and meaningful penalties for proven violations.

DHS already maintains relationships with SEVP-certified institutions and their international student offices. These existing systems provide an opportunity to improve oversight without effectively pricing legitimate students out of practical training.

Before imposing these fees, DHS should publish an itemized cost justification, a clear revenue-allocation explanation, evidence connecting the proposed amounts to fraud reduction, and a comparative analysis of less burdensome alternatives.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and adopt targeted, evidence-based compliance measures that distinguish fraudulent activity from legitimate academic and professional training.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees as an unjustified financial barrier.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Harm to Research, Entrepreneurship, and American Innovation**

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees because they would undermine the research and innovation ecosystem that has historically strengthened the United States.

OPT is not exclusively a pathway into large corporations. Eligible graduates also pursue practical training through university research laboratories, research assistant positions, nonprofit organizations, early-stage startups, and other work directly related to their academic studies.

Many of these organizations operate with limited budgets. A university laboratory may have funding for a graduate research assistant but not an additional $70,000 institutional fee. A nonprofit may be able to offer meaningful training but lack the resources to offset such a financial barrier. A promising startup may be able to provide valuable technical experience without possessing the financial capacity of an established corporation.

The proposed fee therefore risks excluding talented graduates from precisely the organizations that can generate significant scientific and social value despite limited immediate revenue.

International students have also contributed substantially to American entrepreneurship. NAFSA reports that former international students founded approximately one-quarter of U.S. startup companies valued at $1 billion or more. Restricting access to post-study training could weaken the pipeline through which future entrepreneurs develop skills, professional networks, and innovative ideas.

The United States benefits when talented graduates conduct research, commercialize discoveries, establish businesses, and contribute to emerging industries. Their contributions can generate new employment opportunities for American workers rather than merely compete for existing positions.

Importantly, OPT is temporary practical training, not permanent residence. Standard post-completion OPT generally lasts up to 12 months, with an additional 24-month extension available to eligible STEM graduates. Participation does not guarantee an H-1B visa or a green card.

It is difficult to justify imposing up to $100,000 in institutional fees for temporary training opportunities that provide no guarantee of long-term immigration status.

I urge DHS to consider the effects on university laboratories, nonprofits, startups, and the national innovation ecosystem. The Department should withdraw the proposed fees and pursue targeted compliance improvements that preserve legitimate research and entrepreneurial opportunities.

Source: NAFSA, America Is Losing International Student Talent; Institute of International Education, Open Doors 2025.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm research, startups, and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Pre-Completion OPT, CPT, and Contradictory Policy Incentives**

I oppose the proposed OPT fee structure, particularly its treatment of pre-completion OPT and subsequent practical training under Sections V.A and VI.

The proposed rule would impose a $70,000 institutional fee when a student first participates in OPT, regardless of whether the training occurs before or after graduation. A subsequent OPT participation would trigger an additional $30,000 fee.

This creates an extraordinary financial disincentive for students seeking legitimate pre-graduation practical experience.

For example, a student who uses pre-completion OPT for a summer internship could trigger a $70,000 fee before graduation. If the student subsequently seeks post-completion OPT, another $30,000 could apply. A short internship and later graduate employment could therefore result in $100,000 in institutional fees.

DHS itself acknowledges in the proposed rule that pre-completion OPT participation is expected to decline, while stating that it cannot reasonably predict the magnitude of that decline.

That admission should prompt further analysis before the Department adopts a policy with potentially severe consequences for students and universities.

The proposal is especially concerning when considered alongside broader DHS scrutiny of Curricular Practical Training (CPT). If the Department seeks to strengthen CPT oversight, it should ensure that legitimate alternatives remain practically accessible. A regulatory framework that restricts one training pathway while imposing a $70,000 barrier on another risks eliminating meaningful opportunities for lawful experiential education.

Practical training is an integral component of many academic programs. Internships allow students to apply classroom knowledge, acquire professional skills, and contribute to American employers and research institutions.

The Department should also distinguish temporary training authorization from permanent labor immigration. OPT does not guarantee an H-1B petition, selection, or permanent residency. Requiring extraordinary institutional payments for a limited period of training is disproportionate to the benefit conferred.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure, assess its combined effects with existing CPT and OPT requirements, and develop coordinated oversight measures that preserve legitimate internships while targeting actual misconduct.

A sound regulatory system should encourage compliance, not make lawful participation financially impossible.
