comments.title: Comment Submitted by Susanna Fessler
comments.commentText:
The proposed fee is not closely targeted to the fraud DHS identifies. DHS describes serious misconduct involving fraudulent employers, shell companies, false employment documentation, suspect worksites, and other improper employment arrangements. DHS reports that one recent investigation identified more than 10,000 F-1 students working for highly suspect employers. Yet DHS expressly states that the proposed fee "would not be tied to a specific employer." That distinction is important; a student seeking initial post-completion OPT does not need to have secured employment before applying. An institution therefore could be required to pay $70,000 before the employer whose legitimacy is a central focus of DHS's fraud concerns has even been identified. Institutional payment does not establish whether a future employer is legitimate, a worksite exists, employment is related to the student's field, or the student is actually performing the reported work.
The proposed fees also would not directly fund the enforcement measures needed to address the identified fraud. DHS states that the receipts would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and would not be retained or used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). DHS nevertheless estimates annual collections of $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. Those funds therefore would not automatically provide additional employer verification, site visits, investigators, designated school official (DSO) training, or other compliance resources. Moreover, these annual collections estimates appear unrealistic to the extent that they fail to account adequately for the deterrent effect of the proposed fees: charges of this magnitude could lead institutions that cannot pay them to forgo OPT recommendations and would discourage students from pursuing OPT at all, reducing participation and the resulting collections.
DHS considered alternatives including expanded site visits, reporting requirements, and training plans, but rejected them in part because the proposed fee can be implemented with less administrative burden on the government. Administrative convenience does not justify the proposed fee.
Implementation also would not simply involve an additional transaction by a DSO. Payments of this magnitude could involve multiple offices, including a university's Comptroller, Student Accounts, accounts-payable and accounts-receivable processes, additional financial controls, and staffing. DHS itself acknowledges that institutions may need additional administrative review, budget processes, recordkeeping, tracking, and payment controls.
As a result, the proposal would effectively add institutional financial capacity as a prerequisite to an OPT recommendation even where the student otherwise satisfies the substantive requirements for practical training. Financial selectivity is not equivalent to immigration compliance.
The proposal also would undermine U.S. competitiveness in the global market for talent. International students increasingly have attractive alternatives when determining where to pursue higher education, and countries including Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland, and New Zealand continue to offer pathways that connect higher education with post-graduate employment opportunities. Prospective students may take future access to practical training into account when selecting a university or country of study, and DHS acknowledges that SEVP-certified institutions could experience declines in F-1 enrollment if prospective students are deterred by the proposed fees, with potential effects on university revenue.
The resulting impact would extend well beyond higher education institutions. International students contribute to local economies through tuition, housing, consumer spending, and workforce participation. A decline in enrollment would adversely affect communities, employers, research enterprises, and innovation ecosystems throughout the country.
More targeted alternatives are available. Where risks involve illegitimate employers, false worksites, fabricated employment, or concealed employment arrangements, DHS could expand risk-based employer verification, targeted site visits, scrutiny of entities displaying fraud indicators, improved data matching, or other compliance mechanisms directed at identified sources of fraud. Unlike the broader site-visit and reporting alternatives DHS rejected, measures directed at employers and entities displaying fraud indicators would concentrate government resources where the risk is demonstrated rather than apply to all OPT participation. DHS already utilizes STEM OPT employer oversight mechanisms, including site visits and training-plan requirements, that provide examples of targeted approaches to strengthening compliance.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is untargeted, overly burdensome, and does not directly fund fraud enforcement.

comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to submit my formal public comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to introduce a $70,000 fee for the initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) period and a $30,000 fee for the STEM OPT extension.
We are deeply concerned about the devastating, short-sighted impact this rule will have on families, American higher education, and the broader United States economy.
1. Creating an Insurmountable Financial Barrier for Families
International families already make immense financial sacrifices to send their children to the United States, paying full out-of-state tuition, standard university fees, and high cost-of-living expenses. A $70,000 to $100,000 fee for post-graduation training is not a standard administrative charge—it is a punitive extraction. It turns what should be a merit-based opportunity into a luxury accessible only to the ultra-wealthy. This rule throws the future of brilliant, hard-working students into complete uncertainty, making their multi-year academic investments a sudden question mark.
2. Destructive Impact on American University Funding
International students are a vital economic pillar for U.S. colleges and universities. The revenue from their tuition directly subsidizes domestic student programs, campus infrastructure, research laboratories, and financial aid. If this rule is finalized, global applications to U.S. institutions will collapse overnight. Families will simply refuse to invest in a U.S. degree if the essential path to post-graduation practical experience is locked behind an impossible paywall. The resulting multi-billion-dollar shortfall will cripple the budgets of American universities, forcing them to cut programs or drastically raise tuition on domestic American students to survive.
3. Severe Harm to the United States Economy and Global Talent Retention
The U.S. economy thrives because it has historically attracted the world's brightest minds. The OPT and STEM OPT programs serve as a crucial bridge that allows American companies to recruit top-tier, U.S.-educated talent in critical fields like artificial intelligence, engineering, biomedical research, and advanced technology.
By effectively dismantling the OPT program, the United States will actively push this elite talent pool directly into the arms of competitor nations like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, all of which offer welcoming, affordable post-study work pathways. Pushing this talent away will stunt innovation, weaken American corporate competitiveness, and ultimately harm the U.S. GDP.
Conclusion
For the past decade, We have witnessed firsthand how hard work, education, and innovation drive the United States forward. This proposed fee structure undermines those very values. It punishes families who play by the rules and will severely damage American universities and the economy. We strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to immediately withdraw this economically harmful and counterproductive proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this rule. The NPRM never analyzes what the fee would do to invention, patenting and research output in the United States. The word "innovation" appears once, in a quotation of the 2016 STEM OPT rule that DHS now sets aside. Earlier comments noted in passing that OPT has value no payer captures. Inventive work is the clearest case, and the rule's cost method cannot measure it.

1. The UMRA economy finding points to the wrong section
UMRA section 202(a)(4) asks for the rule's effect on "Productivity, Economic Growth, Full Employment, Creation of Productive Jobs, and International Competitiveness." DHS's entire answer is one sentence: it "has provided discussions of the effect of this rule on the economy in the Regulatory Impact Analysis of this rule. See Section VII, subpart B." Section VII, subpart B is the Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis. The RIA is subpart A. Neither discusses productivity growth, research, patents or competitiveness. The statement points to analysis that does not exist.

2. The "transfer" assumption fails for inventive work
The benefits section says that if OPT participation falls, "there could be transfers to other workers who may perform the same job functions." The cost section says employers able to replace OPT workers "with other equivalent workers would not experience opportunity costs." That logic treats every job as a fixed slot that someone else can fill. Research and engineering jobs do not work that way. An idea is not used up when one person has it. A new design or method raises the output of coworkers, later inventors and other firms. If an inventor leaves the country, the job may be refilled, but the inventions that person would have made, and the gains to collaborators, are not handed to the replacement. They are lost or produced abroad. DHS's proxy, which sets lost value at the unpaid fee, cannot register any of this, because spillovers to third parties never enter a fee negotiation.

3. The evidence DHS did not address
Published research finds that skilled immigrants contribute a large share of U.S. invention. Hunt and Gauthier-Loiselle (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 2010) estimate that a 1 percentage point rise in the immigrant college graduate share of the population raises patents per capita by 9 to 18 percent. Kerr and Lincoln (Journal of Labor Economics, 2010) find that higher H-1B admissions increased invention by immigrant scientists and engineers, with limited effects on native inventors. Bernstein, Diamond, McQuade and Pousada (NBER Working Paper 30797, 2022) estimate that immigrants are about 16 percent of U.S. inventors but produce about 23 percent of innovation output, and that their presence raises the output of native collaborators. DHS cannot ignore this work while asserting that lost OPT jobs simply pass to other workers.

4. The fee lands on the innovation pipeline
STEM OPT exists for training in science and engineering. Each extension requires a Form I-983 naming "learning objectives" and a training plan (NPRM footnote 53). The proposed $30,000 subsequent fee applies to every STEM OPT recommendation. DHS's low scenario assumes schools keep paying for all STEM students and drop non-STEM students. Even that scenario has schools paying about $8.41 billion a year after the transition period. DHS gives no evidence that schools can or will spend that sum, so it has no basis to assume the STEM pipeline survives intact. If it does not, the losses fall on the fields where spillovers are largest.

5. Reversal without engagement
In 2016 DHS relied on "the widely accepted proposition that" educational exchange and "a focus on STEM innovation" are "positive contributors to the U.S. economy and U.S. workers" (NPRM text at footnote 98). The NPRM cites participation growth and fraud, but it never says that proposition is false. A change in position must account for the facts underlying the prior policy (FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502 (2009)). The innovation effects are such facts.

6. Requests
DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should first re-propose with:
(a) a real UMRA 202(a)(4) analysis of effects on productivity, research and patenting;
(b) a cost method that counts spillovers to coworkers and other firms, not only the unpaid fee;
(c) a response to the published patent and inventor evidence, including the studies above;
(d) an estimate of how many STEM OPT recommendations schools would actually fund at $30,000 each; and
(e) consideration of exempting STEM OPT, which already carries training plans, E-Verify and site visits, from any fee while DHS pursues targeted enforcement against the employers it identifies.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the rule due to flaws in economic and innovation impact analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose DHS's proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. I urge the Department to withdraw this proposal.

The proposed fees are extraordinarily disproportionate, lack a demonstrated relationship to actual administrative costs, and would create substantial financial barriers for international students, universities, and American employers. Although DHS identifies fraud prevention and immigration integrity as its objectives, the proposed fee structure does not effectively target fraudulent conduct. Instead, it imposes the same financial burden on legitimate students and institutions, regardless of their compliance records.

1. The proposed fees lack a reasonable cost-based justification.

DHS estimates that the proposal could generate approximately $12.4 billion in annual fee collections under its primary estimate. Such a substantial amount requires a transparent explanation of how the $70,000 and $30,000 fees were calculated.

The administrative activities associated with OPT include eligibility review, SEVIS record maintenance, and compliance monitoring. DHS has not adequately demonstrated how these activities justify charges of tens of thousands of dollars per student.

The Department should provide an itemized accounting of OPT-related administrative costs, explain the methodology behind the proposed amounts, and demonstrate that the fees are proportionate to the actual government services and enforcement costs involved.

2. The proposed fees do not distinguish legitimate participation from fraud.

DHS identifies fraudulent employers, shell companies, fictitious employment arrangements, and nonexistent worksites as major concerns. However, the proposed fees apply universally, without distinguishing between legitimate employment and fraudulent arrangements.

A student employed by an established American company, performing genuine work related to their academic training, would trigger the same fee as a student associated with a fraudulent employer.

If the Department's concern is employer-related fraud, enforcement should focus on employer verification, worksite inspections, supervision requirements, and investigations of suspicious employment arrangements.

A universal fee does not address the specific sources of fraud identified by DHS.

3. The initial fee is disconnected from actual employment.

Students applying for initial post-completion OPT are not required to have secured employment before receiving a DSO recommendation. Therefore, the $70,000 fee may be imposed before a student has even received a job offer or selected an employer.

At that stage, there may be no employer, worksite, compensation arrangement, or actual training relationship to evaluate.

DHS should explain how a fee imposed before an employment relationship exists can effectively prevent fraudulent employment arrangements. The proposed mechanism is poorly aligned with the Department's stated enforcement objectives.

4. The proposal would harm American universities and employers.

Universities would face substantial financial liabilities for recommending otherwise eligible students for OPT. Institutions may respond by limiting OPT recommendations, increasing tuition or student fees, reducing international student services, or declining to support eligible students.

Although schools are formally responsible for paying the fees, DHS acknowledges that these costs may be transferred to students or employers.

This would particularly disadvantage small businesses, startups, university spin-offs, and technology companies that cannot absorb substantial additional recruitment costs. Employers may choose not to hire qualified international graduates because of the financial uncertainty associated with OPT.

The result could be reduced hiring, fewer research and development opportunities, and weaker innovation in industries such as robotics, artificial intelligence, semiconductor engineering, and advanced manufacturing.

5. The fees would undermine U.S. competitiveness in STEM fields.

The United States competes globally for engineers, researchers, and other highly skilled professionals. OPT provides international graduates with an opportunity to apply their academic training in American workplaces.

A $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would make the United States less attractive to international students and discourage employers from recruiting qualified graduates.

The STEM OPT extension is particularly important for industries that require specialized technical skills and practical experience. Imposing an additional $30,000 fee for an eligible extension could discourage universities from supporting students who have legitimate employment and training arrangements.

DHS should consider the long-term consequences for university enrollment, research activity, workforce development, and American technological competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a graduate student in speech-language pathology (SLP), a healthcare field that diagnoses and treats disorders related to communication, voice, and swallowing. I am opposed to ICEB-2026-0100 because of the negative effects it will have on my profession and on healthcare as a whole.

Many of my fellow graduate students hold F-1 visas and hope to practice SLP in the US after graduation, which they can only do if they complete a year of fellowship training (i.e., an OPT). This proposed financial barrier will keep my classmates from contributing the demonstrated skill and expertise that only they can bring to this field, at a time when demand for healthcare workers is increasing faster than we can keep up with as a country.

In order to practice as an SLP, one must complete a clinical fellowship year, which qualifies as an OPT for international students holding an F-1 visa. In this sense, it is not an "optional" training period as Section D1 of the proposal describes; yet, these positions fall into this wide category. Our field needs more practitioners than are graduating into the field each year, and international students help meet this growing demand. In addition to their labor, international students' diverse perspectives and backgrounds help the field grow, and ensure culturally and linguistically appropriate care for all people who need it. This proposal will reduce the number of qualified professionals across healthcare disciplines in what is a growing shortage of healthcare professionals nationwide.

US healthcare is facing dire staffing shortages across disciplines, and SLP is no exception. Because of the US's aging population and the over-twofold increase in childhood language delays since the COVID-19 pandemic, the demand for SLPs is skyrocketing, with the Bureau of Labor Statistics predicting that SLP as a field will grow by over 15% over the 2024–2034 decade. Meanwhile, SLP graduate programs are already failing to keep up with current demands, with 55% of surveyed SLPs reporting that job openings exceeded applicants in their area in 2025. More people need more SLPs than are graduating into the workforce each year, and that is only going to worsen as the population continues to age and children continue to experience COVID-related language consequences. We need international students to help fill these gaps.

International healthcare workers have bolstered the healthcare workforce in the midst of growing professional shortages, and are historically more willing to take on lower-paying jobs in underserved areas when compared to their US-born counterparts. International SLP students take on a special commitment to practicing in the US, as an SLP certificate is not valid in other countries.

In a field as demographically homogeneous as SLP, international students are key to ensuring culturally and linguistically appropriate care for all Americans. 80% of SLPs identify as white, and over 90% are women. A 2021 report found that less than 10% of SLPs are bilingual, while nearly a fifth of all Americans are bilingual. People who speak languages other than English and come from other racial and ethnic backgrounds need care that is culturally and linguistically appropriate, and it will only become harder for them to find it if fewer international students enter the workforce in the coming years. A diverse SLP workforce is key to the growth and health of the field, and including international students will help us meet these demands.

International students in healthcare fields train to fill the growing gaps in our healthcare system, and are a vital piece of ensuring that Americans receive the care they need. The passage of ICEB-2026-0100 would keep the American healthcare system from accepting help that it badly needs, and throw a wrench in the lives of people working to provide it.

re: Optional Practice Training Fees

Thank you for the opportunity to discuss this sensitive matter with you. I TOTALLY AGREE with the fees, but rather, have OPT abolished. Foreign students looking to study in the states can do so; however, once degree is received, the training should be applied to their home country. The visa-hopping starts to become mishandled.

Protecting American Students and Ensuring Fairness in the Optional Practical Training Program
The United States must reconsider the financial and regulatory structure of the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program to ensure that the interests of American students, graduates, and workers are adequately protected.

American students invest significant financial resources, time, and personal sacrifice to obtain an education from American institutions. They graduate with student loan obligations, enter an increasingly competitive employment market, and expect that their education will provide a fair opportunity to compete for professional positions in their own country.

However, the expansion of employment opportunities available through OPT raises important questions about fairness, workforce competition, and the government's responsibility to protect the value of an American education.

The issue is not whether international students deserve educational opportunities or whether their contributions to American universities should be recognized. International students contribute meaningfully to academic institutions and the American economy. The issue is whether a federal employment authorization program should operate without sufficient financial accountability and safeguards to ensure that American graduates are not placed at an unnecessary competitive disadvantage.

Employers should not have an economic incentive to select a temporary foreign worker over an equally qualified American graduate simply because the employment arrangement carries different payroll tax obligations or other cost advantages.

Furthermore, the American government should not be expected to absorb the administrative, regulatory, and enforcement costs associated with an expanding employment authorization program without requiring a more meaningful financial contribution from the institutions and stakeholders that benefit from its operation.

Increasing OPT fees would be a reasonable policy mechanism to strengthen program accountability, finance oversight, discourage fraudulent participation, and ensure that OPT remains focused on legitimate practical training.

The United States should also examine whether employers participating in OPT are providing genuine educational and professional training opportunities or simply using the program as an alternative source of labor.

Ultimately, the question is one of national economic fairness.

Why should an American student who has invested in an American education face a potentially uneven employment playing field in the very country whose educational system and workforce development programs that student has helped support?

The United States can welcome international students while simultaneously prioritizing the economic interests of its citizens. These objectives are not mutually exclusive.

Increasing OPT fees, strengthening employer accountability, and establishing stronger domestic workforce protections would send an important message: America welcomes global talent, but participation in its employment system must be financially responsible, transparent, and consistent with the interests of its domestic workforce.

The value of an American education should not be diminished by a federal policy framework that fails to adequately consider the American graduates it is also intended to serve.

Thank you.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees under 8 CFR 214.13(i).
Optional Practical Training (OPT) serves an important purpose in the U.S. education and employment system. It allows eligible international students to apply the knowledge and skills they have developed through their education in real-world professional settings. This creates a valuable connection between universities and industry, allowing businesses, research institutions, and other organizations to benefit from specialized training while contributing to innovation and economic growth in the United States.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would seriously undermine this system. Although the fees would technically be paid by educational institutions rather than students or employers, this distinction does not eliminate their economic impact. In fact, requiring schools to pay such substantial amounts before they can even recommend a student for OPT creates a significant financial barrier to employment authorization.
First, this proposal would place an unreasonable financial burden on American universities. Universities already invest considerable resources in educating students, supporting research, maintaining laboratories, and developing relationships with industry. A $70,000 fee for each student seeking initial OPT participation could force institutions to redirect substantial resources away from education and research. Schools with limited budgets, particularly smaller universities and public institutions, may simply decide that they cannot afford to support OPT participation for certain students. As a result, access to employment opportunities could depend less on a student's qualifications and more on the financial resources of their university.

Second, American businesses, especially startups and small companies, could lose access to qualified talent. Many smaller organizations operate with limited budgets and cannot absorb the indirect costs associated with this proposal. Although the fee is paid by the school, employers may find that universities are less willing or able to recommend international graduates for OPT. This could discourage companies from recruiting these candidates in the first place. In fields such as biotechnology, healthcare, engineering, and advanced technology, where specialized skills are essential, restricting access to qualified candidates could delay research, product development, and business expansion.

Third, restricting employment opportunities for international graduates does not automatically create employment opportunities for American workers. Hiring is driven by business needs, available budgets, and the qualifications required for a position. If an employer cannot hire a qualified candidate because the associated financial barriers make the position impractical, it does not follow that the employer will simply hire another candidate. The position may remain vacant, the hiring plan may be canceled, or the entire project may be postponed or moved elsewhere. In these situations, American workers do not necessarily gain employment. Instead, the U.S. economy may lose investment, productivity, and potential job creation.
The structure of the proposed fees also raises concerns about proportionality. The same substantial fee applies regardless of an institution's financial capacity, the employer's size, the nature of the position, or the actual risk of fraudulent employment. Furthermore, the subsequent $30,000 fee applies to later OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions, even when the student continues working for the same employer. This creates additional costs without necessarily reflecting any change in the employment arrangement or the level of risk involved.

If the primary concern is fraud within the OPT program, the government should focus on identifying and addressing fraudulent employers, sham employment arrangements, and violations of existing requirements. Stronger employment verification, targeted audits, more effective monitoring of questionable worksites, and meaningful penalties for proven violations would address these problems more directly. A blanket financial barrier imposed on every legitimate OPT participant is not a substitute for effective enforcement.

DHS should also provide clear evidence explaining why fees of this extraordinary magnitude are necessary and how they are reasonably connected to the identified problems. The potential consequences for universities, employers, research activities, and the broader U.S. economy deserve much more consideration.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and consider targeted anti-fraud measures instead. Immigration enforcement and the protection of U.S. workers are important objectives, but they should not come at the expense of legitimate educational opportunities, American businesses, research institutions, and the country's long-term economic competitiveness.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they create financial barriers for universities.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the fees in proposed 8 CFR § 214.13(i) and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. A school would have to pay $70,000 before recommending a student for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation. For a graduate who completes initial OPT and then pursues a STEM extension, that is $100,000. A public university could verify that a placement offers excellent training in the student’s field and still have to turn it down because it cannot afford to recommend the student. Paying the fee tells DHS little about what the student will learn, what the employer will pay, or whether the employer has displaced a U.S. worker.

I share DHS’s concern about employers exploiting workers. This proposal could make that problem worse. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students or employers. A graduate who borrows heavily to pursue OPT may feel unable to walk away from unpaid wages or unsafe conditions. An American coworker on the same shift has a stake in whether that graduate feels free to speak up. DHS could protect both workers more directly by investigating employers with repeated complaints, auditing placements that show signs of sham training, and giving students a confidential way to report misconduct.

DHS should also reconsider how it treats students who have already enrolled. In its September 14, 2026 order in Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. DHS, the District of Massachusetts postponed the effective date of a separate rule governing the duration of admission. On page 38, the court explained that DHS had inadequately considered the commitments students had already made by enrolling in multiyear programs and paying tuition. That reasoning bears directly on Section VI of this proposal. A student can choose a university for its teaching, its research, and the opportunity to put that education into practice. OPT can matter to that decision even when it is one of several reasons for enrolling. Sixty days’ notice before the fees take effect gives a senior no way to revisit the choice they made as a freshman.

I urge DHS to withdraw both fees. Students who pursue legitimate training, employers who follow the rules, and U.S. workers who report abuses all deserve an enforcement policy that responds to what happens in the workplace.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS should withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. The proposal establishes that fraud warrants enforcement, but it does not establish that these charges would effectively distinguish fraud from lawful participation.

The central flaw is the assumption that willingness to pay demonstrates legitimacy. Under Section IV.C, schools would become more selective because they must pay the fee. Yet schools may transfer the entire cost to students or employers. That weakens the financial accountability on which DHS relies. A qualified student with a legitimate training opportunity may be unable to pay, while a well-funded fraudulent operation may afford the charge. Reducing participation is not evidence of improving compliance. DHS should demonstrate how the fee changes the proportion of fraudulent participation, rather than simply reducing the number of people to monitor.

The amounts themselves lack a convincing justification. Section IV.C compares them with educational expenses and H-1B charges, but neither comparison establishes an appropriate price for OPT. Tuition purchases instruction and institutional services; it does not justify an additional government charge of similar size. Nor does lawful participation in OPT become circumvention merely because it costs less than a different immigration program. DHS should identify the specific statutory authority for imposing charges of this scale primarily to discourage participation, and explain why substantially lower amounts would not achieve its objectives.

The proposal also leaves its stated resource problem unresolved. DHS acknowledges that ICE cannot retain the receipts and that the revenue would not be specifically dedicated to OPT oversight. The fee therefore does not itself finance the employer verification or investigations DHS says are needed. Administrative convenience cannot substitute for evidence that a broad financial barrier is more effective than targeted enforcement.

Section VII.A compounds these weaknesses by using unpaid fees as a proxy for lost opportunities and assuming that parties can share the expense when OPT’s benefits exceed its price. This confuses economic value with immediate access to funding. Benefits may accrue over years, extend beyond the paying parties, or be impossible to coordinate among a school, student, and prospective employer. The analysis needs to account for these constraints rather than treating nonpayment as evidence of limited value.

Finally, Sections V.C and VI provide inadequate protection for existing commitments. Applying a charge to a future recommendation does not eliminate its effect on students who already enrolled, graduates who accepted employment, or current OPT participants seeking STEM extensions. A 60-day transition cannot meaningfully accommodate decisions made over several years.

DHS should compare targeted employer verification, risk-based inspections, and sanctions for documented violations against the proposed fees using evidence of effectiveness and total costs to affected parties. The present proposal has not justified replacing those measures with an exceptionally high financial threshold for every participant.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
DHS should withdraw this rule. Its own analysis shows the rule would shut down OPT for most students and employers, not regulate it.

1. DHS admits the rule will cut participation. DHS projects that the fees will cost between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion a year. It also concedes that “some schools may decline to fund OPT.” More than half of SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. They cannot pay $70,000 per student, so their students will lose access.

2. The fee has no relationship to cost. An OPT work authorization application already carries a USCIS filing fee of a few hundred dollars. A $70,000 fee is more than 100 times that amount. DHS has not shown any administrative cost that justifies it, and it should explain what statutory authority allows a fee this far above the cost of the service.

3. The fraud rationale does not hold up. DHS cites a 2020 investigation that led to 15 arrests. Roughly 289,000 students were on OPT or STEM OPT in 2024. Charging every one of them $70,000 because of 15 cases is not proportionate. DHS already has SEVIS, I-983 training plans, and site visits, and those tools target misconduct directly.

4. U.S. healthcare and research will lose workers they cannot replace. International graduates in biostatistics, public health, data science, and the life sciences support clinical trials, drug and device development, hospital analytics, and university research. Academic medical centers, nonprofit hospitals, and grant-funded labs cannot pay $70,000 per hire, so these positions will go unfilled.

5. The economic cost is large. International students contributed about $43 billion to the U.S. economy in 2024–25. In an IIE survey, 92% of college leaders said international students would likely choose other countries without OPT. Canada, the U.K., and Australia are ready to take them.

6. The process is unfair. Schools must pay before recommending a student. No refund is allowed once work authorization is issued, and refund decisions cannot be appealed.

The rule imposes billions of dollars in costs to address a problem that targeted enforcement already handles. DHS should withdraw it.

I am writing to express my strong support for the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to implement a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) school certifications and a $30,000 fee for subsequent amendments and STEM extensions. This regulatory update is a long-overdue mechanism to ensure fiscal responsibility, program integrity, and the protection of the domestic labor market.
Implementing these fees is justified and necessary for the following critical reasons:
• Ensuring Full Cost Recovery and Agency Efficiency: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) is primarily a fee-funded agency. The administrative burden of vetting, monitoring, and managing the compliance of thousands of educational institutions and hundreds of thousands of OPT/STEM OPT participants is immense. For too long, the true operational costs of auditing these programs have been subsidized by other fee-paying categories or backlogged resources. This fee ensures that the institutions directly utilizing and benefiting from the program bear the actual cost of its oversight.
• Enhancing Program Integrity and Oversight: The OPT and STEM OPT programs have grown exponentially, making robust oversight difficult. By securing a dedicated, substantial revenue stream from these fees, DHS can deploy the necessary personnel, advanced data tracking, and site-visit infrastructure to eliminate fraudulent "visa mills" and ensure participating institutions are providing legitimate, high-quality training that complies with federal regulations.
• Encouraging Institutional Accountability: Higher education institutions benefit heavily from marketing the OPT program to attract international enrollment. Charging a meaningful fee for certification ensures that only institutions fully committed to strict regulatory compliance, student vetting, and dedicated career oversight will participate. This filters out bad actors and protects the reputation of legitimate American higher education.
• Rebalancing the Domestic Labor Market: The OPT program, particularly the STEM extension, effectively functions as a massive, tax-exempt guest-worker program that competes directly with recent American graduates. Because employers and universities are exempt from paying certain payroll taxes (such as FICA) on OPT students, there is an artificial financial incentive to prefer foreign graduates over domestic talent. This fee structure creates a necessary economic counterbalance, ensuring that the program is used as a specialized training tool rather than a cheap labor loophole.
For the security of our immigration system, the fiscal health of the managing agencies, and the protection of the domestic workforce, I urge the Department to finalize and implement this rule without delay. comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed rule introducing a $70K initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and a $30K extension fee. As an international student currently planning my higher education, this proposal drastically diminishes the appeal of the United States (US) as a destination for global talent and directly undermines the competitiveness of American universities.

The US higher education institutions are globally renowned for their academic and research excellence. The opportunity to pair this world-class education with practical, hands-on experience at leading American companies has historically made the US the premier choice for international students. However, education is a significant financial investment, and the ability to pursue post-graduation training through OPT is a critical component of that investment's value.

Imposing a $70K fee for the opportunity to gain entry-level work experience is financially prohibitive for the vast majority of international students. By creating an insurmountable financial barrier to post-study work, the US government is effectively signaling that it does not value or welcome the contributions of global students.

Furthermore, this policy will cause severe, lasting damage to US universities, which rely heavily on the tuition and fees paid by international students to fund academic programs, campus infrastructure, and domestic scholarships. If international enrollment plummets due to these prohibitive costs, American institutions will face massive revenue shortfalls that will ultimately degrade the quality of education for domestic students as well.

This fee structure is also an unnecessary intervention in the domestic job market. Opponents may argue this protects local workers, but the reality is that this rule will not make a meaningful difference for US students. Domestic graduates already hold a massive, permanent advantage in the job market because they do not require visa sponsorship, upfront government fees, or complex immigration paperwork. Employers will naturally continue to favor domestic candidates for the vast majority of roles due to this lack of administrative burden, meaning this rule only serves to punish international students rather than protect American workers and to the detriment of the US economy.

Moreover, the assumption that every international student utilizing OPT intends to remain in the US permanently is flawed. For many of us, the primary goal of OPT is simply to gain a few years of high-caliber, practical experience at world-class companies before returning to our home countries or moving to other global markets. Viewing OPT purely as a gateway to permanent immigration mischaracterizes how international students view the program; it is an educational extension that allows us to apply our degrees in a real-world setting, which also benefits American companies.

If this rule is finalized, the US will lose high-caliber students to other global economies. The United Kingdom for example, offers an attractive Graduate visa program that allows graduates to live and work flexibly without facing tens of thousands of dollars in upfront government fees. American classrooms will lose vital international perspectives, research labs will lose dedicated talent, and US companies will lose access to a highly motivated pool of global graduates that power the US economy.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this economically damaging proposal and instead maintain accessible pathways for international students to transition to work experience which will contribute to America's continued position as a leading education destination. I am saddened to think that the US will no longer be seen in the great light it has been basking in thus far.

Sincerely,
Anonymous

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ponnusamy Kaliyannan
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing as a concerned parent to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, including STEM OPT extensions.

My elder son enrolled at the Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech) in Fall 2024 to pursue his undergraduate degree in Computer Science. He expects to graduate in Spring 2027.

When he enrolled, our family made significant educational, financial, and career decisions based on the regulations and opportunities available at that time. The possibility of obtaining lawful practical training after graduation was an important part of our planning.

We understood that OPT required government approval. However, we could not have anticipated a $70,000 fee being introduced more than two years after he began college.

Now, just months before graduation, this proposal creates uncertainty about his future. Our family has invested substantial financial resources, and my son has committed years toward completing his degree.

**1. Reliance Interests and Grandfathering — Section VI**

DHS acknowledges that students already enrolled in American universities are differently situated from prospective students. Nevertheless, the proposal would apply new fees to future OPT recommendations, even for students who began their education years earlier.

My son enrolled in Fall 2024, while this proposal was published in October 2026. Applying these fees near graduation does not adequately recognize our existing commitments.

Had these fees been known in 2024, our family would have evaluated our educational decisions differently.

I request that DHS grandfather students enrolled before October 8, 2026, allowing them to pursue eligible initial OPT and STEM OPT extensions under the existing fee framework.

**2. Inadequate Transition Period — Section V.C**

The proposed 60-day transition period is insufficient for students who have already invested years in their education.

Students approaching graduation cannot easily change universities, recover tuition expenses, or reverse career decisions.

A meaningful transition should recognize enrollment dates rather than only future OPT recommendation dates.

**3. Excessive Financial Burden — Sections IV.C and V.A**

The proposed fees could total $100,000 for initial OPT followed by a STEM OPT extension.

Families already invest heavily in tuition, housing, health insurance, and educational expenses.

Although universities would pay these fees, DHS acknowledges that costs could be passed to students, families, or employers.

This could make practical training inaccessible to qualified students because of financial limitations.

**4. Academic Merit and Fair Opportunity**

OPT eligibility should depend on academic qualifications, immigration compliance, and genuine training related to a student's field of study.

A university's ability to pay $70,000 does not determine whether a student is talented, qualified, or compliant.

Financial capacity should not replace academic merit in determining access to practical training.

**5. Targeted Fraud Prevention — Section IV.A**

I support DHS's efforts to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers.

However, legitimate students should not face extraordinary financial barriers because of misconduct committed by others.

Stronger employer verification, risk-based inspections, institutional oversight, and enforcement against fraudulent organizations would more directly address these concerns.

**6. Impact on American Higher Education**

American universities attract talented students through educational excellence, research, and professional opportunities.

Unexpected OPT fees could affect enrollment decisions, legitimate training opportunities, and the ability of institutions and employers to support graduates.

DHS should carefully evaluate these consequences.

**My Requests**

I request that DHS withdraw or reconsider the proposed fees, grandfather students enrolled before October 8, 2026, protect eligible STEM OPT extensions, reconsider the 60-day transition period, and prioritize targeted fraud prevention.

For our family, this proposal directly affects my son's future. He began college in Fall 2024 hoping to complete his education and gain legitimate practical experience after graduation.

We have invested years of effort and substantial financial resources. Changing these requirements shortly before graduation creates hardship and uncertainty.

I urge DHS to protect students who made educational commitments in good faith under existing regulations.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Parent of a Georgia Tech Student

comments.commentText: I am a graduate student researcher in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Yale University, and I regularly work with international students and researchers from Morocco, Japan, Namibia, Germany, Canada, and China. I study paleomagnetism to understand Earth's history, and I frequently collaborate with researchers worldwide. Scientific research in the United States is the best in the world because of our facilities, resources, and the minds of our researchers, whether they are from the US or come to the US to study. The new rule outlined in Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 will drive international students and researchers away by making it prohibitively expensive to study and work in the United States. Nobody benefits from this policy. Throughout US history, we have innovated and prospered most when we remained open-minded and welcoming to researchers and thinkers from anywhere. By creating a system that encourages students and researchers to come to the United States, our science will benefit, our economy will benefit, and scientific breakthroughs will flourish. I urge the DHS to withdraw this proposal for the betterment of the present and future of the United States.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Proposed Rule "Optional Practical Training Fees," Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees.

1. This is a de facto ban presented as a fee. DHS expects the fee to make schools "more selective in determining which students are qualified to participate in OPT," yet it also projects $8.4-16.5 billion in annual payments. Both cannot be true: if schools stop recommending OPT, the revenue and cost estimates are wrong; if they pay, the burden is enormous. A $70,000 charge bearing no relationship to administrative cost (compare the $350 SEVIS fee) functions as a prohibition. If DHS intends to end or sharply restrict OPT, it must say so and justify that choice directly, including the reliance interests that students, schools, and employers have built over decades, rather than calling it a fee.

2. It drives taxpayer-funded talent and jobs abroad. Much STEM doctoral training is paid for by federal research grants. A rule that shuts down OPT sends researchers trained with U.S. tax dollars to competitor countries just as they become productive. International students contributed about $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 356,000 U.S. jobs in 2024-25 (NAFSA).

3. It rewards the wrong schools. Legitimate public and nonprofit universities are the most likely to stop recommending OPT. Schools that market work authorization as their main product can pass the cost to students, which DHS acknowledges schools may do. A flat fee risks pushing OPT toward the very actors DHS says it is targeting. DHS already has targeted tools: certification reviews, site visits, STEM OPT training plans and wage rules, and enforcement against specific schools.

If DHS proceeds, any fee should be tied to documented costs, charged at most once per student per degree level, and exclude students already enrolled.

Respectfully submitted,
Anonymous
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, arguing they act as a ban and harm the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposal. A lawful agency fee must be tied to the cost of a service provided to an identifiable recipient
(Independent Offices Appropriation Act, 31 U.S.C. 9701). The NPRM contains no cost analysis
linking $70,000 or $30,000 to any government cost. The current Form I-765 adjudication fee is
about $500 — the proposal is roughly 140 times that cost.
Worse, the NPRM admits the amounts are punitive and deterrent rather than cost-based: it states
that schools may pass the fee on to students and that doing so "would further discourage misuse
of OPT" (91 FR at 64576). The proceeds would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts; the
NPRM concedes "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected"
(91 FR at 64577) — not one dollar would fund the fraud enforcement the rule claims to serve. A
charge designed to deter behavior and raise general revenue is a tax, and the power to tax
belongs to Congress alone. DHS's own estimates put annual transfers at $8.4–16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4
billion per year , across 2,478 affected institutions (91 FR at 64584). Under the major questions
doctrine, an agency action of this economic and political magnitude requires a clear statement of
congressional authorization (Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023); West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S.
697 (2022)). INA § 214(a)'s general authority to prescribe the "time and conditions" of admission
has never before been read to authorize multi-billion-dollar per-student exactions.
The closest precedent has already been struck down: in June 2026, a federal court vacated the
administration's $100,000 H-1B charge as an unauthorized tax, and courts have since declined to
stay or have separately enjoined it. The OPT fee shares the same defects.No reasoned basis for the amounts. The NPRM offers no explanation of why $70,000 and
$30,000 are the correct figures rather than any others.
Circular cost-benefit analysis. DHS "assumes these opportunity costs are equal to or less
than the proposed fee per OPT instance" (91 FR at 64585) — valuing a lost year of skilled
professional work at exactly the amount of the fee DHS invented.
Gross mismatch of means and ends. DHS's own evidence shows fraud concentrated among
a small minority of bad actors — even its 2026 probe identified roughly 10,000 suspectparticipants out of about 194,554 OPT employment authorizations in 2024 (around 5%). The
fee punishes the other ~95% across every field and treats compliant universities identically to
bad actors. Targeted tools (site visits, training plans, employer verification) were considered
and rejected as too administratively burdensome (91 FR at 64577). Convenience is not a
reasoned basis for a blanket punitive fee.
Irrational compounding. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and then post-completion
OPT triggers $70,000 + $30,000 = $100,000 for one person, although any fraud risk is per
person, not per recommendation.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees are unlawful, punitive, and exceed agency authority without cost justification.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Hossein Talebi Khiavi
comments.commentText:
Many U.S. universities rely on international PhD graduates to fill postdoctoral research positions, and Optional Practical Training (OPT) is an important pathway that allows these highly trained researchers to continue contributing to American research institutions after completing their doctoral degrees.
Postdoctoral researchers play a critical role in advancing scientific knowledge, innovation, and the global competitiveness of U.S. universities. After years of rigorous academic training, they bring specialized expertise, advanced research skills, and valuable experience to research projects. At this stage, they are not simply receiving additional training; they are actively contributing the knowledge and skills they have developed throughout their academic careers to the benefit of U.S. universities and the broader scientific community.
I am deeply concerned that imposing significant additional fees on OPT would create unnecessary financial barriers for international PhD graduates seeking to continue their research careers in the United States. Such a policy could harm not only these researchers but also the universities, laboratories, and research programs that depend on their expertise.
Furthermore, U.S. universities invest substantial financial and institutional resources in educating and training international doctoral students. Creating financial obstacles that discourage these graduates from remaining in the United States would undermine the long-term return on those investments. Rather than benefiting from the highly skilled researchers they have helped train, American institutions risk losing valuable scientific talent to other countries.
Ultimately, this policy could weaken the U.S. research ecosystem, reduce its ability to attract and retain international talent, and negatively affect America's leadership in science and innovation.
I strongly urge policymakers to reconsider the proposed OPT fees and recognize that retaining highly trained international researchers is not merely an immigration issue, but a strategic investment in the future of American science, higher education, and economic competitiveness.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that additional OPT fees create financial barriers and harm U.S. research and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Theresa McCromick
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

To the Department of Homeland Security,

As the Chair of the Department of Chemistry at Portland State University (PSU), I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed fee increases for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and to urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

Our graduate program relies heavily on talented international students, who use OPT to transition from their academic training into the U.S. workforce. However, the current proposal fails to examine how public research universities—and the state governance structures that fund them—will be impacted. In its federalism discussion, DHS lists the effect on state governments as “N/A” and notes that it did not consult state officials. This overlooks the financial reality of public access institutions like PSU, where half of our funding comes from the state and the other half comes from student tuition.

Graduate students earning stipends of less than $30,000 per year cannot reasonably afford a $70,000 fee. Absorbing this cost would fall to the university, ultimately forcing tuition increases for all students. The far more likely outcome is a sharp decline in international enrollment. Furthermore, the international students who do attend will be forced to leave the U.S. after graduation rather than staying to contribute their advanced skills to our local, state, and federal economies. Depleting both our graduate student pool and our domestic scientific workforce will severely harm American competitiveness in scientific research and development.

While this fee increase is framed as a measure to deter fraud, robust anti-fraud protections are already in place. In my role helping process OPT applications for PSU chemistry students—all of whom I know personally—I have never encountered an application that was improper or failed to benefit the U.S. economy. While bad actors may exist elsewhere, existing vetting mechanisms already ensure that the applications reaching my desk are entirely legitimate.

At PSU, the majority of our chemistry graduates go on to support the domestic semiconductor industry. This proposal directly threatens our program and our ability to train the STEM workforce in this critical national sector.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal in its entirety. I also strongly oppose the alternative proposal on which DHS requested comment, which would assess the $70,000 fee repeatedly at each higher degree level. Any fee structure should be calibrated strictly to the actual administrative cost of program oversight, rather than serving as a punitive revenue measure. Neither students nor public universities can absorb these costs, and implementing them will disproportionately disenfranchise state research institutions.

Sincerely,

Theresa McCormick, PhD
Chair, Department of Chemistry
Portland State University
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee increases, arguing they harm students and universities.

I strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees under DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

As a parent, I am deeply concerned about the impact this proposal will have on students and families who have invested years of their lives and significant financial resources in education in the United States.

The rule would require a school to pay $70,000 before recommending an F-1 student for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT), and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. Students learn how a congregation worships, how a pastor cares for families, and how churches share the Gospel across languages and cultures by doing that work alongside experienced mentors. I am an international graduate student in a STEM field at a U.S. university. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

OPT and the STEM OPT extension are the standard path that allows international graduates to begin working in the fields they trained in at U.S. institutions. Under the proposed rule, a school would owe $70,000 for a student's initial OPT recommendation and another $30,000 for a STEM extension, a total of $100,000 for a single student. The rule also creates serious uncertainty. As proposed, it is unclear whether a STEM extension for a student whose initial OPT began before the effective date would cost $30,000 or $70,000. Students who enrolled years ago under the current rules, and employers who have already made hiring plans, cannot reasonably plan around a new cost of this magnitude that did not exist when they made their decisions.

I respectfully ask DHS to:
1. Withdraw the proposed fees in their entirety.
2. At minimum, exempt STEM fields and STEM OPT extensions, where the benefit to the U.S. workforce is greatest.
3. At minimum, exempt students already enrolled in U.S. programs before any final rule takes effect, and clarify how STEM extensions would be treated.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees" — Comment in Opposition

I am an F-1 student who completed a STEM-designated master's program at Trine University and am currently working in the United States under post-completion Optional Practical Training, which began in June 2026. I work as a senior full-stack software engineer. I plan to apply for the 24-month STEM OPT extension in early 2027. I write to oppose the proposed fees as they would apply to students in my position.
Under the proposal, my university would have to pay $30,000 before its designated school official may recommend me for the STEM OPT extension, and DHS itself acknowledges that schools may pass this cost on to students or employers. My current OPT filing cost roughly $500. A $30,000 charge — 60 times higher — for the same 24-month work authorization is not a processing fee; it is a de facto barrier that prices ordinary STEM graduates out of the program.

The proposed grandfathering does not protect me. My initial OPT recommendation was issued before any effective date, yet my STEM extension — a routine, expected continuation of the same training period — would trigger the full $30,000 simply because of when the recommendation is entered into SEVIS. I have done nothing different from students whose extension recommendations happen to fall before the cutoff; the only difference is timing.

The pass-through uncertainty is already causing real harm. DHS states that schools may recover the fee from students, from the broader student body, or from employers, with no limits on the method. Employers making hiring and sponsorship decisions now face an open-ended $30,000 liability attached to any F-1 STEM hire, which discourages exactly the early, good-faith sponsorship the immigration system should encourage.
DHS's own estimate — $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual fees, premised in part on schools simply stopping OPT recommendations rather than paying — concedes that the rule would shrink or eliminate the program for many students rather than merely fund oversight. A fee designed to improve program integrity should not be set at a level its own authors expect institutions to avoid by exiting the program.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. At a minimum, any fee should be capped near actual adjudication cost, should not be passed through to students, and should not apply to STEM extensions that continue an OPT period already recommended and approved before the rule's effective date.

Respectfully,
Leo
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they are writing to oppose the proposed OPT fees as an F-1 student.

Last, No reasoned basis for the amounts. The NPRM offers no explanation of why $70,000 and $30,000 are the correct figures rather than any others. Circular cost-benefit analysis. DHS "assumes these opportunity costs are equal to or less than the proposed fee per OPT instance" (91 FR at 64585) — valuing a lost year of skilled professional work at exactly the amount of the fee DHS invented. Gross mismatch of means and ends. I am writing to express my concern regarding the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Patric Gerard
comments.commentText:
Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

Optional Practical Training Fees (Proposed Rule)Introduction

I am an American citizen submitting this comment in strong support of the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. I am particularly concerned about the long-term effects of large-scale guest-worker programs on employment opportunities for U.S. students and workers, especially in STEM fields. While the proposed fees are a useful interim step, I believe OPT should be terminated altogether.Background

This comment addresses the proposed rule that would require SEVP-certified schools to pay a $70,000 fee for the initial OPT recommendation of an F-1 student and $30,000 for any subsequent recommendation (including STEM OPT extensions). The fees would be paid by the school before a Designated School Official could recommend the student for OPT in SEVIS. I support these fees as proposed and urge the agency to finalize them promptly.Analysis

OPT was never authorized by Congress. It was created by administrative rulemaking and expanded over time into a multi-year work authorization program for foreign students after they complete their studies. The F-1 visa category was intended for temporary study, not as a pathway to U.S. employment. There is no clear statutory basis for granting open-ended work authorization under OPT, no prevailing-wage requirement, and no numerical limit on the number of participants.This structure disadvantages American workers. Employers hiring certain OPT participants can avoid the employer share of Social Security and Medicare (FICA) taxes, creating a direct cost advantage over hiring a U.S. worker for the same role. In practice, this functions as a subsidy for employing foreign graduates rather than Americans. Data consistently show that a large share of U.S. STEM graduates do not end up working in STEM occupations; large-scale OPT and related guest-worker programs contribute to this mismatch by increasing labor supply in precisely those fields without corresponding protections for domestic workers.The program also creates incentives for “pay-to-stay” and other schemes that weaken the integrity of the student visa system. Schools and employers have financial reasons to maximize OPT participation, while American graduates face increased competition for entry-level and early-career positions without the same tax or regulatory advantages. The proposed fees would raise the cost of these recommendations, deter low-value or fraudulent participation, and force schools and employers to internalize more of the external costs currently borne by U.S. workers.I recognize that fees alone do not solve the underlying problem. The better policy outcome is for Congress to end OPT entirely (for example, through legislation such as H.R. 2315, the Fairness for High-Skilled Americans Act). Until that occurs, the fees in this proposed rule are a practical and justified measure that reduces the scale of an unauthorized program and prioritizes American students and workers.Recommendations
Finalize the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees as written, without reducing the amounts or creating broad exemptions.
In the preamble to the final rule, clearly restate that the F-1 category was never intended to serve as a work pathway and that OPT lacks explicit statutory authorization.
Coordinate with the Department of Labor and Congress on permanent reforms that would eliminate OPT work authorization and close related loopholes, rather than treating fees as a permanent substitute for ending the program.
Monitor and publicly report on the effect of the fees on the volume of OPT recommendations, STEM OPT extensions, and any displacement effects on U.S. graduates.
Conclusion

I support the proposed OPT fees because they will raise the cost of an administratively created work program that Congress never authorized, reduce the tax subsidy that favors foreign graduates over Americans, and better protect U.S. students and workers. The fees are a necessary interim step. The preferable long-term solution remains the complete termination of OPT. Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong support for the proposed OPT fees and urges the agency to finalize them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Vicky Boss
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees. I oppose the proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it.

I am a graduate student at Northeastern University, currently interning at TikTok on large-scale advertising systems, and I expect to graduate in Spring 2027. OPT is the practical training my degree is designed to lead into, and the only lawful way for me to continue that field-related work after graduation. If schools cannot pay $70,000 to recommend OPT, I would lose that path entirely, despite having completed my U.S. degree and training in the U.S.

1. The charge is a tax, not a fee. A lawful agency fee must be tied to the cost of a service provided to an identifiable recipient (31 U.S.C. 9701). The proposal contains no cost analysis linking $70,000 or $30,000 to any government cost. The current Form I-765 adjudication fee is about $500, so the proposal is roughly 140 times that cost. Worse, the proposal admits the amounts are punitive and deterrent rather than cost-based: it states that schools may pass the fee on to students and that doing so "would further discourage misuse of OPT" (91 FR at 64576). The proceeds would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts; the proposal concedes "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected" (91 FR at 64577), so not one dollar would fund the fraud enforcement the rule claims to serve. A charge designed to deter behavior and raise general revenue is a tax, and the power to tax belongs to Congress alone.

2. An exaction of this scale requires clear congressional authorization. DHS's own estimates put annual transfers at $8.4-16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion per year, across 2,478 affected institutions (91 FR at 64584). Under the major questions doctrine, an agency action of this economic and political magnitude requires a clear statement of congressional authorization (Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023); West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)). INA section 214(a)'s general authority to prescribe the "time and conditions" of admission has never before been read to authorize multi-billion-dollar per-student exactions. The closest precedent has already been struck down: in June 2026, a federal court vacated the administration's $100,000 H-1B charge as an unauthorized tax. The OPT fee shares the same defects.

3. The rule is arbitrary and capricious. The proposal offers no explanation of why $70,000 and $30,000 are the correct figures rather than any others. Its cost-benefit analysis is circular: DHS "assumes these opportunity costs are equal to or less than the proposed fee per OPT instance" (91 FR at 64585), valuing a lost year of skilled professional work at exactly the amount of the fee DHS invented. The means also mismatch the ends: DHS's own evidence shows fraud concentrated among a small minority of bad actors, roughly 10,000 suspect participants out of about 194,554 OPT employment authorizations in 2024, around 5%. The fee punishes the other roughly 95% across every field and treats compliant universities identically to bad actors. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and then post-completion OPT triggers $70,000 + $30,000 = $100,000 for one person, although any fraud risk is per person, not per recommendation.

4. It punishes the wrong people. The fraud DHS describes concerns fake employers and shell companies falsifying employment, not a university's recommendation. Taxing the school's recommendation does nothing to catch fraudulent employers; it only deters compliant universities from recommending legitimate students.

5. OPT is not "optional" for many graduates. For many F-1 students, OPT is the degree-related practical training that completes their education: the supervised, field-related work experience their degree program is designed to lead into, and in many fields the only lawful way to do it after graduation.

6. A less restrictive alternative already exists. STEM OPT already requires formal training plans, employer reporting, and site visits. Extending verification requirements to post-completion OPT would target fraud directly, at its actual source. DHS rejected such measures as administratively burdensome, but the agency's convenience does not justify shifting $12.4 billion per year onto students and universities. International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 355,736 American jobs in 2024-25 (NAFSA); new international student enrollment had already dropped by 17 percent from fall 2024 to fall 2025. Finalizing this fee would lock in that decline and hand U.S.-trained talent to competitor countries.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and asks DHS to withdraw it due to high fees.
