comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing in opposition to this proposed rule.

Read its design carefully, because the design is the confession. If DHS wanted to recover the cost of OPT, it would charge the student, as it already does with the $410 filing fee for the I-765. Instead, this rule charges the school $70,000, payable before the school official is even permitted to enter the recommendation. That structure has one purpose: to make universities do the excluding. No student will ever receive a denial under this rule. No official will ever have to look at a 23-year-old and say her future is cancelled. Her school will simply stop participating, OPT will die in a budget meeting, and the Department's hands stay clean. That is not fee-setting. It is a ban built with plausible deniability, by people who did not want to defend a ban in the open.

Consider who pays the price. F-1 students are the most documented, most tracked, most compliant people in the immigration system. Their addresses are on file. Their employers are reported. Their status is verified term by term. They broke nothing. They paid full tuition, followed every rule they were handed, and made decisions that cannot be undone — turning down other countries, taking on debt, building years of a life here — in reliance on the terms they were offered. This rule touches no one who broke the law. It lands only on the people who obeyed it, because they are the ones standing in the open, where they are easy to reach. That is not enforcement. It is punishing compliance because compliance is convenient to punish.

The amount itself admits the intent. $70,000 is more than a year of tuition at most universities, more than many graduates will earn in their first year of work. The act being "paid for" — an official entering a recommendation into an existing database — costs almost nothing. Nobody at DHS calculated $70,000. Somebody chose it, the way you choose the height of a fence: high enough that nothing gets over. A price set above what anyone can pay is not a price. It is a wall, described in the language of accounting so its builders can call it bookkeeping.

And the charge returns. $30,000 more for every later recommendation, including the STEM extension. Even in the fantasy where one wealthy school pays once, the toll comes back two years later. The cruelty is not a side effect of this design. It recurs on schedule, because it is the design.

Behind all of this are students who are mid-degree right now, 19 and 20 years old, who chose this country in good faith. They cannot un-borrow the loans. They cannot recover the years. This rule reaches back into decisions already made by people with no power and no vote, and reprices their future at a number chosen to be impossible. There is a word for changing the terms on the powerless after they can no longer walk away, and that word is not "fee."

Withdraw this proposal. If the Department wants to end OPT, let it say so in plain words and take responsibility for saying it. The students this country invited are owed at least that much honesty.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed rule functions as a ban and harms compliant F-1 students and universities.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sivmey Srin
comments.commentText:
DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100
RIN 1653-AB01
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Optional Practical Training Fees
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing as an international student currently pursuing my degree in the United States to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees.
The proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and an additional $30,000 for STEM OPT extensions are completely detached from economic reality. They will effectively dismantle the OPT program, decimate America's ability to attract global talent, and inflict severe financial distress on international students and the universities that host us.
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule based on the following critical flaws:
• Unprecedented Financial Barrier for Students: While the rule technically levies this fee on universities, institutions will inevitably be forced to pass these astronomical costs down to students. International students already pay premium tuition rates and are restricted in their ability to work off-campus. Adding a $70,000 to $100,000 financial hurdle just to gain practical experience in our fields of study will price out all but the wealthiest individuals, destroying equity and diversity in higher education.
• Destruction of Practical Learning and Career Pathways: OPT is not a loophole; it is an integral, complementary component of American higher education. Forcing students or their employers to pay up to $100,000 to utilize this benefit makes it completely unviable.
• Severe Harm to the U.S. Economy and STEM Innovation: The U.S. has long been a global leader because it retains the brightest minds educated at its world-class universities. By placing a massive financial penalty on OPT, DHS will drive top international talent to competing nations like Canada, the UK, and Australia, which actively incentivize international graduates to stay and work.
• Flawed Rationale and Benchmarking: DHS’s attempt to benchmark OPT fees against H-1B structures is legally and conceptually flawed. F-1 students are not H-1B visa holders; we are paying customers of the U.S. education system seeking a temporary period of practical application.
As a student funding my education through family savings, a fee of this magnitude would mean I would have to leave the country immediately upon graduation without the chance to apply my skills, rendering my investment in my U.S. education incomplete.
A 30-day comment window is entirely insufficient for the public to analyze and respond to an economically significant rule of this magnitude. This proposal does not protect U.S. workers; it simply punishes students and weakens American universities. I strongly request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule entirely.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (91 FR 64566), Proposed OPT Fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees on SEVP-certified schools. The fees bear no relation to the cost of any service. They rest on contradictory estimates, they are uneconomic for schools by simple arithmetic, and they would push U.S.-trained talent abroad without protecting American workers. DHS should withdraw the proposal.

1. Fee is unrelated to cost
Students now pay about $470 to file for OPT. The school's role is a SEVIS entry by its own staff. The proposed $70,000 is about 149 times that filing fee, and initial OPT plus STEM OPT would rise from $940 to $100,940. DHS projects $8.4-16.5 billion a year in fee payments, far beyond any plausible cost of overseeing OPT. That makes this a penalty, not a user fee, and DHS says one purpose is to discourage OPT use. DHS should identify what authority permits a fee this far above cost, charged to schools that are not the applicants.

2. Revenue estimate contradicts the policy goal
Let N(F) be the number of OPT recommendations at fee F, with N falling as F rises. Revenue is R(F) = F x N(F). DHS's $8.4-16.5 billion projection implies about 120,000-236,000 fee-paying recommendations a year, roughly today's level. So DHS assumes the fee barely changes behavior, while saying its aim is to change behavior. The Economic Innovation Group projects a 35% drop in international graduate applicants under a $100,000 fee, and 80% of surveyed students said they would reconsider staying. Both cannot hold: if the fee deters, revenue is overstated; if revenue is accurate, the fee does not deter. DHS's cost estimate spans $32 million to over $8 billion, a factor of 250, which shows it never estimated N(F).

3. Schools would lose money
A school recommends OPT only if its net margin on the student covers the fee: m x T >= F, where T is total tuition and m is the margin after costs. For an illustrative STEM master's with T = $80,000, initial OPT requires m >= 87.5%. Adding STEM OPT (F = $100,000) requires m >= 125%, which is impossible. For PhD students, tuition is usually waived, so each fee comes directly out of research budgets. DHS itself says over 56% of SEVP-certified schools may be small entities.

4. Pass-through is a confiscatory tax
If schools pass the fee on, the effective tax on the graduate's work is F / (w x t). At an illustrative salary of $85,000, 12 months of OPT is taxed at 82%, and 36 months of OPT plus STEM OPT at 39%. An employer facing this can hire the same graduate in Toronto or London, or offshore the work. The job then leaves the U.S.; it does not go to an American.

5. The displacement premise is weak
The rule treats jobs as a fixed quantity. Economists call this the lump-of-labor fallacy. Peri, Shih and Sparber (2015) link foreign STEM workers to higher wages for college-educated natives. Hunt and Gauthier-Loiselle (2010) find immigrant graduates raise patenting. Immigrants founded or co-founded over half of U.S. billion-dollar startups (NFAP). Studies that find some firm-level substitution, such as Doran, Gelber and Isen (2022), support targeted measures, not dismantling the program. Those measures already exist: STEM OPT requires E-Verify, a Form I-983 training plan, comparable terms of employment, and DHS site visits. DHS should enforce them rather than charge a fee it does not dedicate to fraud detection.

6. Lost investment, stronger competitors
U.S. universities and taxpayers invest heavily in training these graduates. This rule ensures the return is realized elsewhere, in Canada, the U.K., and strategic competitors such as China, weakening long-term U.S. technological strength.

7. Alternatives were not analyzed
DHS calls effects on universities and competitiveness too speculative and does not adequately weigh less burdensome options such as SEVIS data matching, risk-based employer audits, and enforcing existing STEM OPT rules, as regulatory analysis and the Regulatory Flexibility Act require.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees in full.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and argues they should be withdrawn.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security,

Introduction and background:
I am a PhD student in STEM at an American R1 university, here on an F-1 Visa, writing to oppose the proposed OPT fees ($70k for initial OPT, $30k for subsequent OPT). In my comment, I will focus specifically on the impact of this proposed rule on graduate students.

Analysis:
Research in my field is often funded by Department of Defense and private industry grants, due to its strong applicability in defense and profitable commercial technologies. These are also the fields in which I and students in similar programs are likely to make contributions, if allowed to remain in the United States through OPT. The fees proposed, particularly if passed down to students as the document acknowledges is probable, would make it financially untenable for students to participate in OPT. Thus, students in my position would likely have to leave the US and aim to make these contributions elsewhere.

The majority of graduate students, myself included, are financially self-supported by stipends (paid from a variety of sources including fellowships, scholarships, TA-ships, or research grants) which are significantly below $70k/year. That is, even the initial OPT fee of $70k would significantly exceed a year’s wage for a PhD student. Most students I know budget carefully, often choosing to live with roommates to reduce costs. The $70k fee is not an amount that students can realistically be expected to save up. The alternative—that the university pays the OPT fees instead of the student—seems very unlikely given that this same money could support a student actively working for the university rather than a student who (in the case of post-completion OPT) is most likely leaving the institute. The document states that DSOs “can elect not to pay the fee for a particular F-1 nonimmigrant who is not a strong candidate for OPT.” I would add that universities/colleges can elect not to pay the fee regardless of how strong a candidate is—after all, what incentive do they have to pay for a worker they will not be retaining themselves? Finally, the document suggests that the cost could be passed on to prospective employers instead. I can’t speak to the likelihood of an employer agreeing to this but, from a personal standpoint, it is a hope I would not be prepared to financially rely on.

Conclusion:
If they were to pass, these proposed fees would create at best strong financial uncertainty and at worst an impossibility for PhD students wanting to use OPT to exercise their highly specialized research expertise in the US. DHS proposes this rule to deter adverse actors—I would argue that it will deter all actors, including those for which the OPT program was designed.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Zachary Clifton
comments.commentText:
Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Optional Practical Training Fees

I write as an American citizen from Kentucky and an undergraduate at Yale College. My family came to this land before it was the United States. In the three centuries since, people have kept coming for the opportunity this country promises. There was nothing morally right in my ancestors’ timing, and there is nothing morally wrong in the timing of those who ask for that promise now. Some of my closest friends and the most remarkable people I know are international students. This rule would treat them as suspects and price them out of the training that their education is meant to include. I oppose it in its entirety. My reasons follow, with references to the sections of the proposal.

1. The fee is not tailored to the fraud it cites (Section IV.A). Nearly every example of abuse in the proposal involves shell employers, staged worksites and fraudulent offer letters. Yet the fee is charged to schools, for every student, before any employer is even identified; the proposal says the fee “would not be tied to a specific employer.” The investigation the Department highlights found about 10,000 students working for suspect employers. More than 190,000 students reported OPT employment in 2024 alone, and more than 165,000 more were in STEM OPT. A $70,000 charge on every student is not a reasonable response to misconduct by a small set of employers.

2. The fee raises serious legal questions. The Department says it set the fee to “closely align” with H-1B fees. On June 8, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 H-1B fee, holding that it was a tax Congress never authorized (State of California v. Mullin, No. 25-cv-13829). This proposal has the same features: a very large charge, revenue sent to the general Treasury, and a stated purpose of reducing participation. INA 214(a) lets the Secretary set the “time and conditions” of admission. It does not give the Secretary the power to tax.

3. It selects for wealth, not merit (Sections IV.C and VI). The Department says the fee will lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students.” A $70,000 price tag does not measure promise. It measures who can pay. The Department admits schools may pass the cost on to international students, to all students, or to employers. That means American students like me could end up paying it through tuition. The Department itself compares the fee to one or two extra years of education. In practice, OPT would become a privilege of the wealthy, and talented students from modest backgrounds would go to countries that welcome them.

4. The Department’s own numbers show severe harm. By its own estimate, the rule would cost about $4.1 billion a year (primary estimate), with lost-participation costs of up to about $8 billion a year, and would transfer about $109 billion over ten years. It also estimates that 116 small institutions would lose more than 20 percent of their annual revenue in the first year, and that 841 small institutions would lose more than 1 percent. It considered exempting small institutions and rejected the idea. It also says it cannot confidently predict how much participation would fall. A rule this large, resting on admitted uncertainty, needs far more justification than this one gives.

5. The structure is arbitrary (Section V.A; Section VII.A.5.d(3)). A student who does a summer internship through pre-completion OPT and then post-completion OPT would cost the school $100,000. The same 12 months taken all after graduation would cost $70,000. The Department expects this to discourage pre-completion OPT, which is the form most closely tied to a student’s ongoing studies. A rule that claims to protect OPT’s educational purpose should not penalize its most educational use.

6. The process is inadequate. The Department admits this is an economically significant rule, yet it allowed only about 30 days for comment. Executive Order 12866 says comment periods should generally be at least 60 days. The Department also says it did not consult state, local or tribal governments, even though about 1,044 public institutions would be affected.

If the Department has evidence of fraud by particular employers or schools, it has tools to go after them: site visits, training-plan requirements, employer verification, SEVP decertification and criminal prosecution. I urge it to withdraw this proposal and use those tools against the wrongdoers, not to charge every international student and every school for the misconduct of a few.

This country made a promise to the people who came before me. I ask the Department not to break it for the people who are asking for it now.

Zachary Clifton 
Yale College, Class of 2028, a native son of Kentucky

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Emily Scott

Public comment on the proposed Optional Practical Training fees

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am the F. F. Blicke Collegiate Professor of Pharmacy at the University of Michigan, where I teach and conduct research in medicinal chemistry and pharmacology. My lab studies how human cytochrome P450 enzymes affect the way our bodies process medicines and how these enzymes can be targeted to develop better treatments. I am writing in my personal capacity to urge DHS to withdraw its proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee rule in its entirety. The proposal would require schools to pay $70,000 for a student’s initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I am concerned that fees of this size would put OPT out of reach for many otherwise eligible scientists. Federal Register proposed rule

Keeping research projects moving

Several postdoctoral researchers in my lab have worked under OPT. In experimental research, it takes time to learn a technique well enough to troubleshoot an experiment and interpret the results with confidence. As postdocs gain that experience, they can take on more responsibility and help move projects forward. If the fees lead universities to make fewer OPT recommendations, labs like mine will have fewer opportunities to bring in researchers with the right scientific background. When a position goes unfilled, the experiments that depend on that person’s work can be delayed.

Helping scientists start careers in the United States

The postdocs I have worked with used their time on OPT to learn techniques and gain research experience they went on to use in the pharmaceutical industry. I have seen how a period of practical training can connect university research to the skills employers need. Here in Ann Arbor, that connection matters because our research labs help train the scientists that pharmaceutical and biotechnology employers can hire. Making it harder for graduates to take their first research positions in the United States would weaken that connection and make it harder for U.S. employers to benefit from the scientists we train here.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in full and preserve access to OPT. Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong concern about the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. I am concerned that a fee this large could have significant economic consequences for the United States itself.

The economic impact of this proposal is bigger than whether a particular job is ultimately filled by an international student or an American worker. When OPT participation falls, the United States can lose the economic activity that comes with these students staying, working, earning, spending, and contributing to the economy after graduation.

International students already spend substantial amounts of money in the United States while earning their degrees. They pay tuition, rent apartments, buy food and other goods, use transportation, and spend money in the communities where they live. If the cost of OPT makes the United States less attractive as a place to study, some students may choose other countries instead. That means the economic impact begins before graduation, through lost enrollment, tuition revenue, and local spending.

American universities could also be affected. Many universities rely on international enrollment, and the opportunity to gain practical work experience after graduation is an important part of the value of a U.S. degree for international students. If OPT becomes financially difficult to offer, some prospective students may decide that studying in the United States is no longer worth the cost. Over time, that could reduce enrollment and the revenue that supports American educational institutions.

There is also a broader loss of economic value when people who were educated in the United States leave immediately after graduation rather than working here. Their education was partly supported by the U.S. economy, and OPT allows them to continue contributing through their work, income, consumption, and taxes. Reducing that participation means the United States may receive less economic benefit from the investment already made in educating these students.

The proposed fee could also have a disproportionate effect on smaller universities and nonprofit institutions that do not have the financial resources to absorb such a large cost. If these institutions are unable or unwilling to pay the fee, fewer students may be able to participate in OPT, further reducing the economic activity associated with the program.

I believe the economic consequences of this proposal deserve much more consideration. For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fees will harm the US economy, universities, and international student enrollment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed fee.

International students often pay higher tuition than domestic students, in addition to housing, transportation, university fees, living expenses etc. They can't access federal financial aid, and many scholarships are restricted to citizens. Even available scholarships may only reduce tuition to the in-state rate rather than cover the cost of education. Beyond tuition, international students support local businesses through everyday spending and provide significant revenue to universities. Reduced international enrollment could therefore affect educational institutions, local businesses, and surrounding communities. The proposed fees could make the US less attractive to international students, resulting in lost tuition revenue for universities.

CPT and OPT authorize eligible students to work under specific conditions, but they do not provide employer-sponsored immigration status. Many employers remain reluctant to hire international candidates, even when they are currently authorized to work, because of anticipated future H-1B sponsorship costs, administrative requirements, and immigration uncertainty. Some exclude international applicants from internships, co-ops, and entry-level positions altogether. Consequently, qualified graduates may be rejected because of their immigration statues rather than their qualifications. Sponsorship is neither automatic nor guaranteed. Employers make selective decisions based on business needs and the value a candidate brings. Many international graduates never receive sponsorship and must leave the country when their work authorization expires. It is therefore an oversimplification to claim that international graduates broadly displace American workers. They often have access to a narrower pool of employers and face barriers that domestic candidates do not. It is also important to recognize the circumstances of international students before characterizing them as competition for American workers. They have a lot of immigration and employment restrictions, pay out of pocket, and pursue an education in a country where English isn't their first language. Their presence does not automatically mean that an American worker has lost an opportunity. In many cases, employers hire international graduates because they possess specialized technical abilities, or qualifications that are difficult to find in the domestic labor market. Those who eventually receive H-1B sponsorship do so through an employer's decision to pursue that process, not through an automatic entitlement. Rather than viewing these graduates as a threat to American workers, they should be recognized as an important part of the skilled workforce that helps meet the needs of the US economy.

Some may say that F-1 students who are nonresident aliens for U.S. tax purposes may be exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes on qualifying authorized employment, potentially saving employers up to 7.65% of wages. However, this exemption does not apply to all international students. F-1 students are generally exempt from the substantial presence test during their first five calendar years in the United States. After that, they may become resident aliens for tax purposes, in which case the FICA exemption generally no longer applies. Resident alien status for tax purposes does not mean U.S. citizenship. This limited tax provision should not be portrayed as a universal employer advantage or used to suggest that international students as a group have an unfair employment advantage.

The proposed fees do not distinguish between legitimate OPT participants and institutions or employers involved in misconduct. A university recommending an eligible student who fully complies with program requirements would face the same fee structure as an institution associated with potential violations. Furthermore, the proposed amounts are not clearly tied to the actual administrative or investigative costs of individual cases. DHS should explain how it calculated these fees and why less burdensome alternatives would not achieve the same objectives. Universities can verify student eligibility and fulfill their compliance responsibilities, but they cannot reasonably be expected to investigate every employer's internal practices or prevent all employment fraud. Instead of imposing extraordinary costs on every institution, DHS should strengthen risk-based audits, verify legitimate employment arrangements, investigate repeat offenders, and impose meaningful penalties on those actually responsible for violations.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposal to increase Optional Practical Training (OPT) application fees. I believe the proposed fee adjustment is unwarranted, unreasonable, and an unnecessary barrier that harms the accessibility, equity, and competitiveness of the U.S. higher education and workforce systems.
The OPT program provides significant value to international students by allowing them to gain practical work experience in the United States, enhance their professional skills, and improve their future career opportunities. Given that these students already pay exorbitant international tuition rates and significantly contribute to local economies, it is unreasonable to expect them to bear an even heavier financial burden for basic administrative processing.
While USCIS operates primarily on a fee-funded basis, relying on skyrocketing fees for students is an unsustainable mechanism. Instead of penalizing applicants, the government should look toward federal appropriations or internal efficiency measures to secure staffing, technology, and customer service resources. Increasing fees penalizes students for agency inefficiencies and rising application volumes.
A higher OPT fee does not guarantee program integrity; rather, it creates an exclusionary system where only wealthy applicants can afford to participate. True program integrity comes from streamlined, transparent regulations, not from inflating costs that deter qualified, diverse talent from applying. Robust oversight should be funded through broader fiscal management, not by placing a premium on educational benefits.
Furthermore, the proposed increase is far from modest when added to the already immense financial hurdles international students face, including high tuition, living expenses, and existing visa fees. Many applicants have not yet secured employment and do not have access to competitive salaries when applying. In that context, the proposed fee increase represents an undue burden and a significant financial barrier rather than a reasonable investment.
It is also critical to note that historical fee increases have rarely resolved longer processing times, backlogs, or poor service quality. Raising costs without guaranteeing faster timelines forces students to pay more for the same broken system. A truly functional agency should focus on reducing processing delays to benefit applicants, employers, and educational institutions, rather than exploiting a captive applicant pool.
For these reasons, I strongly oppose DHS's proposal to increase OPT fees and urge the Department to reject the fee adjustment. Ensuring that the U.S. remains an attractive and equitable destination for global talent is in the best interests of applicants, employers, educational institutions, and the growth of the U.S. economy as a whole.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by WholeRen Education
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01 — "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 FR 64566 (October 8, 2026)

Comment of Andrew Chen, Chief Executive Officer, WholeRen Education

I am the CEO of WholeRen Education. We advise international students and their families on studying in the United States, and we work directly with U.S. schools and universities. Optional Practical Training (OPT) is the bridge between the education our students receive here and the U.S. workforce that education was designed to serve. I write in opposition to the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, and I ask DHS to withdraw them.

1. The proposed charges are a tax, not a fee. A designated school official's OPT recommendation is an administrative certification entered in SEVIS. The actual cost of that service is minimal, and the proposed $70,000 charge bears no relationship to it. DHS's own analysis estimates the rule would collect between $8.4 and $16.5 billion per year — revenue on a scale that has nothing to do with recovering the cost of processing recommendations. Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, agency fees must be tied to the cost of the service provided; a charge designed to raise general revenue is a tax, and taxation is the province of Congress, not of the Department. The same defect affects the structure of the charge: because the fee must be paid before the recommendation can be entered at all, it operates as a toll on access to a benefit Congress created.

2. In practice, the rule would end OPT for most students without any change in the statute. OPT is part of the F-1 program established by Congress at INA § 101(a)(15)(F) and implemented for decades at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10). No school can absorb $70,000 per student, and no school will simply absorb it: institutions will restrict which students they recommend, pass the cost on to students and families, or decline to recommend at all. Community colleges and smaller institutions — the schools least able to pay — will be hit first and hardest. A benefit that exists on paper but is priced out of reach has been eliminated in fact, and that decision belongs to Congress.

3. The harm falls on U.S. employers, universities, and communities, not only on students. International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy and support hundreds of thousands of American jobs. OPT and the STEM OPT extension are the pipeline through which U.S. employers — hospitals, manufacturers, technology firms, and research institutions — hire graduates they have already effectively interviewed through their degree programs. Meanwhile, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia are actively competing for the same students, and survey data consistently show cost is now the single largest factor in students' destination choices. This rule would hand those countries a generation of talent the United States educated.

4. A flat fee does not target fraud. Every compliant school and every legitimate student would pay the same punitive charge as the rare bad actor. ICE already possesses the tools aimed at actual fraud: SEVP certification review, on-site visits, and decertification of non-compliant schools. A universal $70,000 toll punishes the compliant, consumes institutional resources that would otherwise fund exactly the advising and oversight that keep the program clean, and does nothing to identify wrongdoing.

5. On the question DHS specifically posed: DHS asked whether the full $70,000 should be charged again each time a student advances to a higher degree level and begins a new period of OPT. It should not. Re-imposing the charge at each level would compound every problem above and further penalize precisely the long-term, high-achieving students — master's and doctoral graduates in research fields — whom the United States most benefits from retaining.

Conclusion. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee schedule. If the Department believes a fee is needed to administer OPT recommendations, it should propose one anchored to the documented cost of that administration, as federal fee law requires.

Andrew Chen
Chief Executive Officer, WholeRen Education
andrew.chen@wholeren.com
Newton, Massachusetts

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule requiring an initial $70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation plus $30,000 for STEM extensions fundamentally undermines U.S. national security, global competitiveness, and domestic job creation under the guise of program integrity.

While DHS frames this exorbitant fee structure as a deterrent against fraud, its practical execution will dismantle the primary talent pipeline driving critical American industries, including artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, aerospace, and biotechnology. International students constitute a vital portion of graduate researchers in STEM disciplines across U.S. universities. Depriving these scholars of a predictable post-graduation pathway to apply their training locally will starve American research labs and private-sector R&D of top-tier technical minds.

Crucially, the proposal’s premise that high financial barriers foster "program integrity" is flawed. A $70,000 - $100,000 price tag does not filter candidates based on academic merit or field relevance; it filters them based on access to wealth. High-caliber talent from developing nations will be priced out, while lower-merit applicants backed by substantial capital can easily comply. This shifts U.S. talent acquisition from a meritocracy to a pay-to-play system, severely degrading the overall quality of the workforce remaining in the U.S.

Furthermore, driving international talent to competing nations, such as Canada, the UK, China, and Germany, inflicts long-term economic damage on American workers. High-skilled foreign graduates are catalysts for domestic employment; they launch innovative enterprises, secure patents, and expand high-tech manufacturing capacity inside the U.S. Forcing these innovators offshore means the jobs, tax revenues, and intellectual property they generate will benefit foreign economies instead.

DHS must recognize that the OPT program is not a loophole, but a vital engine of U.S. economic and technological leadership. Imposing punitive six-figure surcharges will yield negligible gains in program integrity while inflicting self-inflicted damage on America’s innovation ecosystem. DHS should withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The DHS proposed rule requiring an initial $70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations alongside a $30,000 fee for STEM extensions is arbitrary, capricious, and fundamentally destructive to the national interest of the United States. While DHS frames this policy as a mechanism to "prevent fraud" and "protect American workers," its practical implementation will deliver a devastating blow to U.S. technological supremacy, compromise national security, reward foreign wealthy elites over true merit, and inflict severe economic harm on American workers and higher education institutions.

1. Dismantling National Security & Technological Superiority:
The primary battleground of global power today is technological innovation, specifically in artificial intelligence, semiconductor design, quantum computing, data science. International students comprise over 70% of graduate students in key STEM disciplines at top U.S. research universities. OPT is the essential operational runway allowing these scholars to transition their research from university labs to the American industrial base. By placing a $70,000 to $100,000 price tag on post-graduation practical training, DHS will effectively shut off the primary talent pipeline feeding U.S. critical technology sectors. Foreign adversaries, most notably China, are actively spending billions to build competing research ecosystems. This rule directly hands those nation-states a strategic advantage by driving world-class technical talent out of the U.S. and straight into competing global markets.

2. The Fallacy of "Program Integrity" via Wealth Selection
DHS asserts that forcing colleges to pay $70,000 will incentivize them to be "more selective" and deter recommendations for candidates with "questionable qualifications." This administrative premise is fundamentally flawed. Higher education institutions cannot absorb six-figure fees per student and will be forced to pass these financial burdens onto the applicants or employers. As a result, this fee structure does not select for academic quality or specialized skill; it selects strictly for financial wealth. High-caliber talent, brilliant researchers, and promising innovators from modest financial backgrounds in developing nations will be priced out of the U.S. system entirely. Conversely, lower-merit applicants with access to substantial capital will easily bypass the barrier. Replacing a meritocratic talent pipeline with a pay-to-play framework actively degrades the overall quality of the U.S. workforce and directly contradicts DHS’s stated objective of improving program integrity.

3. Economic Damage and Job Destruction for American Workers
DHS’s claim that this rule "protects American workers" ignores overwhelming empirical economic research. High-skilled immigrants do not displace American labor; they serve as job creators and economic multipliers. National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) studies demonstrate that foreign-born STEM graduates drive local innovation, file key patents, and found high-growth enterprises that create thousands of net-new domestic jobs for U.S. citizens. Forcing these innovators offshore eliminates the downstream employment opportunities, tax revenues, and corporate investments they would have generated within American borders.

4. Administrative Arbitrariness and Institutional Destabilization
The threat by DHS to shut down the OPT program entirely if these unprecedented fees are not implemented constitutes improper regulatory coercion. Imposing a $100,000 cumulative fee on a free administrative recommendation, a process historically accompanied only by nominal filing fees, lacks rational connection to the actual administrative cost of processing the benefit. Passing these unmanageable costs onto colleges destabilizes the U.S. higher education model, threatening the financial health of public and private research universities that rely on global tuition funding to subsidize domestic student aid and faculty initiatives.

For these reasons, DHS should immediately withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are destructive, economically harmful, and damage U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule on Optional Practical Training Fee recommendations is fundamentally flawed. Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), agency rule-making must be grounded in reasoned decision-making and supported by substantial evidence. DHS justifies this exorbitant financial penalty by claiming it is necessary to "prevent fraud and abuse" and force colleges to act as financial gatekeepers. However, an analysis of federal data, existing regulatory frameworks, and DHS’s own record demonstrates that systematic fraud within the OPT program is virtually non-existent, rendering the proposed fee structure arbitrary, capricious, and legally untenable.

1. DHS Fails to Provide Empirical Evidence of Widespread Fraud
In its proposed rule-making, DHS cites a handful of isolated enforcement actions, such as a 2020 operation involving 15 individuals, to characterize the entire OPT program as compromised. Attempting to justify a blanket $100,000 regulatory penalty on nearly 300,000 annual OPT participants based on a fraction of a percent of non-compliance is an extreme administrative overreach. Out of more than 1.1 million active international students and hundreds of thousands of OPT beneficiaries, instances of intentional fraud represent an statistically negligible percentage—far below one-hundredth of one percent (0.01%). Imposing structural, multi-billion-dollar costs across higher education to address an anomaly that existing law enforcement mechanisms already successfully catch fails any standard of cost-benefit analysis.

2. Existing Oversight Mechanisms Already Ensure Rigorous Compliance
DHS’s assertion that colleges must be financially penalized to force "selectivity" ignores the extensive regulatory regime already governing OPT. The Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) provides real-time, mandatory reporting. Designated School Officials (DSOs) are legally required to verify that an applicant’s proposed practical training directly relates to their major field of study before issuing a Form I-20 recommendation. Furthermore, STEM OPT extensions require a formal, signed Form I-983 Training Plan executed by both the university-backed candidate and a vetted U.S. employer, outlining specific learning objectives, oversight protocols, and wage protections. The federal government already possesses full transparency and robust auditing authority over OPT; adding a $100,000 fee adds zero oversight capacity, it merely creates an arbitrary financial gate.

3. Conflating Administrative Non-Compliance with Systemic "Abuse"
DHS repeatedly conflates minor, technical administrative reporting delays, such as a graduate taking several weeks to update an address change or employer name in SEVIS, with deliberate fraud. Honest delays in a complex administrative system do not constitute systemic bad-faith abuse. By framing routine record-keeping variances as evidence of widespread corruption, DHS fabricates a crisis to rationalize an unlawful revenue grab. Threatening to terminate the entire OPT program if these non-statutory fees are not collected demonstrates an absence of factual justification, relying on regulatory coercion rather than empirical evidence.

4. Arbitrary Penalization Stripped of Rational Connection
Under established administrative law, an agency must establish a direct, rational connection between the facts found and the choice made (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.). DHS has failed to produce any evidence demonstrating how charging universities $70,000 to $100,000 per student deters fraudulent actors, who could simply pass costs along or seek illicit work outside legal channels, while severely penalizing the vast, law-abiding majority of students and institutions.

Because DHS’s premise of rampant OPT fraud is demonstrably unsupported by data, the proposed rule lacks a valid regulatory purpose. DHS must immediately withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fee is exorbitant, legally untenable, and based on a lack of evidence of widespread fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Joe Johnson
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AB01)

I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees, and I ask DHS to withdraw this rule. I am a U.S. citizen and recent college graduate, and I have seen firsthand the struggles international students face when they leave their homes and families to study at American universities. Visa rules already limit the work experience they can get while in school. OPT is their chance to show American employers that their degree means they can do the job. It is already limited to one to three years, depending on field of study. Employers know that keeping these graduates long term means sponsoring them, and sponsorship already carries its own costs. OPT lets an employer see a graduate's work first and then decide whether sponsorship is worth it. Charging a fee before a graduate can prove themselves breaks that process and keeps employers from hiring the best person for the job.

The fee works as a ban. OPT is not a niche program. About 72 percent of foreign graduates use it (Peterson Institute for International Economics, 2025), which makes it the main bridge between an American degree and an American job. DHS itself expects the fee to produce a smaller pool of participants (91 FR 64566). For most students, schools, and employers, $70,000 is not a fee they can pay. A price this high does not regulate OPT. It ends it for most students.

The fee does not target fraud. DHS points to shell companies and suspect employers (91 FR 64566), but the fee is charged for every student at every school, no matter who the employer is. A student hired by a hospital or research lab pays the same as one placed by a fake company. The answer to bad employers is vetting, site visits, and enforcement against those employers.

The money would not pay for oversight. The proposal sends fee revenue to the general Treasury, and ICE would not keep it (91 FR 64566). The fee does not fund the enforcement work used to justify it. A fee unrelated to the cost or integrity of the program is a penalty, not a fee.

American students and families will pay too. DHS acknowledges schools may pass the fee on to all students, or to employers (91 FR 64566). That means higher costs for domestic students, or schools refusing to recommend OPT at all.

The evidence shows OPT helps American workers. A study found no evidence that OPT reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers, and found more OPT participants were associated with lower

unemployment among U.S. workers (Zavodny, National Foundation for American Policy, 2019). Another found that OPT increases innovation and does not harm native workers (Neufeld, Niskanen Center, 2019). That fits a larger pattern. Immigrants make up about 16 percent of U.S. inventors but account for about 30 percent of American innovation since 1976 (2018 Stanford study, cited by Mercatus Center). International students and their families also contributed $42.9 billion and 355,736 jobs to the U.S. economy in the 2024 to 2025 academic year (NAFSA International Student Economic Value Tool).

We would be paying to train talent and then sending it away. International students are some of the most valuable workers this country can attract. Immigrants earn 52 percent of STEM doctorates in the U.S. (Mercatus Center). American universities spend years training these students, and OPT is how that education becomes work for American employers, tax revenue, and new companies. A $70,000 charge at that step hands this talent to competing countries.

I also oppose the alternative of charging the $70,000 initial fee again when a student moves to a higher degree level (91 FR 64566). It would punish the students seeking the most advanced training.

If DHS keeps any fee, it should cover only the actual administrative cost of a recommendation, and fraud should be handled through targeted enforcement against employers who abuse the program. I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

Sources

Mercatus Center, "Reforming Optional Practical Training (OPT) to Enhance Technological Progress and Innovation" (citing a 2018 Stanford University study for the inventor figures).

Peterson Institute for International Economics, "Skilled immigration on the chopping block: Effects of eliminating Optional Practical Training" (2025).

DHS/ICE, "Optional Practical Training Fees," Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026), Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

Madeline Zavodny, "International Students, STEM OPT, and the U.S. STEM Workforce," National Foundation for American Policy (March 2019).

Jeremy L. Neufeld, "Optional Practical Training (OPT) and International Students After Graduation," Niskanen Center (March 2019).

NAFSA, International Student Economic Value Tool, cited in NAFSA issue brief on the Keep Innovators in America Act.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and asks DHS to withdraw the rule, arguing it acts as a ban on hiring.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. I believe these fees are completely unreasonable and would bring serious damage to American universities and the U.S. economy. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

First, I do not think these fees reflect the actual cost of processing OPT applications. OPT has been part of the F-1 student program for many years. It allows students to gain work experience related to what they studied. However, DHS has not clearly explained why universities or students should pay $70,000 or $30,000 for this process. These amounts are far beyond normal administrative costs. Instead of covering processing expenses, these fees would simply prevent many qualified students from participating in OPT.

Second, this rule would also create a huge financial burden for American universities. According to DHS's own analysis, 841 out of 1,389 small institutions would face costs higher than 1% of their annual revenue, and 116 institutions would face costs above 20%. These are not small numbers. Many universities already have limited budgets, and adding such large expenses could force them to reduce academic programs, spend less money on research, or increase tuition. This policy would hurt not only international students, but also the universities and American students who study there.

Third, I believe this proposal would harm the U.S. economy. According to NAFSA, international students contributed about $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs during the 2024–25 academic year. These numbers do not even include OPT participants. International education brings a lot of economic benefits to the United States. If OPT becomes too expensive, fewer students may choose to study in America. Universities could lose enrollment, local businesses could lose customers, and American companies could lose talented graduates. I don't see how this would benefit the country.

Finally, I think DHS has not fully considered the long-term impact of this proposal. Its analysis does not properly measure how many opportunities could be lost, or how much universities and employers could suffer. The impact is not just about whether someone can afford the fee. It also affect university funding, research opportunities, employment, and future economic growth. These consequences should be seriously considered before introducing such an extreme policy.

OPT is an important part of American higher education. Charging $70,000 or $30,000 would make this program almost impossible for many people to access. I believe the negative consequences would be much greater than any possible benefits.

I am writing to express my unequivocal support for the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations under DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (91 FR 64566). Implementing these fees is an urgent, necessary measure to protect struggling American graduates, restore fairness to the entry-level job market, and eliminate documented fraud within the F-1 nonimmigrant visa program.
First, this rule is vital to protect U.S. workers, particularly recent domestic college graduates who are facing a severe entry-level hiring crisis. According to labor market data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the unemployment rate for recent college graduates has risen well above the national average, reaching 5.2% to 5.8% overall. In technical fields where OPT and STEM OPT participation is heavily concentrated, the displacement of domestic entry-level talent is even starker: recent U.S. Computer Engineering and Computer Science graduates face unemployment rates of 7.5% and 6.1% to 7.0%, respectively, while entry-level software engineering job postings have plummeted by 65% since 2022.

Furthermore, American graduates are suffering from chronic underemployment and failing to secure jobs that match their majors. Data from the New York Federal Reserve and the Strada/Burning Glass Institutes demonstrates that 41.5% to 42.5% of recent U.S. college graduates are underemployed—working in positions that do not require a college degree—including nearly 20% of Computer Science majors and over 25% of Information Systems and Mathematics majors. At the exact time nearly half of American graduates cannot land degree-appropriate entry-level roles, the number of foreign graduates utilizing OPT has doubled over the past decade to more than 290,000 annually. Worse still, because F-1 OPT workers are exempt from FICA payroll taxes, U.S. employers are given a built-in ~7.65% financial incentive to hire foreign trainees over American graduates who have invested heavily in their higher education.
Second, as DHS and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) thoroughly documented in this NPRM, the unchecked expansion of OPT has created massive vulnerabilities to systemic fraud that outstrip current oversight resources. HSI investigations have already uncovered over 10,000 F-1 students on OPT tied to highly suspect employers, including coordinated clusters of fraudulent shell companies operating out of residential addresses to sell sham employment and bypass H-1B visa caps. Requiring SEVP-certified institutions to remit $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT will immediately deter bad-faith actors, hold institutions accountable for the legitimacy of their recommendations, and properly fund rigorous site visits and compliance enforcement.
The OPT program was never intended by Congress to serve as a massive, tax-advantaged guest-worker pipeline that crowds out new American graduates from launching their careers. I strongly urge DHS and ICE to finalize and implement Published Document 2026-20660 without delay and without reducing the proposed fee amounts.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly supports the proposed OPT fees to protect U.S. workers and reduce fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100) to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a deeply flawed policy that functions as a de facto ban on experiential learning. While curbing immigration fraud is a legitimate government interest, these exorbitant fees will indiscriminately punish genuine international students, devastate U.S. university enrollment, and erode the United States' position as the premier global destination for higher education.

An Astronomically Unreasonable Price Tag
A $70,000 fee for a single year of practical training authorization is objectively unreasonable. For context, this figure exceeds the median annual income of a U.S. household and surpasses the total four-year tuition costs of many public universities. The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) explicitly states that these fees are designed as a "deterrent," but setting the cost at a punitive level untethered to actual administrative processing costs transforms the fee into a financial blockade. By forcing educational institutions to pay this upfront—which will inevitably be passed on to the students through specialized fees or tuition hikes—the rule ensures that only the ultra-wealthy, rather than the most academically talented, can afford to fully participate in the U.S. educational system.

Depriving Genuine Students of Crucial Educational Development
Practical training is not an ancillary loophole; it is a fundamental component of modern higher education. Genuine students rely on OPT to apply theoretical classroom knowledge to real-world environments, a requirement for mastery in fields ranging from engineering and medicine to business and the arts. By placing a $70,000 to $100,000 premium on this experience, the proposed rule deprives legitimate, law-abiding students of the hands-on training that makes U.S. degrees globally valuable. The rule unjustly punishes hundreds of thousands of legitimate students for the fraudulent actions of a localized minority of "visa mills" and shell companies. Punishing the entire student population with an insurmountable financial burden is a failure of regulatory precision, substituting targeted law enforcement and compliance audits with a blunt financial instrument.

A Devastating Impact on U.S. University Enrollment
The global market for international students is highly competitive. If the U.S. attaches a $70,000 penalty to post-graduate practical training, prospective students will simply take their talent, intellect, and tuition dollars to countries with welcoming, affordable post-study work policies, such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. This mass diversion of international students will trigger a severe enrollment crisis for U.S. universities.

International students contribute tens of billions of dollars to the U.S. economy annually, and their tuition often subsidizes academic programs, faculty salaries, and research facilities that directly benefit domestic American students. The NPRM's own Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis notes that 56% of regulated SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. A sudden, drastic collapse in international enrollment will force many of these small and mid-sized institutions into deep financial distress, leading to program cuts, layoffs, or closures.

Combating fraud requires precise school oversight, strict employer verification, and targeted investigations—not astronomical price tags that commodify access to education. Implementing a $70,000 OPT fee will not protect the integrity of the U.S. education system; it will hollow it out by driving away the world's brightest minds and plunging U.S. academic institutions into an entirely preventable financial crisis.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are exorbitant, act as a de facto ban, and harm students and universities.

I am writing to submit this formal comment in support of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish new fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. The proposed framework—requiring a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent extensions—represents a necessary step toward aligning foreign student employment authorizations with the broader goals of U.S. workforce protection and immigration system integrity.
This regulation addresses several critical vulnerabilities in the current immigration system:
• Protection of the Domestic Labor Market: As outlined by DHS, the current structure allows for a massive influx of post-graduation foreign labor that can distort local job markets. By introducing a substantial regulatory fee, the rule helps ensure that domestic citizens and permanent residents can compete on an equitable playing field for entry-level positions, particularly in high-demand sectors.
• Mitigation of Systemic Fraud and Abuse: Proponents emphasize that the open-ended nature of the current OPT framework has historically been exploited by unaccredited "visa mills" and shell companies utilizing fraudulent employment letters. A significant financial threshold will naturally incentivize Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) certified schools to exercise far greater scrutiny and selectivity before making recommendations in the SEVIS database.
• Preventing H-1B Cap Circumvention: Currently, the OPT program operates without a numerical cap or prevailing wage requirements, allowing some employers to utilize it as an unregulated alternative to the H-1B visa program. Aligning the financial commitment of OPT with the costs associated with primary employment visas removes the incentive for organizations to bypass congressionally mandated H-1B limits and fee structures.
• Enhancing Institutional Accountability: By making educational institutions the primary entities responsible for filing the fee, the rule ensures that universities remain active participants in monitoring compliance, rather than treating post-graduation work authorization as an unvetted benefit.
For these reasons, I support the implementation of the proposed fee adjustments to strengthen oversight and ensure the OPT program aligns with its original, temporary educational objectives.
Thanking you
Nags CVN

comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it.
1. Current OPT and STEM OPT rules already serve the national interest.
OPT lets graduates of U.S. universities apply their training at U.S. employers. STEM OPT already includes safeguards: employers must attest that trainees have not replaced U.S. workers. The evidence shows the program works as intended: (niskanencenter)
A study of the 2008 STEM OPT extension found it increased domestic STEM employment by 4.4% to 5.8% and domestic wages by 2.4% to 3.3% (Gong, Guo, and Pang). (virginia)
An NFAP analysis of 2008-2016 data found no evidence that OPT reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers. OPT participants are under 1% of workers with a STEM bachelor's degree. (fosterglobal) (thepienews)
Niskanen Center data show average STEM wages in 2021 were 36% higher than in 2014, even though the STEM OPT population was 187% larger. (niskanencenter)
2. OPT participants build American companies and jobs.
NFAP found that 25% of U.S. billion-dollar startups have a founder who first came as an international student, and those companies averaged 860 jobs each. In AI, 18 of the top 43 U.S. AI companies had a founder who began as an international student. OPT is how many of these future founders gain their first U.S. work experience. (americanbazaaronline) (immigrationresearch)
3. The fees would sharply reduce OPT and STEM OPT participation.
Today the USCIS filing fee is $470 online or $520 on paper. The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT period and $30,000 for each later one, so a STEM graduate using all three years would cost a school $100,000. Under the rule, no OPT recommendation can be entered, and USCIS may not grant work authorization, until the fee is paid. Few schools, especially small colleges and community-focused institutions, can absorb this. Schools will either stop recommending OPT or pass the cost to students and employers. An analysis from the Institute for Progress estimates the fee would reduce OPT and STEM OPT participation by 23% to 99%. DHS's analysis assumes schools will not reduce recommendations, which is unrealistic at these prices. (us proposes 70000 work training fee for foreign students 10 08 2026 +4)
4. Fewer participants means real harm to the American economy and its people.
Employers: Companies, especially startups and research teams, lose access to trained graduates in STEM, healthcare, and research.
Universities and domestic students: 92% of U.S. institutions report that without OPT, international students would likely choose other study destinations. Economist Michael Clemens estimates a $100,000 fee could cost U.S. universities up to $4 billion a year in lost revenue. International tuition helps fund seats for domestic students. (2025 data and the global student trajectory +2)
Communities: International students and their families boosted the economy by nearly $43 billion and more than 355,000 jobs in 2024-25. A rule that discourages enrollment puts those jobs at risk. (quorum)
5. The rule's justification and process are inadequate.
DHS cites fraud prevention, but its own assumption that STEM recommendations will continue means the fee would not deter fraud among STEM graduates. DHS has not shown that deterring fraud requires fees totaling $100,000, or analyzed less burdensome alternatives such as employer vetting and targeted enforcement. A change this large deserves more than a 30-day comment period. (ifp)
Request. DHS should withdraw the rule. If it proceeds, it should set any fee based on actual administrative cost, exempt STEM OPT extensions, adopt targeted anti-fraud measures instead, grandfather current students, and extend the comment period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international graduate student in the United States, and I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation.

When I decided to pursue my education in the United States, OPT was an established part of the F-1 student framework. I understood that, if eligible, I could apply for practical training related to my field without a new fee of tens of thousands of dollars for a university recommendation. The availability of OPT was an important factor in my decision to come here. I have invested a substantial amount of money, time, and effort in my education, based on the system that existed when I enrolled. Introducing a financial barrier of this magnitude after students have already made life-changing decisions is deeply unfair. It undermines the reasonable expectations on which many of us relied.

Even if universities are formally responsible for paying the $70,000 fee, that does not mean students would be protected from its consequences. Universities have limited budgets and competing obligations. A charge of $70,000 for recommending just one student could lead schools to restrict OPT recommendations, decline to support otherwise eligible students, divert funding from educational services, or pass costs along through higher tuition or other charges. Some schools could not absorb these expenses. If a university refuses or cannot afford to pay, the student loses the practical opportunity to pursue OPT, regardless of academic performance or professional qualifications. The financial burden may be imposed on schools, but the resulting harm would fall heavily on students.

The amount is extraordinary. Seventy thousand dollars exceeds the annual salary of some entry-level jobs. It is difficult to understand why access to practical training should depend on an institution's ability to pay an amount that may be greater than a graduate's first year of earnings. This proposal could turn an established educational opportunity into one available primarily to students at institutions with sufficient resources, making access depend on a school's resources rather than student merit.

This uncertainty has already had a serious impact on my mental and physical well-being. I have experienced significant anxiety, emotional distress, and physical effects of stress. I came here to learn, build my skills, and prepare for a meaningful career. Instead of focusing fully on my studies and professional development, I now worry that an opportunity I have worked toward for years could become inaccessible through circumstances beyond my control. This is real suffering that affects my daily life. I have also witnessed serious anxiety and frustration among international students around me. Many of us have made enormous personal sacrifices, followed the rules, and planned our futures around the educational pathways available when we arrived. The possibility of such a sudden change has created widespread insecurity in our community.

I recognize that DHS has a legitimate interest in preventing fraud and protecting program integrity. I support appropriate oversight and enforcement against actual misconduct. However, imposing an enormous fee on every participating institution is not a targeted way to address fraudulent activity. It risks discouraging legitimate universities from supporting students who comply with the rules. Employer verification, targeted investigations, and stronger reporting or monitoring requirements deserve careful consideration as alternatives that focus more directly on the source of misconduct.

I ask DHS to give meaningful weight to the reliance interests of students already pursuing U.S. degrees. Students cannot simply reverse years of financial investment, relocate their education, or redesign their careers without significant cost. An analysis focused only on which party is legally required to pay the fee would miss the indirect consequences for students whose schools might no longer recommend them for OPT. DHS should examine these effects carefully, including how the proposal could affect universities with fewer resources and students who enrolled before the fee was proposed.

OPT allows students to apply the knowledge developed in American classrooms to professional work in their fields. International students contribute through tuition, living expenses, research, and participation in university communities. Making OPT practically inaccessible would diminish the opportunities associated with an education in the United States and could discourage future students from choosing American institutions.

For these reasons, I strongly oppose the proposed rule and respectfully request that DHS withdraw it. Thank you for considering my personal experience and concerns.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are unfair and create severe financial and institutional barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i))

I am an engineering student at a U.S. university, and I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. The $70,000 and $30,000 fees are not a reasoned response to the problems DHS identifies.

1. The fee has no cost basis and funds nothing it is meant to fix. DHS says it chose an amount "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas," and the money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts because "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected." A charge set to match a different program, unrelated to the cost of any service, and deposited as general revenue is a tax in all but name (see National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 1974). The time-and-conditions provision of INA 214(a) does not clearly authorize DHS to collect an estimated $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year, and a measure of that economic significance requires clear congressional authorization (West Virginia v. EPA, 2022).

2. The fee is not tailored to fraud. It attaches to the school's recommendation, not the employer, so it costs the same whether a graduate works for a shell company or a legitimate firm. DHS's fraud evidence, such as 10,000+ students working for "highly suspect employers," involves a small fraction of the roughly 195,000 OPT participants in 2024, yet every student is charged. Tools that target fraud directly (training plans, employer attestations and site visits, as already used in STEM OPT) were set aside because a fee would be "immediate and effective." But a fee that funds no enforcement and cannot tell fraudulent employment from legitimate employment is "effective" only by suppressing participation across the board. That is not a "rational connection between the facts found and the choice made" (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 1983).

3. The worker-protection rationale does not support the amount. DHS cites the 7.65% employer FICA savings. For a graduate earning $80,000, that is about $6,100 a year; the $70,000 fee is more than eleven times that, and it applies equally to graduates who have been in the U.S. long enough to owe FICA. If FICA parity is the concern, the fix is legislation or a wage condition, not a flat charge.

4. Pre-completion OPT is priced irrationally. The initial fee applies "whether it is pre-completion or post-completion OPT." Both draw on the same 12-month entitlement, yet splitting it between a summer internship and post-graduation work would cost $100,000, or $130,000 with a STEM extension. DHS itself expects schools to shift away from pre-completion OPT, curtailing it through price rather than reasoned rulemaking. Pre-completion OPT should be exempt.

5. Reliance interests are dismissed, not weighed. Current students enrolled, paid tuition and borrowed money based on OPT as it has existed for decades. DHS concedes current students "are in a different position than prospective F-1 nonimmigrants," yet protects only those recommended before the effective date and simply declares that its concerns "outweigh any stakeholder's reliance interest." Conclusory statements do not suffice (Encino Motorcars v. Navarro, 2016; DHS v. Regents, 2020). At minimum, DHS should exempt every student enrolled before the effective date.

6. DHS admits it does not know the rule's effects. Its annualized cost estimate ranges from $32 million to $8.2 billion, a more than 250-fold spread, and DHS "cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation." It finds "a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities," with 841 small institutions facing impacts above 1 percent of revenue, yet rejects an exemption for small institutions. It also acknowledges that schools may pass the cost on to students generally, including Americans, through higher tuition.

7. The threat to end OPT is not a justification. DHS says that without the fees it "may shut down the program entirely." A rule must stand on its own reasoning; the possibility of a more drastic action does not make this one reasonable.

DHS should withdraw proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i). If it proceeds, it should (a) limit any fee to the documented cost of OPT oversight, (b) target employers with fraud indicators through site visits and attestations, (c) exempt pre-completion OPT, and (d) exempt all students enrolled before the effective date.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, arguing the fees are exorbitant, unjustified, and lack legal authority.
