comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

As someone who understands the challenges international students face while pursuing higher education in the United States, I believe this proposal could create serious barriers to education, professional development, and economic opportunity.

1. Financial and Educational Impact

International students already make substantial financial investments in American education, including tuition, housing, health insurance, and living expenses. OPT provides an important opportunity to apply academic knowledge in professional environments. Introducing exceptionally high fees could discourage universities from supporting eligible students and potentially lead to additional institutional charges being passed on to students.

2. Negative Impact on American Universities

Universities, particularly smaller institutions, may struggle to absorb such substantial per-student fees. This could affect their ability to support international students and make American higher education less attractive to talented individuals worldwide.

3. Impact on American Businesses and Innovation

International graduates contribute to important sectors such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, healthcare, engineering, and scientific research. Startups and small businesses also benefit from access to qualified graduates. Making OPT participation financially difficult could reduce opportunities for employers to recruit skilled talent and weaken America’s competitive position in emerging technologies.

4. Disproportionate and Unjustified Financial Burden

Although these proposed fees are formally charged to educational institutions rather than directly to students, their economic consequences could ultimately affect students and universities. DHS should provide clear evidence explaining how the proposed amounts were calculated and demonstrate why such substantial fees are necessary to achieve its enforcement objectives.

Fraud prevention and immigration compliance are legitimate government responsibilities. However, enforcement should target fraudulent institutions, employers, and employment arrangements rather than create excessive financial barriers for legitimate students.

5. Recommended Alternatives

I respectfully urge DHS to:

* Withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure.
* Establish reasonable fees based on actual administrative and enforcement costs.
* Strengthen SEVIS monitoring and verification systems.
* Target fraudulent employers and institutions through evidence-based enforcement.
* Consider exemptions or reduced fees for financially disadvantaged institutions.
* Conduct a comprehensive economic impact assessment before implementing such a policy.

Conclusion

International students contribute to American universities, local economies, research, entrepreneurship, and technological innovation. OPT serves as an important bridge between education and professional experience.

The United States should continue attracting talented students and encouraging them to contribute their knowledge and skills to the American economy.

I support responsible immigration enforcement and the protection of American workers. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an international graduate student at a U.S. university, writing to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees [proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2)] and the requirement that schools pay them before a DSO may recommend a student for OPT [proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)]. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

I am qualified to comment because I have lived every stage of the pathway this rule would put out of reach. Over eight years in the United States, I studied as an F-1 undergraduate; worked full time at a U.S. firm on OPT, the STEM OPT extension, and then an H-1B; and have now returned on an F-1 visa for a graduate degree as I prepare to re-enter the U.S. job market.

My U.S. education opened the door to a career I loved, and OPT allowed me to walk through it. My employer selected me through the same competitive process as my American peers and invested in my growth. Over four years, I became a trusted contributor, co-authoring more than five research abstracts and three manuscripts with colleagues in health economics and outcomes research. Those collaborations also gave me lasting friendships and mentors who shaped who I am. None of this would have been possible without the work authorization that F-1 status provides.

Under the proposed rule, that same path would have required my school to pay $100,000 ($70,000 for my initial OPT and $30,000 for my STEM extension) before I could work a single day. Today, the only OPT-related cost is a filing fee of roughly $500. Because students typically request OPT before graduation, often before receiving a job offer, the $70,000 would be owed before a student knows whether, or where, they will work. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass this cost on to “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers.” For most international students, that would put OPT out of reach; for employers, it would make an international graduate far more expensive to hire than an equally qualified domestic candidate, regardless of merit.

This is not abstract for me. I am recruiting for internships and full-time roles right now. From my first job search in college, I know how long and uncertain the process already is for international students, and today’s market is tighter than the one I entered four years ago. Employers who would gladly hire me on the strength of my experience may simply stop considering candidates who need OPT, turning a difficult search into a nearly impossible one for me and many classmates.

DHS states that the fee would ensure “only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate” and would reduce fraud. I respectfully argue that a flat fee can do neither. It does not measure qualification or detect fraud; it measures only who can pay. I was hired on my qualifications, yet under this rule I would have faced the same $100,000 barrier as anyone else. Meaningful safeguards already exist: during my STEM OPT extension, my employer and I completed a formal training plan, submitted periodic evaluations, and were subject to reporting requirements and possible site visits.

The rule would also weaken U.S. universities’ ability to recruit the world’s most talented students. For prospective international students, the chance to gain practical experience after graduation is a core part of the value of a U.S. degree. A fee of this magnitude signals that they are not welcome to stay, and many will choose countries with post-study work pathways instead, taking with them tuition revenue that sustains programs and financial aid. And because the cost could be passed on to “all students,” American students could end up paying for this rule as well.

The consequences reach the broader economy and fields that serve the public. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-2025 academic year. In healthcare, my own field, international graduates contribute to research and innovation that improve patient care and public health.

I chose the United States eight years ago because it offered a world-class education and a real chance to put it to work. That choice paid off in both directions: I built a career, and my employer, colleagues, and community gained someone committed to contributing. This rule would close that door to the next student ready to do the same, and to students like me trying to walk through it again.

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,
An international graduate student
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566, Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I am submitting this comment anonymously. I am a lawful permanent resident, yet I do not feel safe putting my name on it. I mention that because it matters to the record: many of the F-1 students this rule would affect have told me they’d like to comment but are afraid to do so. What DHS hears from them is probably much quieter than what they actually think.

Why this matters to me

I came to the United States in the late 1990s as an F-1 student. I picked a U.S. liberal arts education because it let me explore before committing to a path, which wasn’t an option where I grew up. OPT then let me spend three years working with children with special needs, in a field that couldn’t fill its jobs.

When I decided on graduate school, OPT was the deciding factor in choosing the U.S. I wanted a career in higher education administration, and I was counting on practical training to put my degree to work. A graduate degree without that wouldn’t have been worth the cost. CPT and OPT gave me the experience, and the professional network, that launched my career.

Today I am a designated school official at a large public university. I have spent two decades helping international students and scholars come here to study, do research, and contribute. That work depends on the same pathway that brought me here.

What our students are telling us

Our office recently surveyed our current F-1 students. About 600 responded, roughly 37 percent of those we reached. Around three-quarters are graduate students, and nearly three-quarters are in STEM fields.
77 percent said that if these fees had been in effect, they would not have chosen to study in the U.S.
98 percent said they would not be willing or able to pay.

This is a hypothetical, self-reported survey at one institution, so I offer it as one data point. But it comes from students who did choose the U.S. Those weighing several countries today may feel even more strongly. Many of the students who said the fees wouldn’t have changed their decision told us they would have looked at other countries first.

Below are select, lightly edited excerpts of their written feedback::

A doctoral student on a research stipend of about $25,000 a year put it plainly: “How can I possibly afford fees totaling $100,000?” Another wrote, “If I had $70,000, I would not have left my country.” A graduate student said, “Nobody who has access to the kind of money that is being asked for is in need of any kind of training.”

Others were thinking about the country’s loss. One PhD student in a highly specialized engineering field wrote that the fee “feels like getting taxed for having more skills than the rest.” Another said, “I would definitely go somewhere that appreciates my talent and hard work, because I will eventually contribute to the community and country where I live.” An undergraduate wrote, “With other developed nations having much better skilled working pathways I would never come here if this rule comes into play.”

Several also saw the effect on universities. One said the policy “limits the influx of international students,” which “reduces the vast amount of tuition that flows into schools.”

This isn’t just our campus

The national research points the same way. NAFSA’s comment letter summarizes much of it, so I’ll only touch on a few pieces:
Michael Clemens’s analysis (IZA Discussion Paper 18933) estimates that a $100,000 charge on OPT could cut OPT starts by roughly 80 percent in central scenarios where universities bear the cost.
The Institute for Progress projects large long-term GDP losses.
IIE’s Fall 2025 survey found that 92 percent of responding institutions expect many students would study elsewhere without OPT.
Hoover/Stanford research shows how heavily international graduates figure in U.S. STEM research and in founding leading AI firms.

These are projections, and projections carry uncertainty. But they all point in the same direction. The U.S. is competing for talent with countries offering clearer, more predictable paths after graduation, and fees this large would hand students to them.

What I’m asking

I respectfully ask the agency to:
Withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees.
Reconsider the financial barriers these fees would create for international students.
Carry out a real assessment of the effects on international enrollment, U.S. universities, employers, and the country’s ability to attract talent.
Weigh the long-term economic, scientific, and societal contributions of international graduates, rather than treating OPT only as an immigration benefit.
Handle any legitimate administrative or program costs through reasonable, proportionate fees, not charges that shut out qualified students.

Respectfully,

An international education professional and former international student
comments.reason: The commenter argues the rule harms F-1 students and draws on personal experience to oppose the proposed OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yatish Hosmane Revanasiddappa
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees, particularly their application to international students who have already invested substantial amounts in American higher education.

I personally paid approximately $100,000 in tuition to pursue my education in the United States. I made this investment with the reasonable expectation that I could apply for OPT to gain practical work experience and potentially recover some of my educational expenses.

Had I known that OPT could become subject to a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee, I would never have made this financial commitment.

My concerns are:

Unfairness to existing students: Students have already spent years and substantial amounts on tuition. They cannot reverse these investments because regulations change midway through their education.

Financial burden: DHS acknowledges that universities may pass these fees to students or employers. Even if universities pay directly, they may decline to recommend otherwise eligible students for OPT.

Inadequate transition period: The proposed 60-day transition does not adequately protect students who made financial commitments years earlier under a different regulatory framework.

Economic consequences: Restricting access to practical training could discourage future international enrollment, reduce university tuition revenue, and limit the contributions of international graduates to American research and innovation.

Disproportionate response to fraud: Legitimate students who comply with immigration requirements should not face extraordinary financial barriers because of misconduct by others. Targeted verification and enforcement would address fraud more directly.

How are students like me supposed to recover our $100,000 educational investments if the practical training opportunities we reasonably anticipated become financially inaccessible?

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider these fees and, at a minimum, exempt students who enrolled before the rule takes effect, including from subsequent OPT and STEM OPT fees.

International students made these investments in good faith. Changing the financial conditions after those investments have already been made is fundamentally unfair.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are an unfair financial burden and will harm international students and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I would like to present a case for grandfather arrangements for protecting current international students who have already made life changing decision to come study in the US based on an existing set of rules which are now proposed to be dramatically changed. Fraud and misuse of these should always be countered but the significant impact on current fee paying student who have been fully legally compliant and arrived in good faith and done nothing wrong should also be considered.
The United States has long been regarded as a beacon for talented students from around the world. Families make life-changing decisions based on that reputation. Students commit years of their lives and families commit substantial financial resources, often paying some of the highest university tuition fees in the world, in reliance on a reasonably stable educational and post-graduation framework. A critical part of that framework is the opportunity for practical training through CPT and OPT. These programmes are an integral component of the educational experience. Students choose the United States, rather than other leading destinations with the understanding that practical training opportunities form part of the value proposition of a U.S. education.

The U.S. Government has every right and responsibility to combat fraud, prevent abuse, and protect domestic workers and students. However, if significant new fees are imposed on colleges it will impact the international students, it would be fundamentally unfair to apply them immediately to students who are already enrolled and who made their educational decisions in good faith under a different set of expectations. These students cannot simply reverse those decisions. Many have already invested years of study, substantial financial resources, and forgone opportunities elsewhere.

Fraudulant schemes and dishonest arrangements should continue to be investigated and prosecuted, but the basis principles of innocent till proven guilty cannot be forgotten. The present arrangements penalises ALL students and universities.

It is important to distinguish between the overwhelming majority of legitimate students and the small minority who may seek to misuse the system. Where abuse occurs, it requires participation by institutions that fail to uphold appropriate standards or local bad actors.

In an age of advanced data analytics and artificial intelligence, bad actors can so easily be found without penalising the vast majority of genuine students and universities.

International students provide significant benefits to America. They contribute financially to universities and local communities. More importantly, many go on to become innovators, researchers, entrepreneurs, physicians, engineers, and business leaders whose contributions create jobs, advance technological progress, and strengthen the American economy. America's history demonstrates that talented immigrants and international graduates have often generated economic value far exceeding the direct revenues "lost" employment disguised as education schemes.

The issue is also about trust. Students currently studying in the United States accepted an implicit promise: that the fundamental framework under which they enrolled would not be materially altered without adequate notice or transitional protections. Preserving that trust is essential if the United States wishes to maintain its position as the world's leading destination for higher education and innovation. No grandfathering period imposes significant hardship on students and families who acted in good faith and relied upon the stability and predictability historically associated with American higher education.

The typical profile of an international student in an top American college is one of dedication, high levels of accomplishment and significant potential. They would have options in other parts of the world and scholarships in their own countries. Instead they chose a degree from America which carries a price tag of over USD 400K over 4 years plus all associated costs of visiting, travel etc. This is not small money and it is all contributing to the American economy. The significant additional fees proposed will end up being passed on to students, and will raise the actual cost of the education, because work experience is critical and intrinsic. There is no legally binding contract, but there is certainly a well understood mutual agreement for educational services between the students families and the american education system, which includes an existing set of rules for CPT and OPT, for approx USD 400K over the course of 4 year degree. 100K is suddenly being added to this vulnerable population with no recourse. At less expensive colleges the percentage of "extra charge" is even higher.

Please consider the principles of fairness and good-faith administration.

comments.commentText:
As an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI), I strongly oppose the proposed changes to Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT. This is my own opinion and does not represent my employer. Throughout my career, I have advised and mentored several international graduate students and postdoctoral researchers whose ability to remain in the United States through OPT and STEM OPT was critical to their professional development and to the success of the scientific projects on which they worked. These programs provide a vital bridge between advanced STEM education in the United States and participation in the American scientific workforce. The proposed fees would effectively eliminate that bridge for many institutions and students.

In astronomy and astrophysics, scientific progress depends on attracting exceptional talent from around the world. Major research facilities, including space missions, observatories, and national laboratories, rely on highly trained scientists regardless of country of origin. International students who earn degrees in the United States have already demonstrated their commitment to this country by investing years of study and research at American institutions. Many of the students I have advised made substantial contributions to U.S.-funded research programs during their OPT or STEM OPT periods. Had these pathways not existed, the United States would have lost talented researchers at the very moment when they were prepared to make their greatest contributions.

The proposed rule would also place an extraordinary financial burden on universities by requiring payment of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and an additional $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions. For most universities and research organizations, these costs are simply untenable and would inevitably reduce opportunities for international students regardless of their qualifications or potential. Rather than protecting U.S. competitiveness, the proposal would encourage highly skilled graduates to pursue careers in other countries, taking with them expertise in fields that are strategically important to the United States.

The United States has long been the world's premier destination for scientific training because it combines excellent educational opportunities with pathways that allow talented graduates to contribute to the nation's research enterprise. OPT and STEM OPT are an essential part of that system. Weakening these programs would damage U.S. leadership in science, reduce the return on federal investments in research and education, and diminish the talent pool available to American universities, laboratories, and technology companies. For these reasons, I urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

comments.commentText:
As an international student getting closer to graduation, I find it frustrating that OPT could become even more expensive. Studying in the United States is already a major investment, and many international students, including myself, have spent years working hard, paying tuition, and making sacrifices to build a better future.

What bothers me the most is that we put so much time and money into earning a degree, but when it’s finally time to use what we’ve learned, there are even more obstacles in our way. Finding employment is already challenging because of the restrictions international students face. Making OPT more expensive would only add to that stress.

I also think people sometimes overlook how much international students bring to the United States. We come from different countries with different experiences, ideas, and skills. We spend money on education, housing, food, and other expenses while studying here. When we graduate and enter the workforce through OPT, we also have the opportunity to support American businesses, contribute our skills, and help the U.S. economy grow. I believe this benefits both international students and the country as a whole.

Personally, I don’t think it’s right to encourage students from around the world to pursue an American education and then make it increasingly difficult for them to gain experience afterward. We aren’t asking for guaranteed jobs or special treatment. We just want a fair opportunity to put our education to use.

I hope DHS takes these concerns seriously and considers the financial and personal impact that additional OPT fees could have on students who have already invested so much in their future.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that making OPT more expensive adds unfair financial stress and obstacles for international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566)

I urge this administration to enact the proposed fees immediately. I've read a lot of the public comments here from academia–all in opposition to the OPT fees. A common argument they make is that these fees will hinder their ability to attract the “world’s greatest talents”. They claim America needs these international students to stay competitive, and that US students don’t have the skills.

Wow. What an indictment of their own institutions.

These comments from academia are a public and shameless proclamation of THEIR OWN FAILURE to educate US students with the skills necessary for employment–and that failure is actually used to justify the need to import international students. I suggest these letters be posted on their admissions website as a black box warning to US students: “We’ll take your money and four years, but you won’t leave our university with any employable skills–even we don’t think so.”

Every one of these universities fighting against OPT fees should answer some questions:
--Where were these “world’s best” talents taught? Was it here in the US? And if so, why didn’t the program produce an equally talented US student? Are they suggesting that US students are intellectually deficient when compared to foreign students?
--If, instead, there are foreign universities creating these “world’s best” students, why aren’t US citizens clamoring to go? And why would these foreign students even want to study in America? Clearly, they got a much better, and less expensive, education in their own country.
--Finally, and just as importantly, if these are incredible, rare, unbelievable, unicorn talents, then why would they even need an OPT arrangement? Let them compete with US students for jobs–and if their skills are so far advanced, I’m sure companies would be happy to arrange for OPT and pay the fees.

I’d love academia to put some action behind their words. They’re so convinced that foreign schools are providing the skilled workers we need–they should admit defeat, stop taking taxpayer funds, and shut down. I suggest they go overseas to figure out what magical pedagogy is happening and bring some of that secret sauce back to the US. By their own admission, American universities can attract the world’s best, but can’t produce them.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation.

I am an international PhD student in Geosciences, approaching the completion of my doctoral degree. Over the past several years, I have dedicated myself to scientific research in the United States. My research has involved collaborations with scientists at multiple U.S. universities and has contributed to our understanding of the physical processes shaping the Earth, such as earthquakes.

As I approach graduation, I am actively seeking postdoctoral research opportunities at U.S. universities and research institutions. My goal is to continue contributing to American scientific research, building on the expertise and collaborations I have developed during my doctoral training. OPT provides an essential pathway for international graduates like me to transition from doctoral studies to research careers.

The proposed fees would create an almost insurmountable financial barrier to this transition. Unlike positions in some high-paying industries, academic postdoctoral appointments are typically supported by limited research grants and institutional funding. Neither individual researchers nor many academic institutions could reasonably afford an additional $70,000 simply to enable a recent PhD graduate to begin working. As a result, qualified international researchers could lose opportunities to continue their work in the United States, regardless of their scientific contributions or the willingness of American institutions to employ them.

I am particularly concerned about the broader consequences for U.S. scientific competitiveness. American universities invest substantial resources in training international doctoral students, who contribute to research, publications, teaching, and scientific innovation throughout their studies. If these graduates are effectively prevented from continuing their careers in the United States, the country risks losing highly trained researchers just as they are beginning to make independent scientific contributions. This would undermine the return on years of investment in graduate education and weaken the research communities that depend on international collaboration and specialized expertise.

For me personally, this proposal creates significant uncertainty about my future. After years of doctoral training in the United States, I hope to continue my academic career here and contribute to the scientific community that has supported my development. It is deeply discouraging to face the possibility that my career opportunities may be determined not by my research qualifications or scientific potential, but by an extraordinary financial barrier beyond my ability to overcome.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed fees and preserve an accessible OPT pathway for international graduates. Maintaining this pathway is important not only for students like me, but also for the universities, research institutions, and broader scientific enterprise that benefit from their contributions.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment in Support of the Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (Focus on Fraud and Domestic STEM Unemployment)
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to submit this formal comment in strong support of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish new fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. The proposed framework—requiring a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent extensions—is a critical, market-stabilizing measure needed to curb pervasive visa fraud, eliminate systemic displacement of domestic graduates, and protect American entry-level tech workers.
The critical need for this fee structure is demonstrated by the severe economic challenges facing American tech graduates alongside documented systemic issues within the program:
• Addressing High Unemployment Among Domestic STEM Graduates: While tech corporations frequently cite a lack of domestic talent, recent data reveals a stark contraction in entry-level hiring that has disproportionately harmed U.S. citizens. While the general national unemployment average is low, recent college graduates in computer science and computer engineering face an unemployment rate hovering around 7% to 8%. Flooding this already compressed labor market with hundreds of thousands of uncapped OPT guest-workers actively deprives qualified American graduates of the entry-level roles required to build their careers.
• Combatting Pervasive "Pay-to-Stay" and Shell Company Fraud: This proposed fee acts as a necessary firewall against the rampant fraud degrading the integrity of the F-1 visa system. In May 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and HSI exposed over 10,000 potential OPT fraud cases. Federal audits revealed extensive networks of fraudulent IT staffing agencies, vacant offices, residential "phantom addresses," and "pay-to-play" schemes where foreign nationals paid under-the-table fees to shell corporations simply to maintain visa status without performing legitimate work. By forcing a significant financial commitment up front, the proposed rule effectively dismantles the economic model underpinning these fraudulent networks.
• Preventing the Disenfranchisement of U.S. Citizens via Foreign Outsourcing: Recent DHS site visits confirmed that multiple alleged OPT employers were utilizing U.S. corporate addresses as a front while training and managing their OPT workers entirely via managers located overseas in places like India. This practice completely subverts the educational purpose of "practical training" within the domestic economy, effectively converting a student visa program into an unregulated offshore outsourcing pipeline that operates on American soil.
• Removing Arbitrary Cost Advantages and Corporate Incentives: Under current tax codes, employers are entirely exempt from paying the 7.65% FICA (Social Security and Medicare) payroll taxes on OPT workers. In fields like software engineering and computer science, this loophole makes hiring a foreign graduate thousands of dollars cheaper than hiring an American citizen graduate. The $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure properly offsets this financial distortion, neutralizing the systemic economic incentive for tech corporations to bypass domestic talent.
The OPT program has evolved far beyond a temporary training benefit into an institutionalized, cap-exempt labor system plagued by systemic exploitation. This proposed rule restores balance, encourages schools to stringently vet their corporate partnerships, and protects domestic grads during an incredibly difficult entry-level tech market.
Sincerely,
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong support for the proposed rule to establish new OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment in Support of the Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (Focus on Fraud, Healthcare, and STEM Workforce Impact)
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to submit this formal comment in strong support of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish new fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. The proposed framework—requiring a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent extensions—is a critical, market-stabilizing measure needed to curb pervasive visa fraud, eliminate systemic displacement of domestic graduates, and protect American workers across highly specialized fields, including software engineering and healthcare.
While public attention frequently focuses on tech labor distortions, the current uncapped OPT framework has increasingly expanded into the medical and clinical sectors, introducing severe regulatory vulnerabilities and unfair competition that harm American medical graduates:
• Addressing Fraudulent Clinical Placement and "Ghost Residency" Schemes: The healthcare and medical research fields have seen a rise in regulatory exploitation mirroring the IT staffing fraud exposed by federal agencies. Unaccredited clinical research firms, fraudulent medical staffing agencies, and shell consulting companies have manipulated the OPT framework to orchestrate "pay-to-stay" schemes for foreign medical graduates (FMGs). In these arrangements, individuals pay under-the-table fees to shell corporations for fraudulent employment letters and falsified clinical hours to maintain immigration status. Requiring a significant upfront fee will effectively eliminate these illicit corporate actors by rendering fraudulent visa-brokering economically unviable.
• Protecting U.S. Medical Graduates from Structural Displacement: The traditional paths for foreign medical training in the U.S. (such as J-1 or H-1B clinical visas) are strictly regulated, requiring rigorous credential verification, ECMFG certification, and adherence to prevailing wage standards. In contrast, the expansion of OPT and STEM OPT in medical research, clinical laboratory, and healthcare administrative roles allows foreign graduates to bypass these standard vetting processes. This influx compresses employment opportunities for U.S. citizen medical students, pre-med graduates, and couples with a 7% to 8% unemployment rate facing recent domestic tech and STEM graduates who compete for essential clinical and technical research roles.
• Eliminating the Unfair Corporate Financial Incentive Over U.S. Doctors and Researchers: Under current tax codes, healthcare employers and private research facilities are entirely exempt from paying the 7.65% FICA (Social Security and Medicare) payroll taxes on OPT workers. This regulatory loophole provides medical groups, laboratories, and corporate healthcare chains an automatic financial incentive to hire foreign graduates over equally qualified U.S. citizen medical graduates. The proposed fee framework properly offsets this distortion, removing the financial benefit of bypassing domestic talent.
• Restoring Integrity to Medical Training Safeguards: Medicine requires the highest level of institutional oversight to protect patient safety and labor standards. Allowing a student visa program to operate as an unregulated, cap-exempt secondary guest-worker pipeline in medical and technical fields undermines the specialized visa pathways established by Congress.
The OPT program has evolved into an institutionalized labor system vulnerable to exploitation. This proposed rule restores structural balance, requires educational institutions to strictly vet their healthcare and technical partnerships, and ensures that the domestic workforce is not structurally disadvantaged.
Sincerely,

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposed rule, “Optional Practical Training Fees” (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), and urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The charge is a tax that Congress has not authorized. DHS projects $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year in collections, to be deposited in the general Treasury, not used for OPT oversight. DHS says it set the amount to “closely align with the H-1B fees,” not to recover any cost. A federal court has already held the $100,000 H-1B payment to be an unauthorized tax (State of California v. Mullin, D. Mass. June 8, 2026), and the Supreme Court confirmed this year that the power to regulate does not include the power to tax (Learning Resources v. Trump, 2026). None of the statutes DHS cites authorizes a revenue charge on schools. DHS should explain which statute does, and why it did not use the cost-based fee authorities Congress provided (8 U.S.C. 1356(m), 1372(e); 31 U.S.C. 9701).

2. A flat charge does not prevent fraud. Every school pays the same amount for every student, whether compliant or not. The fraud DHS describes involves employers, yet a school must pay before a student may even have a job offer, so it cannot screen an employer that does not yet exist. No revenue funds investigators or site visits. DHS also contradicts itself: it says the charge is meant to “discourage” OPT use, but its revenue estimate assumes STEM OPT participation will not decline at all.

3. The rule ignores the reliance of students already enrolled. The fee applies to any recommendation made after the effective date, so students who enrolled under current rules would be fully subject to it. I am an international graduate student in computer science at a U.S. public university, expected to graduate in 2027, so any OPT recommendation for me would fall after this rule’s effective date. I chose to study here with the understanding that practical training was part of the educational path the regulations offer, and I have planned my coursework, finances and future around that understanding. Practical training is where what I learn in the classroom is tested against real problems, and I have already seen how much it adds to an education that coursework alone cannot provide. Nothing about my eligibility or my conduct would change under this rule; what would change is whether my university decides that I am worth $70,000. I do not believe that is a fair or rational way to decide who may complete their education. DHS calls these expectations “speculative.” They are not.

4. Better alternatives exist, and 30 days is not enough. DHS could extend STEM OPT safeguards (E-Verify, training plans, site visits) to all OPT, target the employers its own investigations flagged, or set a cost-based fee to fund oversight. It rejected these in conclusory terms. A 30-day comment period for an economically significant rule that was not on DHS’s regulatory agenda falls short of the 60 days Executive Order 13563 calls for. DHS should withdraw the rule, or at minimum reopen comment for 60 days and publish the data behind its fraud claims.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it due to unauthorized taxation and flawed logic.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strongest opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorization.

I am deeply concerned about the devastating consequences this proposal could have for international students, American universities, scientific research, and the future competitiveness of the United States.

First, these extraordinarily high fees would create an overwhelming financial barrier to legitimate employment opportunities for international students. International students already make substantial financial and personal sacrifices to pursue their education in the United States. Many spend years contributing to American universities through research, teaching, and academic service. Requiring tens of thousands of dollars for access to practical training would effectively place these opportunities beyond the reach of many qualified graduates, regardless of their academic achievements, professional abilities, or potential contributions to society.

Second, the proposal threatens the United States' ability to attract and retain highly trained researchers and professionals. International graduate students play important roles in American scientific research, particularly in biomedical sciences, engineering, and technology. Many spend five or more years developing specialized expertise, contributing to federally funded research, publishing scientific discoveries, and training future generations of researchers. OPT provides a crucial opportunity to apply this expertise after graduation. Creating such substantial financial barriers would risk driving highly trained individuals away from the United States precisely when they are prepared to contribute their skills to its research institutions and workforce.

Third, the proposal undermines the purpose of practical training as an essential component of international education. OPT and Curricular Practical Training (CPT) provide legitimate pathways for international students to gain practical experience related to their academic studies. These opportunities should remain accessible based on educational qualifications and compliance with existing regulations, rather than an individual's financial resources. Although this particular proposal concerns OPT fees, I urge DHS to preserve meaningful access to both OPT and CPT.

Finally, this proposal would create significant uncertainty for international students who have already committed years of their lives to studying and conducting research in the United States. Students make educational and career decisions based on the reasonable expectation that established practical-training opportunities will remain meaningfully accessible. Abruptly introducing such substantial financial barriers would disrupt career planning, undermine confidence in the U.S. higher education system, and discourage future international students from choosing American institutions.

International students are not merely temporary visitors to American universities. We are researchers, educators, colleagues, and contributors to the scientific and intellectual communities in which we study. Our contributions should not be overlooked, and our opportunities should not be determined by our ability to overcome extraordinary financial barriers.

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed OPT fee increases and preserve fair, accessible, and practical opportunities for international students to gain professional experience in the United States.

Thank you for considering my comment.

After graduation, OPT and STEM OPT provide an important opportunity to apply the knowledge and skills we gained through our academic programs in real-world professional environments.

The proposed fees could make universities reluctant to recommend international students for OPT because of the enormous financial burden. Even though the fees would initially be paid by educational institutions, the proposed rule acknowledges that universities may transfer these costs to students or employers. This could make employers less willing to hire international graduates and could make universities less willing to support their practical training opportunities.

This is particularly concerning for STEM graduates. The 24-month STEM OPT extension is an important opportunity for students to gain additional professional experience, contribute to research and innovation, and develop specialized skills. An additional $30,000 fee for a STEM OPT extension could discourage universities and employers from supporting qualified graduates, regardless of their academic performance, qualifications, or professional potential.

I also believe this proposal could negatively affect the competitiveness of American universities. International students choose the United States because of its world-class education system, research opportunities, and professional development opportunities. Excessive financial barriers after graduation could discourage talented students from choosing American universities in the future. I understand the government's responsibility to prevent fraud, protect U.S. workers, and maintain the integrity of the immigration system. However, these objectives should be achieved through effective monitoring, compliance requirements, employer oversight, and targeted enforcement rather than extremely high fees that could affect legitimate international students.

I respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security reconsider and withdraw this proposed fee structure. If additional fees are considered necessary, they should be reasonable, proportionate to actual administrative costs, and structured so that they do not prevent qualified students from accessing legitimate practical training opportunities.

I also strongly encourage DHS to protect students who are already enrolled in U.S. universities, have completed their degrees, or are currently participating in OPT or STEM OPT from unexpected financial burdens resulting from new regulations.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
it exceeds DHS's fee authority; and it cannot achieve its stated anti-fraud goal.

1. A price cannot separate abuse from legitimate participation. The fee is charged identically for every student, whether the student works for a shell employer or is a lawful STEM graduate whose U.S. employer depends on their skills. It screens by wealth, not by compliance or merit. A fraudulent operation can price in the cost or route around it, while a talented student from a modest background is shut out. Fraud is specific conduct and calls for targeted tools: employer verification, E-Verify, I-983 training plans, site visits, and SEVIS reporting. DHS considered extending these STEM OPT safeguards to initial OPT and rejected them only as insufficient "as an initial response." Discarding the targeted alternative for a blanket charge on everyone is not reasoned decisionmaking.

2. The fee is untethered from its stated purpose. DHS cites fraud but identifies no fraud data supporting the amounts, and the revenue would not fund fraud detection. The amount was set to be "comparable to the H-1B fee," not derived from any cost or risk analysis. DHS also states that a main purpose is to "discourage aliens from using the OPT program" and calls the fee "an immediate first step in a graduated strategy." A fee meant to suppress a program DHS concedes is lawful, rather than to recover the cost of a service, is a policy change disguised as a fee.

3. DHS lacks authority to impose a deterrent charge of this size. Agency user fees, under the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (31 U.S.C. 9701) and DHS's immigration fee statutes, must be tied to the government's costs or the value of a specific service. Under National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), a charge exceeding those bounds is a tax, and only Congress may tax. Revenue estimated at $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year, flowing to the general Treasury for a DSO recommendation and SEVIS entry, cannot plausibly reflect cost. Courts have already blocked the comparable $100,000 H-1B fee on this basis.

4. The economic analysis is inadequate. DHS estimates costs anywhere from $32 million to over $8 billion a year. A range that wide is not an estimate. DHS also sets aside effects on universities and U.S. competitiveness as too speculative, even though it acknowledges schools may pass costs to American students through higher tuition or stop supporting OPT. Failing to analyze the rule's main consequences is arbitrary and capricious under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

5. Small entities and procedure. DHS reports that more than 56% of SEVP-certified schools may be small entities, triggering a real Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis of less burdensome alternatives. A rule of this economic magnitude also warrants at least the 60-day comment period recommended under Executive Order 12866, not 30 days.

6. Harm to the United States. Roughly 194,000 OPT and 95,000 STEM OPT participants were active in 2024. They fill hard-to-staff STEM roles, pay payroll taxes, and form the pipeline for future U.S. innovators and founders. International tuition subsidizes domestic students and sustains graduate programs. Research projects that a $100,000 STEM OPT cost would cut international graduate applications by about 35%. That talent would go to competitor countries, not to American workers.

[Optional: one or two sentences on your own experience, e.g., how OPT led to your current U.S. role and what you contribute.]

DHS should withdraw the rule. If it proceeds, it should (1) identify statutory authority for a non-cost-based fee; (2) document the fraud it seeks to address and show how the fee targets it; (3) adopt targeted compliance measures instead of a blanket charge; (4) quantify effects on universities, employers, and domestic students; and (5) reopen comment for at least 60 days.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee exceeds DHS authority, is untethered from its stated purpose, and harms students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a United States citizen, I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to establish a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT recommendation.

This rule is a necessary step to protect American workers, reduce fraud, and restore integrity to a program that has grown far beyond its original purpose.
Documented Fraud Requires Strong Action
In May 2026, ICE reported identifying more than 10,000 F-1 students linked to highly suspect employers—many involving phantom worksites, empty buildings, residential addresses listed as job sites, “pay-to-stay” schemes, and offshore management of purported U.S. training. These findings came from a review of only the top 25 OPT employers and were described by ICE officials as “only the tip of the iceberg.”
Earlier investigations have uncovered similar patterns, including shell companies and large-scale visa fraud operations involving thousands of students. The Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman has previously warned that the OPT program is especially vulnerable to fraud because compliance resources have not kept pace with its rapid expansion.
A substantial fee paid by the recommending school will create a real financial incentive for Designated School Officials to verify the legitimacy of proposed training before recommending students. Without such a cost, the current system continues to enable abuse.

OPT Has Become a Large-Scale Labor Pipeline

According to ICE’s 2024 SEVP data, nearly 195,000 foreign students held OPT work authorization and over 95,000 held STEM OPT authorization in a single year. The total number of foreign students with practical training authorization has grown into the hundreds of thousands. What began as a limited educational benefit has become a significant source of temporary foreign labor, particularly in STEM and IT fields, often competing directly with recent American graduates for entry-level positions.
When employers can access this labor at relatively low cost—or through third-party arrangements—the result is reduced opportunities and downward pressure on wages for U.S. citizens and permanent residents. The proposed fees help restore balance by ensuring that the privilege of multi-year work authorization carries a meaningful cost that reflects its impact on the domestic labor market.

The Fee Structure Is Sound

Charging the fee to the SEVP-certified school at the recommendation stage is administratively efficient and places responsibility on the institution best positioned to assess the legitimacy of the training. Depositing the fees into the U.S. Treasury is appropriate for a measure designed to protect program integrity and American workers.

The proposed effective date and grandfathering provisions provide a reasonable transition while preventing a rush of last-minute recommendations intended to circumvent the new requirements.
Conclusion

As a U.S. citizen, I believe American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been repeatedly exploited through fraud and that functions as a low-cost alternative to properly regulated employment visas. The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees are a proportionate and necessary response.

I urge DHS to finalize this rule promptly and without reducing the fee amounts or weakening the requirement that payment precede any SEVIS recommendation for OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly supports the proposed OPT fees to protect American workers and reduce fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to Bureau’s proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees," published on October 8, 2026.

I submit these comments from a critical and deeply personal perspective: I am a high-skilled legal immigrant working in the United States on an H-1B visa. I have paid taxes, contributed to American innovation, and raised my family here. Currently, I have one child attending an American university and another who has recently "aged out" of dependent status. While this rule is framed as a regulatory adjustment for educational institutions, its real-world impact is a devastating financial and humanitarian blow to lawful, high-skilled immigrant families who have followed every rule to contribute to this country.

I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal based on the following severe consequences:

1. Critical Threat to "Aged-Out" Children and Family Unity
Children of long-term H-1B visa holders who grow up in the United States face a precarious future when they turn 21 and "age out" of their dependent H-4 status. For these young adults, transitioning to an F-1 student visa and subsequently utilizing the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program is the primary legal pathway to maintain status, remain with their families, and enter the workforce in the only country they call home. By levying an astronomical $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for extensions, this rule effectively destroys the only viable survival pipeline for aged-out children. It forces unnecessary separation of legal immigrant families, punishing children who have grown up as part of the American fabric.

2. Extreme Financial Duress on Immigrant Households
Universities will be forced to pass these massive new institutional OPT fees directly down to students, this rule creates an insurmountable financial penalty. For a family already managing the high costs of higher education, an unexpected $70,000 to $100,000 surcharge just for a child to gain post-graduation practical training is a financial impossibility.

3. Destruction of the Career Entry Pipeline for the Next Generation
My child currently in college deserves a predictable, fair, and merit-based landscape upon graduation. If universities are forced to restrict OPT recommendations, or if the financial barriers prevent students from applying, the entry-level career pipeline for foreign-born graduates will effectively die. Legitimate students who have worked hard in American classrooms will be barred from gaining the practical experience required to launch their careers, leaving them stranded despite their family's legal status and immense financial investment in American higher education.

4. Misaligned Enforcement and Economic Harm
While the agency’s stated goal is to enhance oversight and curb fraud, punishing compliant, world-class American universities and lawful student applicants is an arbitrary mechanism. It does nothing to target actual bad actors. Instead, by crippling the STEM OPT pipeline, the rule will starve the very American industries—such as technology, engineering, and healthcare—that rely on high-skilled talent. This harms the long-term economic stability of the companies that sponsor legal workers, ultimately damaging the broader American economy.

Conclusion
This proposed rule introduces unprecedented, disproportionate financial barriers that target the most vulnerable segment of the legal immigration community: the children of high-skilled workers. It forces family separation and imposes impossible financial burdens on families who have acted entirely in good faith. I respectfully urge to withdraw this harmful proposal in its entirety.
Thank you for your time and consideration of these comments.

Sincerely,
A parent of aged out and aging out children.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are devastating and urges the agency to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international PhD student studying Computer Science at a U.S. research university, and I am submitting this comment to express concern about the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT), particularly their implications for doctoral graduates pursuing postdoctoral research. I recognize the interest in preventing fraud and maintaining the integrity of the OPT program. However, I believe the proposed fee structure would impose substantial costs on legitimate scientific training, while more targeted enforcement measures could address the stated concerns.

Postdoctoral research is an important stage of scientific training. For many PhD graduates pursuing careers as independent researchers, faculty members, or laboratory leaders, a postdoctoral appointment provides an opportunity to develop research independence, deepen technical expertise, and gain experience directing scientific projects. Appointments lasting one to three years can be particularly valuable for researchers continuing training in their doctoral field or a closely related area. This period often forms an important part of the transition from doctoral training to an independent scientific career.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create a substantial financial barrier to this training pathway. Although these fees would formally be paid by educational institutions, their consequences would extend to researchers seeking OPT authorization. Universities and research laboratories operate within limited budgets, and postdoctoral appointments are frequently supported by research grants. Institutions may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial additional costs. If any portion is passed on to graduates, the burden would be especially severe for scientists who have only recently completed years of stipend-supported doctoral training. Access to postdoctoral opportunities could consequently become dependent on financial resources rather than research qualifications.

Furthermore, the proposed fees could affect the ability of U.S. research institutions to attract and retain scientific talent. The opportunity to pursue doctoral education and continue professional development through postdoctoral research contributes to the international appeal of American universities. International doctoral students contribute to university laboratories, federally funded research projects, scientific publications, and the training of other researchers. Restricting their ability to continue this training after graduation could reduce the return on years of research training already undertaken at U.S. institutions. These consequences deserve consideration when evaluating the proposal's broader costs to the American research ecosystem.

Fraud and abuse within practical training programs warrant appropriate oversight. However, substantial fees applied broadly to institutions recommending students for OPT do not directly establish whether a training opportunity is legitimate. They may instead discourage institutions from supporting qualified graduates regardless of the legitimacy of their proposed employment.

I encourage DHS to consider targeted fraud prevention measures, including stronger verification of employers and training arrangements, risk-based audits of institutions or employers exhibiting indicators of noncompliance, and meaningful penalties for documented misrepresentation. Existing reporting mechanisms could also be strengthened to verify that authorized employment remains directly related to a graduate's field of study. These measures would direct enforcement resources toward potentially fraudulent activity while preserving access to legitimate training opportunities.

I also encourage DHS to assess the proposed fees specifically in the context of postdoctoral appointments and university-based research employment, accounting for academic research funding structures and the financial circumstances of recent doctoral graduates.

My concerns arise from my experience as an international doctoral student preparing for a career in scientific research as a university faculty in my country. While I cannot quantify the nationwide economic effects of the proposal, I can speak to the importance of postdoctoral training and the financial constraints faced by researchers at this stage of their careers. Particularly, post doctoral training available at US universities through short term research positions does not exist in universities in many countries or isn't on par in strength, which makes a graduate degree in the US extremely appealing to future scholars around the globe, particularly in STEM fields.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure and pursue more targeted measures to address fraud and noncompliance. Preserving accessible pathways for legitimate scientific training would support the development of early-career researchers and the continued strength of the U.S. research ecosystem.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create a substantial financial barrier to legitimate scientific training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 – Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an international graduate of a U.S. STEM-designated degree program, currently on post-completion OPT and working full time in a professional role. I respectfully submit the following concerns and ask DHS to address them before issuing any final rule.

1.The rule needs a transition provision for students already on OPT who will seek the STEM extension (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)).

As proposed, a student whose initial OPT was recommended and approved before the effective date would owe the full $70,000 "initial" fee if the STEM OPT extension is recommended on or after the effective date, because no initial fee was previously paid. This treats the continuation of an existing, approved training period as a new entry into the program.

Many students chose STEM-designated programs, accepted employment, and made long-term personal and financial commitments in reliance on the existing 24-month STEM extension. Employers likewise invested in training plans and E-Verify participation. These reliance interests deserve careful consideration. I ask DHS to:
(a) exempt STEM OPT extensions for students whose initial post-completion OPT was recommended before the effective date; or
(b) at a minimum, apply no more than the $30,000 "subsequent" fee to these students; and
(c) apply any new fee only to students who begin a degree program after the final rule is published, so they can make informed decisions before enrolling.

2.The fee does not appear to be tied to the cost of administering OPT.

The proposal indicates the fee is intended to reduce participation, and that revenue would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts rather than supporting program oversight. DHS should explain the legal basis for a fee of this size that is not based on the cost of the service provided.

3.The burden would fall disproportionately on small employers.

DHS should explain why targeted enforcement, improved employer verification, and stronger compliance monitoring would be insufficient or less effective. Legitimate students should not face prohibitive financial barriers because of misconduct by unrelated parties.

Third, the proposed rule could undermine the competitiveness of American higher education and the U.S. economy. Many international students choose American universities partly because of the opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation. The proposed fees would introduce substantial uncertainty into educational and career decisions, potentially discouraging talented students from studying in the United States. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees. This comment applies the Information Quality Act (section 515 of Pub. L. 106-554) and OMB's information quality guidelines (67 FR 8452, Feb. 22, 2002) to the evidence DHS disseminates in the NPRM. This one asks a prior question: can the public verify the evidence at all?

1. This is influential information
OMB's guidelines set a higher bar for "influential" information, meaning information with a clear and substantial impact on important public policy. That bar includes transparency about data and methods, so that qualified outsiders could reproduce the results. The NPRM projects 10-year transfers of $109.4 billion (primary, 3 percent). DHS says that without the fees it "may shut down the program entirely." The evidence behind that choice is influential by any reading.

2. The central fraud finding rests on a video
The headline finding is that an investigation "identified more than 10,000 F-1 nonimmigrant students" working for "highly suspect employers." Its only source is an ICE YouTube video of May 12, 2026 (footnote 67). Every listed key finding is cited to that video by timestamp (footnotes 68 to 74). The docket has no report, dataset or method behind it. DHS does not say how "highly suspect" was defined, what period was covered, how many cases were confirmed, or how many employers were cleared. Footnote 56 describes the same video as showing "10,000 highly suspected employers." A reader cannot tell whether the figure counts students or employers.

3. DHS relies on a news count of data ICE withheld
The figure of nearly 4,000 students at potential shell companies comes from a 2021 NBC Bay Area story (footnotes 64 and 65). That story's own title, as DHS cites it, says "ICE Keeping New Data Private." DHS holds SEVIS employer records. It could report how many OPT participants worked for employers later found noncompliant. It cites a reporter's estimate instead.

4. Labor-market figures are second-hand
The unemployment rates for computer science graduates, the growth in foreign STEM workers, and the foreign share of computer occupations all cite Presidential Proclamation 10973 (footnotes 91 to 93). Footnote 94, for the claim that STEM OPT "far surpassed" DHS's 2016 estimate, is also "Id." to that proclamation. The NPRM does not name the surveys, years or definitions behind these numbers. A proclamation restating figures is not a data source that outsiders can test.

5. Key inputs cannot be reproduced from the docket
Table 2, which drives every cost scenario, appears only as an image. Footnote 128 sources it to an ICE file titled "Total Number of Annual OPT, STEM OPT and CPT Authorizations." The NPRM does not say whether or how CPT was removed. The 56 percent STEM share is "Based on 2021-2024 data," but footnote 129 applies 56.11 percent to a 2022-2024 average, and neither calculation is shown. The small-entity tables use revenue from schools' I-17 filings in SEVIS, which the public cannot see. The NPRM does not say whether any of these inputs or models were peer reviewed, as OMB's Peer Review Bulletin (70 FR 2664, Jan. 14, 2005) contemplates for influential scientific information.

6. Undisclosed data also fails the APA
An agency must disclose the critical data it relies on so the public can respond. Portland Cement Ass'n v. Ruckelshaus, 486 F.2d 375 (D.C. Cir. 1973). In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), the court preliminarily postponed the companion Duration of Status rule. It found DHS likely acted arbitrarily, noting that on fraud the government "relies to a large extent on anecdotes." This NPRM repeats the pattern with less: some of its anecdotes are timestamps in a video.

7. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposal. If it re-proposes, it should first place in the docket:
(a) the HSI investigation's report or data, with its definition of "highly suspect," time period, counts of students and employers, and counts of confirmed violations, referrals and outcomes;
(b) the SEVIS extracts and code behind Table 2, the 56 percent STEM share and the small-entity tables, in machine-readable form;
(c) the primary sources for every labor-market figure now cited to the proclamation; and
(d) a statement of any peer review performed.
It should then reopen comment for at least 60 days. A $109.4 billion rule should rest on evidence the public can read.

I respectfully oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

I am a Master's student in machine learning. Through practical training, I have worked on applying ML to oilfield equipment operations. This work was conducted alongside and in support of U.S. colleagues, and it directly complemented my coursework in a way classroom instruction cannot.

1. The fee is not tailored to the fraud it claims to address.

proposal does not explain why enhancing those tools would be insufficient. DHS has not adequately analyzed less burdensome alternatives.

2. The fee amounts lack a reasoned basis, and the revenue is not tied to oversight.
The proposed fees bear no apparent relationship to the cost of administering or policing OPT. The rule projects $8.4–16.5 billion in annual collections deposited into the general Treasury rather than used for program integrity. A charge of this size, untethered to service costs, functions as a tax, and I urge DHS to explain the statutory authority for imposing it under INA 214(a).

3. The rule would create a two-tier system based on wealth, not merit.
Equally qualified students would be separated by whether they, their families, or their employers can absorb a $70,000–$100,000 charge. Smaller employers and startups — which often cannot pay such sums — would be effectively excluded from hiring international graduates, while only the largest firms could participate.

They cannot, and will not, simply substitute for scholars specializing in international politics and economics. International scholars come to the United States precisely because they are interested in studying and teaching these subjects. Without them, these subfields would become substantially weaker, and universities would struggle to meet the extremely high undergraduate demand for courses on international affairs, trade, and global politics. For example- last year, approximately 150 undergraduates took the course "Intro to International Politics" and more than 300 undergraduates and professional school students took the course on the rise of China. These are American students from all sorts of different majors (including STEM) and professions.

This is not simply about protecting employment opportunities for international graduates. It is about preserving academic fields that American students need and increasingly seek out, particularly as they prepare for careers in government, business, and public policy.

Making post-graduation employment prohibitively expensive would discourage future international scholars from studying in the United States, weakening the very academic programs that educate American students.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee provisions. International scholars do not merely compete for American jobs. They sustain fields of expertise that American universities and students depend on. They help preserve what makes American higher education exceptional - its ability to attract the best minds from around the world, maintain the highest standards of teaching and research, and meet the growing demand for specialized knowledge among American students.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they undermine recruitment and weaken higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jeremie Koenig
comments.commentText:
I write to express my opposition to DHS proposed rule change no ICEB-2026-0100. The proposed restrictions on Optional Practical Training (OPT) would place unnecessary burden on graduating international students and would hurt American competitiveness.

I am an Associate Research Scientist at Yale University, where I work on foundational technologies for software reliability and cybersecurity. I came to the United States from France in 2012 as an F-1 graduate student. After I obtained my PhD, using OPT was a key transitional step that not only allowed me to start applying my skills as an independent researcher, but also allowed me time to secure a more durable position and status. The proposed fee would have likely made this process much more onerous and uncertain, and prevented or dissuaded me from continuing to contribute to U.S. research.

For many decades, the U.S. has been able to attract research talent from around the world. This has been a driving force of American leadership in technological development and innovation. The reputation of American universities draws highly capable and motivated students from almost every country on earth, who then become leaders in their fields thanks to the quality of U.S. higher education. OPT represents an opportunity for these students to start their careers in the U.S., and encourages them to deploy their knowledge and skills here on a longer-term basis—a win–win situation. The proposed rule would disrupt this process by effectively ending OPT for all but the wealthiest students, hurting American competitiveness in the global research and technology landscape.

Therefore I strongly oppose the rule and encourage DHS to withdraw this proposal.
