comments.title: Comment Submitted by Abu Ahmed Ferdous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule to impose a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation.

This proposal would create an extraordinary financial barrier for international students who have invested years of hard work, substantial financial resources, and academic commitment in pursuing higher education in the United States.

International students contribute significantly to American universities, research institutions, innovation, and the national economy. Many students pay full tuition without access to federal financial aid, support university research, contribute to STEM innovation, and help strengthen America's position as a global leader in science and technology.

OPT, particularly STEM OPT, provides an important bridge between academic education and practical professional experience. It allows graduates to apply their knowledge, gain industry experience, contribute to research and development, and build professional skills. It also allows American employers to benefit from graduates trained at U.S. institutions.

A $70,000 fee is disproportionate and unrealistic. Most international students are not wealthy individuals. Many rely on family savings, educational loans, scholarships, and years of personal sacrifice to finance their education. Requiring universities to pay such an enormous fee for each student would likely result in institutions passing the financial burden to students, reducing opportunities, or declining to recommend otherwise qualified graduates for OPT.

This policy could have several serious consequences:

Financial exclusion: It would make practical training opportunities inaccessible to students from modest and middle-income families, regardless of their academic qualifications or professional potential.

Damage to STEM education: International graduates in computer science, engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, biotechnology, and other critical fields contribute to research and innovation in the United States. Restricting their ability to gain practical experience could undermine the country's STEM talent pipeline.

Negative impact on universities: Universities may face substantial financial and administrative burdens, potentially affecting research programs, graduate recruitment, and institutional competitiveness.

Reduced competitiveness: Talented international graduates may choose countries with more accessible post-study employment opportunities, weakening America's ability to attract and retain global talent.

Unfair treatment of legitimate students: Measures intended to prevent fraud should distinguish between fraudulent activities and genuine students who have complied with immigration regulations and completed legitimate academic programs.

I fully recognize the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud, protect U.S. workers, and maintain the integrity of the immigration system. However, these objectives can be achieved through targeted compliance monitoring, stronger institutional oversight, employer verification, and enforcement against fraudulent actors rather than imposing an excessively high financial barrier on every legitimate student.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. If additional oversight funding is necessary, the Department should consider a reasonable, proportionate fee based on actual administrative costs rather than an amount that could effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for ordinary international graduates.

International students come to the United States to learn, conduct research, contribute to innovation, and develop skills. Their legitimate educational and professional contributions should not be undermined by a financial barrier that is beyond the reach of most students.

Please preserve fair and accessible OPT and STEM OPT opportunities for qualified international graduates and protect the United States' longstanding role as a destination for global education, research, and innovation.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees due to financial barriers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 graduate student in Carnegie Mellon University. I am writing to oppose the proposed fee of $70,000 for a school's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation.

First, the basis for this fee is unclear. Processing an OPT recommendation is a SEVIS record entry made by a school official; a $70,000 charge bears no relationship to the actual cost of that service. If the goal is fraud prevention, a flat fee charged to every school and student does not target fraud — it penalizes the compliant majority. Fraud is already addressed through SEVIS reporting, DSO oversight, and employer site visits. DHS has not shown that a fee of this size would prevent fraud more effectively than those existing tools.

Second, the fee would seriously harm U.S. universities. No university can realistically pay $70,000 per graduating international student, so the cost would be passed to students, as the proposal itself acknowledges — or schools would simply stop recommending OPT. Either outcome means fewer international students choosing the United States, heavier financial pressure on universities, possible tuition increases for all students, and research labs losing the graduate researchers they depend on.

Third, the damage extends to the U.S. economy. According to NAFSA, international students contributed about $43.8 billion to the U.S. economy and supported roughly 378,000 jobs in the 2023–24 academic year. OPT is a major reason talented students choose the U.S. over Canada, the UK, or Australia. Pricing those students out means losing their skills, their research output, and the companies and innovations they would have built here.

Finally, my own case shows what this fee means in practice. My plan is to continue as a research assistant in my current lab after graduation. Post-completion OPT is the bridge that makes this possible. My OPT work would be research training directly related to my degree. I cannot pay $70,000, and neither can my lab. For students like me, this fee does not price OPT; it eliminates it, and with it a research path that benefits my university and my field.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yinzhe Lu
comments.commentText:
Re: Comment on Proposed Rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026); DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01

I'm a data analyst working in the United States on an H-1B visa. I first came here as an international student and finished a master's degree here before starting work. I'm writing to ask the Department to withdraw the proposed $70,000 fee for a first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for later ones, or, at the very least, to do the analysis the law requires before finalizing anything. OPT is the bridge between a U.S. degree and a first job in your field of study. This proposal would price that bridge out of reach for most students and most schools, based on a fraud problem the proposal never measures and a fee amount it never justifies.

1. The fee has nothing to do with what OPT costs to run.
A fee should have some connection to the cost or the problem it's supposed to address. This one doesn't. The proposal says the initial fee was "designed to closely align with the H-1B fees to reduce students and employers from using OPT to circumvent the H-1B visa program fees." 91 FR at 64576.

2. The fraud case is asserted, not measured, and a flat price can't tell fraud from legitimate use.
I'm not saying OPT fraud doesn't exist. The proposal cites real enforcement actions, including Operation OPTical Illusion and Homeland Security Investigations' finding of 10,000 highly suspected employers. 91 FR at 64573-64576.

3. The proposal's own numbers show concentrated harm that it mostly leaves unmeasured.
The Department "cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation due to these new requirements." 91 FR at 64583. In the low participation scenario, DHS assumes institutions will pay the initial fee only for students eligible for the 24-month STEM OPT extension, 88,374 students, against a 2024 baseline of 194,554 OPT authorizations, which means non-STEM OPT effectively disappears.

4. "The school pays" doesn't settle who actually pays, and the fee punishes the internships the program exists to provide.
The Department presents the fee as a charge on institutions, but its own text concedes the cost lands elsewhere: "schools may mitigate their budgetary impact by passing the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." 91 FR at 64578. A school that passes a $70,000 charge to a graduating student hasn't made the student more employable. It has made the student $70,000 more expensive to hire, with the cost landing on the party least able to bear it and least responsible for any fraud.

5. The reliance analysis is a conclusion, and the transition is too short for the students already here.
The Department's reliance discussion concludes that "the national interest in protecting American workers and program integrity far outweigh[s] any reliance interests of foreign students, employers ... or educational institutions," and that the F-1 visa "was never intended to provide a pathway to employment in the United States." 91 FR at 64578. That is a policy preference stated as a finding, not the assessment of the nature and extent of reliance that Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California requires. Students currently enrolled chose schools, programs, and financing under a framework in which OPT has existed since 1947 and the STEM extension since 2016; a majority of international students are in STEM fields, and 294,253 were on OPT in 2024-25.

6. The combined burden on the same students is never analyzed, and the alternatives were never genuinely modeled.
The same F-1 student faces, all at once: this fee; the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period (91 FR 57807); the $103,265 H-1B fee NPRM (91 FR 54817); the Department of Labor wage rulemaking; the duration-of-status final rule (91 FR 44976, currently postponed); and the August 2026 CPT broadcast messages restricting internships. The OPT proposal identifies no overlapping rule and performs no cumulative analysis. Each action on its own narrows the path from a U.S. degree to lawful U.S. employment; together, they close it for many students.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask the Department to withdraw the proposal. If it does not, I ask at minimum for: (a) a published fraud-rate estimate and a cost basis for the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts; (b) a supplemental quantitative regulatory impact analysis with distributional effects by stakeholder, institution size, and field of study; (c) analysis of a genuine less-burdensome alternative; (d) grandfather and transition provisions for students already enrolled; and (e) a cumulative-impact analysis, each published for public comment before any final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly asks the Department to withdraw the proposed exorbitant OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I support DHS’s proposal to establish substantial fees for Optional Practical Training, including the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. OPT should provide genuine training directly related to a student’s field of study, not an inexpensive substitute for employment-based immigration or a mechanism for fraudulent employment arrangements.

Sections IV.A–C describe serious oversight concerns, including fictitious employment, nonfunctional worksites, and employer networks that obscure where students actually work. These findings justify stronger accountability. They do not establish that every participant is noncompliant, but they demonstrate why recommendations should require more than routine paperwork and unverified assurances.

I support placing the payment obligation on SEVP-certified schools before they recommend OPT, as proposed in Section V.A. Schools are responsible for evaluating eligibility and maintaining student records. A substantial financial obligation can encourage institutions to examine the educational value and legitimacy of recommendations more carefully rather than treating participation as an automatic benefit.

Protecting U.S. workers should remain an explicit objective. Legitimate practical training should not become a vehicle for replacing workers or avoiding the safeguards associated with employment-based visa programs. DHS should evaluate the fees alongside enforcement of existing training and worker-protection requirements; payment must never be treated as proof of compliance.

To strengthen the final rule, DHS should explain the evidentiary basis for the specific fee amounts and why they are preferable to lower fees or alternative safeguards. The agency should also address its acknowledged risk that schools will pass costs to students, employers, or the broader student body. Financial capacity alone is not a reliable measure of educational merit or lawful conduct.

DHS should also explore a legally authorized connection between SEVIS and IRS wage-reporting systems to help verify claimed paid employment and detect fabricated paystubs used to maintain student status. Where employment is represented as paid, supporting evidence should extend beyond an employer-generated paystub to independently verifiable wage reports and, where applicable, tax withholding and remittance records. DHS should coordinate with IRS and, where appropriate, the Social Security Administration to assess what matching is legally permitted and technically reliable, subject to tax-return confidentiality requirements and any necessary legislative authorization. Such checks should distinguish employee wages from other lawful arrangements and account for reporting schedules, corrected filings, applicable tax exemptions, and lawful unpaid training where permitted. A missing or delayed match, or the absence of tax due, should trigger an opportunity to provide documentation and correct errors—not an automatic finding of fraud or loss of status. Any system should minimize data sharing, restrict access, retain audit logs, and provide meaningful review before adverse action. Fees should complement this evidence-based verification, not substitute for it.
Finally, DHS should publish aggregate results on fraud findings, compliance, participation, and labor-market effects after implementation. Because Section IV.C states that receipts go to Treasury rather than directly to ICE, the agency should distinguish anticipated deterrence from any separately funded enforcement expansion.

I urge DHS to finalize a legally supported, evidence-based OPT fee framework that strengthens institutional responsibility, discourages abuse, and protects U.S. workers while preserving legitimate educational training.
Thank you,
An American
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly supports DHS's proposal to establish substantial OPT fees to increase accountability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Steven Singleton
comments.commentText:
In Docket ICEB-2026-0100, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3) applies the fee to DSO recommendations dated on or after a date 60 days after publication of the final rule, and Section VI says institutions will not be required to pay it for OPT already approved or recommended before that date. That prospective design should be preserved in the final rule, and item 3 seeks a related adjustment for STEM extensions that follow pre-rule OPT.

1. Authority for the charge (Sections III.A, IV.C). Section IV.C describes the fee provisions as promulgated pursuant to INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184, says ICE would not retain the money because "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected," and says the fees go to the Treasury under 31 U.S.C. 3302. National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340-42 (1974), describes heavy assessments meant to discourage an activity as in the nature of taxes traditionally levied by Congress, and Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co., 490 U.S. 212 (1989), reads that decision and its companion to require a clear congressional indication before an agency recovers administrative costs not inuring directly to regulated parties' benefit by imposing financial burdens on them. Both bear on review under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(C). Fix: Explain in Section III.A how the "time and conditions" text of INA 214(a), on which it relies, authorizes a mandatory payment of $70,000 or $30,000 to the Treasury.

2. Basis for the amounts (Sections IV.C, VII.A.6). Section IV.C compares the initial fee to the H-1B fee ("selected a fee amount for OPT comparable to the fee for H-1B visas") and the fees generally to "the educational costs" students incur for one or two years of study. Section VII.A.6 states the expected effect as a belief that the rule "would likely result in more scrutiny" of OPT recommendations. Fix: Docket the analysis that derives each amount and links it to an expected reduction in fraudulent OPT recommendations.

3. Transition fee for STEM extensions (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3); Sections V.A, VII.B.4). Section V.A classes a STEM OPT extension as subsequent OPT, and paragraph (i)(2) sets the $30,000 fee where the student "has previously participated in OPT and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000." Paragraph (i)(3) says schools "must pay the fee of $70,000 for each alien who receives a DSO recommendation for OPT" dated on or after the effective date, and Section VII.B.4 states: "If an OPT fee has not previously been paid for an F-1 nonimmigrant, they are subject to the initial fee of $70,000." A STEM extension recommended after that date for a student whose initial OPT preceded it therefore draws $70,000, the same fee as a first recommendation. Fix: Add to paragraph (i)(3) a sentence providing that a recommendation for a STEM OPT extension for such a student is subject to the $30,000 fee.

4. Small-entity alternatives (Sections VII.B.4, VII.B.6). Of 1,389 small institutions, DHS reports that in the transition year 841 would experience impacts above 1 percent of estimated revenue and 116 above 20 percent. The alternatives discussed are no action, a full small-institution exemption (rejected because, with 56 percent of regulated institutions small, fraud could continue), a repeated initial fee, and expanded site visits or reporting. 5 U.S.C. 603(c)(1) names differing compliance requirements or timetables for small entities. Fix: Add to the final regulatory flexibility analysis a quantified alternative capping a small institution's annual OPT fees at 5 percent of its estimated annual revenue, with the effect on projected collections.

5. Refunds (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2); Section V.A). Both paragraphs say SEVP "may exercise discretion to grant a refund request from a school on a case-by-case basis." The school pays before the student may apply to USCIS, and Section IV.C says the refund provisions let schools "seek a refund if the student does not receive" an employment authorization document. A school meeting that condition still depends on discretion. Fix: In both paragraphs, replace "may exercise discretion to grant" with a statement that SEVP will grant the request, and delete the case-by-case qualifier.

6. Comment period (DATES; Sections VI, VII.A). OMB designated the proposed rule economically significant, and Section VI refers to a 30-day public comment period. The notice sets 60 days, to December 7, 2026, for information collection comments, and E.O. 12866 section 6(a)(1) provides that a comment period should in most cases be not less than 60 days. Fix: Publish a notice extending the comment period on the whole proposed rule to December 7, 2026.

None of this rejects the aim of reducing OPT fraud.
comments.reason: The commenter challenges the statutory authority and legality of the heavy proposed OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jisoo Kim
comments.commentText: I am writing to oppose the proposed new fees for OPT. Having gone through the American higher education system myself, including as a graduate research/teaching assistant wholly supported by stipend, I can speak to the financial realities faced by the vast majority of OPT seekers. Though the fees are targeted at the institutions themselves, institutions will, in all likelihood, pass costs down to the applicants instead. The proposed fees were clearly set to exorbitantly high levels such that OPT seekers and their home institutions will not be able to afford them. Graduate student stipends across the country are designed to cover living expenses, not to start building a nest egg. Very few students build up meaningful savings during graduate school, much less to the tune of $70,000. Furthermore, international students supported by stipend are often prohibited from seeking additional income per the terms of their visa, further preventing the growth of any savings to be able to afford application to OPT.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule, and I urge DHS to withdraw it.

A $70,000 fee for a school to recommend a student for Optional Practical Training — and $30,000 more for each later recommendation, including a STEM extension — is not a fee. It is a price that ends the program for nearly everyone it was built for. Schools cannot absorb a charge of this size across hundreds of students, and DHS itself acknowledges the cost will be passed on: to the F-1 student, to all students, or to employers. A student who has just finished a degree cannot pay $70,000 for permission to work, and most employers will not pay it for an entry-level hire either. The practical result is that OPT becomes available only to the wealthy — or to no one.

That defeats the purpose of OPT. It is the bridge between a U.S. education and skilled work in the United States: the year or three in which a graduate applies what they studied, and an employer evaluates them before sponsoring an H-1B. Under this rule, no company will be willing to sponsor international talent at all — the cost of the pipeline becomes so high that employers will simply stop hiring international graduates, no matter how talented they are. That is the opposite of a merit-based system: it selects on ability to pay, not on skill or contribution. A graduate's future here would depend on whether someone can afford a $70,000 fee, not on what they can do. The result is that engineers, data scientists, and researchers educated at American universities go to Canada, the United Kingdom, and every other country competing for them, along with the tuition, research, and tax revenue they bring.

The STEM extension fee is the sharpest contradiction in the proposal. STEM graduates are the workers the United States says it most needs, and this rule would charge $30,000 extra precisely for keeping them here longer.

DHS's own estimate puts the fees at $12.4 billion a year. That is not cost recovery; it is a wall. I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep OPT accessible to the students and employers it serves.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are too high, will end the program, and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. DHS suggests schools can pass the cost along, but that suggestion assumes a payer exists. I want to ask a practical question the proposal never answers: who actually writes the check, and through what channel?

Start with the student. A university bursar's office charges fees tied to enrollment — tuition, housing, lab fees. There is no billing code for a federal immigration charge triggered by a SEVIS entry, and no mechanism to put a $70,000 levy on a student's account at the moment a Designated School Official clicks "recommend." Nor could the student pay it if there were: international students are barred from federal student loans, private lenders generally require a U.S. co-signer and do not lend against a fee assessed to a third party, and the charge falls due before the student has a job, an offer, or a paycheck. Asking a graduating student to produce $70,000 on the spot for a document that does not yet exist is not cost-sharing. It is a demand with no payer behind it.

The employer is no better. A company hiring through ordinary campus recruiting has no contract with the graduate's university, no purchase order, and no vendor relationship to invoice against. A school would have to send a $70,000 bill to a stranger and hope it gets paid — and when the employer declines, as any procurement department would, the recruiter simply hires the candidate who carries no surcharge. Universities are not debt collectors, and employers are not parties to a SEVIS recommendation.

That leaves the school itself, and here the mechanics fail too. Public universities set tuition and mandatory fees through boards and regents, typically a year in advance; a mid-year levy of millions cannot simply be invented. The international office that runs OPT is a cost center, not a revenue center — it has no income stream from which to pay $70,000 per student, and no grant or appropriation covers it. And the fee is due before the employment authorization document even exists, non-refundable once it issues, so the school pays first and learns later whether the authorization survives.

A fee with no payer is not a fee. It is a shutdown wearing a price tag. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and highlights the impracticality of the high fees on OPT recommendations.

comments.commentText:
In light of the recent recommendations being made by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to require students to pay $70,000 for students first pursuing OPT, and an additional $30,000 for each later recommendation, I am writing to strongly oppose this legislation.

I am deeply concerned about the financial barriers this proposal would create, particularly for students from lower-income backgrounds who have already made enormous personal and financial sacrifices to pursue their education in the United States. Access to professional opportunities should not depend on a student's financial resources or their institution's ability to absorb extraordinary fees. I am also deeply concerned that some institutions will not be able to bear the financial responsibilities of this ruling, thus passing the burden down to students. This reality would make it exceedingly difficult for students to maintain their citizenship and basic dignities as productive employees.

OPT provides international students with an important opportunity to apply their education, gain professional experience, and contribute their knowledge and skills to the U.S. workforce. Introducing such substantial costs risks making these opportunities inaccessible to the very students who may benefit from them most. It could also deepen existing inequalities between students attending well-resourced institutions and those whose schools cannot afford these additional expenses.

This issue is also deeply personal to me. I have loved ones whose futures, professional opportunities, and ability to build stable lives in the United States could be affected by these changes. I have seen how much dedication, hard work, and uncertainty international students experience as they pursue their education and careers. The possibility that additional financial barriers could prevent them from participating in the workforce, despite their qualifications and contributions, is profoundly concerning. Having this hang over the heads of my loved ones is difficult to see and heartbreaking to imagine.

International students enrich our academic communities, workplaces, and society. Policies affecting their ability to gain practical experience should recognize these contributions and avoid creating unnecessary financial obstacles or additional uncertainty about their futures.

I strongly urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve meaningful, equitable access to OPT, regardless of a student's socioeconomic background or institutional resources.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed fees, arguing they create unfair financial barriers for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

First, restricting international graduates from working in the US does not automatically create more employment opportunities for American workers. Hiring should be based on qualifications, skills, and professional competency, not nationality. If the goal is to strengthen the American workforce, investment in education, training, and workforce development would be a more constructive approach than financially penalizing qualified international graduates.

Second, it is unclear how DHS arrived at these high amounts. What specific costs or calculations justify charging $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations? The proposal should provide a transparent, evidence-based breakdown explaining how these figures were determined. Such substantial fees should not be imposed without clear justification.

Third, these fees could place an unreasonable financial burden on universities and students, discourage institutions from supporting OPT participation, and drive highly educated talent toward other countries. This would undermine the US's abilities to attract and retain skilled graduates who contribute to research, innovation, and economic growth.

Finally, DHS should provide credible evidence demonstrating how these fees would actually improve employment outcomes for American workers. Without such evidence, this proposal risks causing significant harm to international students, universities, and the broader US economy without achieving its stated objectives.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue more reasonable, evidence-based approaches to protecting American workers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the high OPT fees place an unreasonable financial burden on students and harm the US workforce.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to modify the proposed rule and explicitly exempt F-1 students who held H-4 dependent status prior to transitioning to F-1 ("aged-out" youth) and have resided lawfully in the United States for 10 or more years from the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees.

1. Involuntary Transition from H-4 to F-1

Unlike traditional international students who apply for an F-1 visa from abroad to enter the United States, these young adults were H-4 dependents first. They were brought to the U.S. legally as children by their high-skilled, tax-paying parents and have lived here continuously for over a decade—attending American K–12 schools and growing up in U.S. communities.
Because of severe employment-based green card backlogs, these youth lose their H-4 status strictly due to turning 21 ("aging out"). They were forced to switch from H-4 to F-1 status solely to maintain lawful presence and finish their college education in the only home they know.

2. Penalizing Lawful, Long-Term Residents Fails DHS’s Stated Purpose

DHS states these fees are intended to deter visa fraud, eliminate "pay-to-stay" programs, and protect U.S. workers. Imposing a $70,000–$100,000 fee on former H-4 children accomplishes none of these goals:
• Already Vetted for Over a Decade: Having spent 10+ years in lawful H-4 status prior to switching to F-1, these students are thoroughly vetted and pose zero fraud risk.
• An Insurmountable Barrier: These students and their families—who have already paid U.S. federal, state, and local taxes for over a decade—cannot afford $70,000 on top of university tuition. Universities will not absorb this cost, effectively barring these American-raised graduates from entering the workforce.

3. Severe Family Separation and Economic Loss

Denying OPT access through an unaffordable fee forces former H-4 youth to self-deport to countries they barely remember, separating them from their parents and siblings who remain lawfully in the U.S. At the same time, the U.S. economy loses qualified graduates whose K–12 education was already funded by American taxpayers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm long-term resident aged-out H-4 youth and urges DHS to exempt them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. The $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees exceed DHS's authority, do not address the fraud DHS describes, and rest on an incomplete analysis.

1. IT IS A TAX, NOT A FEE (Sections III.A, IV.C)
DHS admits the money would go to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt and that ICE cannot keep it. Under 31 U.S.C. 9701 and National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), a fee must reflect the cost of a service; a charge set to raise revenue and deter activity is a tax, which only Congress can impose. DHS chose $70,000 to match H-1B costs, not any cost of processing OPT. WashTech v. DHS (D.C. Cir. 2022) upheld OPT itself, not revenue charges attached to it, and after Loper Bright (2024) DHS's reading of its authority gets no deference.

2. IT DOES NOT FUND OVERSIGHT (Section IV.A)
DHS's central finding is that compliance resources have not kept pace with OPT. Yet the rule adds no investigators, site visits, or SEVIS improvements. A remedy that adds nothing to the stated problem is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

3. IT TARGETS THE WRONG PARTY (Sections IV.A, V.A)
Every fraud example DHS cites involves employers: shell companies, fake worksites, phantom employees. But the fee is "not tied to a specific employer," and for initial OPT schools must pay before the student even has a job, so they cannot screen employers at all. DHS links about 10,000 students to suspect employers, under 3 percent of roughly 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The other 97 percent bear the cost.

4. BETTER ALTERNATIVES WERE REJECTED FOR CONVENIENCE (Section IV.C)
DHS rejected site visits and training-plan requirements mainly because a fee costs DHS less. Mandatory E-Verify and verified worksite data for OPT employers, risk-based site visits, or a cost-based fee retained by SEVP would target fraud directly.

5. THE ANALYSIS IS FLAWED (Section VII)
DHS estimates up to $8.2 billion a year in costs and $12.8 billion in transfers but quantifies no benefit at all. It finds 116 small institutions would lose over 20 percent of revenue, yet offers no relief. Its UMRA section says both that the rule does not exceed the $100 million threshold and that it does.

6. THE STRUCTURE IS ARBITRARY (Section VII.A.5.d)
Fees apply per recommendation, so the same 12 months of OPT costs $100,000 if split for a summer internship and $70,000 if not. DHS's own low scenario assumes non-STEM students lose OPT entirely, with no finding that those fields are more fraud-prone.

7. RELIANCE INTERESTS ARE IGNORED (Section VI)
DHS v. Regents (2020) requires serious weighing of reliance. DHS concedes current students are differently situated (fn. 124) yet calls their interests "speculative." Students who enrolled, paid tuition, and relocated families under existing rules should be exempt.

8. THE COMMENT PERIOD IS TOO SHORT
An economically significant rule with up to $69.9 billion in ten-year costs received 30 days; E.O. 12866 calls for at least 60.

DHS has identified real employer fraud. Targeted enforcement against those employers, not a revenue charge on compliant students, is the lawful response. I urge DHS to withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, arguing the fees exceed authority and harm students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully submit this comment opposing the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

My concerns focus on three fundamental deficiencies in the proposed rule.

1. The Proposed Fees Raise Serious Questions About Statutory Authority and Regulatory Purpose

DHS principally relies on its general authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act, including INA Section 214(a), to establish conditions governing nonimmigrant admissions.

However, authority to regulate immigration status does not necessarily establish unlimited authority to impose extraordinary financial obligations on educational institutions.

The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 charges are not calculated primarily by reference to the administrative cost of processing OPT applications or providing immigration services. Instead, DHS expressly intends these charges to discourage participation.

Moreover, DHS acknowledges that the resulting revenue would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than retained by ICE for fraud detection or program oversight.

These features raise substantial questions regarding the legal and regulatory character of the charges.

I request that DHS identify the specific statutory language authorizing fees of this magnitude, explain whether these charges function as regulatory fees or economic deterrents, and establish the limiting principle governing their amount.

DHS should also explain why an OPT fee benchmarked against costs associated with the H-1B program is appropriate when OPT and H-1B operate under distinct statutory and regulatory frameworks.

2. DHS Has Not Adequately Demonstrated That Financial Exclusion Prevents Fraud

The proposal assumes that imposing substantial financial costs will discourage fraudulent participation and incentivize educational institutions to exercise greater scrutiny.

However, the ability to pay $70,000 does not establish whether a student, institution, or employer complies with immigration requirements.

A legitimate research institution with limited financial resources may be unable to finance the proposed fees, while a well-funded noncompliant participant may remain capable of paying them.

The proposed fee therefore risks distinguishing participants according to financial capacity rather than compliance.

DHS should provide empirical evidence demonstrating that the proposed fee amounts would reduce fraud, including the expected relationship between payment capacity, misconduct, and program participation.

The Department should separately estimate how many legitimate OPT opportunities would be eliminated for each anticipated reduction in fraudulent participation.

Without such analysis, it is difficult to determine whether the proposal addresses misconduct or merely reduces participation in an otherwise lawful educational training program.

3. DHS Has Not Adequately Justified Rejecting More Targeted Alternatives

The proposal acknowledges alternatives such as employer site visits, training plans, expanded reporting, and enhanced verification, but largely rejects them because they may require additional governmental resources.

Administrative convenience alone does not establish that a substantially more restrictive measure is preferable.

Reasonably available alternatives include risk-based audits, enhanced employer verification, targeted enforcement against repeat violators, improved information-sharing, and expanded safeguards modeled on existing STEM OPT requirements.

These approaches could potentially address misconduct directly without conditioning legitimate educational training on exceptionally large payments.

I request that DHS conduct and disclose a meaningful comparative assessment of these alternatives, including their expected costs, effectiveness, and consequences for lawful participants.

DHS should also explain why a uniform $70,000 fee is necessary rather than a lower amount, a graduated fee, or a risk-based compliance framework.

Conclusion

The proposed rule raises serious concerns about the scope of DHS's statutory authority, the evidentiary basis for its deterrence rationale, and the adequacy of its consideration of less burdensome alternatives.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal. At a minimum, DHS should disclose the evidence supporting its fee amounts, meaningfully evaluate alternative measures, and provide a reasoned explanation addressing these concerns before adopting any final rule.

Safeguarding immigration integrity is essential, but regulatory measures should distinguish actual misconduct from lawful participation rather than treating financial exclusion as a substitute for effective oversight.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule's high OPT fees and questions DHS's statutory authority.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose DHS's proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. I support effective fraud prevention, but the proposal does not adequately justify its economic assumptions, treatment of reliance interests, or implementation burdens. I request that DHS address the following issues in any final rule.

1. Economic Analysis and Opportunity Costs

DHS estimates annual fee collections of $8.4–$16.5 billion across its modeled scenarios. For foregone OPT participation, it uses unpaid fees as a proxy for opportunity costs while acknowledging that actual costs may be higher or lower. Yet a government-imposed price is not a demonstrated measure of the economic value of lost practical training.

DHS should explain why this proxy reasonably represents lost educational and economic benefits, rather than merely reflecting the fee DHS has chosen. The analysis should distinguish transfers to the Treasury from real resource costs and foregone benefits, and test sensitivity to different assumptions about students' willingness and ability to pay, institutional budget restrictions, and employer cost-sharing.

Reduced OPT access may also affect international enrollment, tuition-supported academic programs, research continuity, employer partnerships, and opportunities available to U.S. students and workers. I request scenario analyses of these indirect effects, with assumptions and uncertainties disclosed rather than treated as negligible.

2. Institutional Burdens and Reliance Interests

DHS estimates 30 minutes of DSO review and 30 minutes of administrator processing per recommendation, but six-figure or near-six-figure commitments across multiple students may require budget approvals, legal review, financing decisions, system changes, accounting controls, and refund administration. DHS acknowledges that certain transaction and refund costs cannot be quantified.

The agency's own small-entity analysis estimates that 841 of 1,389 affected small entities (about 61%) would face transition-year impacts exceeding 1% of annual revenue; 116 (8.4%) would exceed 20%. DHS should explain how affected institutions could finance payments, especially where public funding or donor restrictions limit allowable expenditures, and whether its administrative-cost assumptions capture the approval process in practice.

DHS also should meaningfully address reliance interests. Students already enrolled, universities maintaining degree programs and research collaborations, and employers coordinating training opportunities may have made long-term commitments in reliance on existing OPT rules. Prospective application to later OPT recommendations does not eliminate these effects. What alternatives, grandfathering provisions, or transition periods did DHS consider, and why were they rejected? Why would 60 days after publication of a final rule be sufficient for institutions to adapt?

3. Unclear Fee Triggers, Unequal Effects, and Public Participation

The NPRM contemplates separate charges for pre-completion and post-completion OPT and further charges for STEM OPT. It also raises questions about additional OPT at higher degree levels and across institutions. DHS should specify, with worked examples, when each $70,000 or $30,000 fee is due, whether a second institution must pay another initial fee, how prior participation is tracked, and when refunds are available. Absent clarity, similarly eligible students may face different barriers based on institutional resources and academic pathways rather than program compliance.

I also request analysis of less disruptive approaches to institutional oversight, including risk-based audits and targeted verification. A 30-day comment period is especially restrictive for institutions needing to gather budget data and consult students, researchers, and employers. DHS should extend the comment period and provide a renewed opportunity to comment if material provisions change.

Conclusion

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule or, at minimum, provide a more rigorous economic analysis, assess reliance interests and less burdensome alternatives, clarify the fee triggers and refund procedures, and allow meaningful public participation. Program integrity should be advanced through evidence-based oversight, not inadequately evaluated barriers to lawful practical training.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and outlines economic concerns regarding the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Kyria Clark
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am submitting this public comment regarding the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees. I would like to raise concerns about the potential economic, educational, and workforce consequences of the proposal.

1. Disproportionate Financial Impact on Educational Institutions

The proposed fees would place an extraordinary financial burden on universities and colleges that support international students. A fee of $70,000 per student could make it financially impractical for many institutions, particularly smaller universities and public colleges, to continue recommending eligible students for OPT.

Educational institutions already invest significant resources in international student services, regulatory compliance, and student supervision. The proposed fees could divert resources away from educational programs and student support.

2. Impact on International Students and Educational Opportunities

International students make substantial investments in their education in the United States. Many finance their education through personal savings, family support, and educational loans.

OPT provides an opportunity for students to gain practical experience directly related to their academic fields. An exceptionally high institutional fee could reduce access to this opportunity, regardless of a student's academic performance, qualifications, or commitment to complying with immigration regulations.

Students who have already committed years of their lives and significant financial resources to U.S. education could face considerable uncertainty about their ability to obtain practical training after graduation.

3. Potential Consequences for the U.S. Economy and Workforce

International graduates contribute skills and expertise to American industries, including technology, engineering, healthcare, research, and other specialized fields.

OPT provides employers with access to graduates who have received education and training at U.S. institutions. Reducing access to OPT could make it more difficult for employers to recruit qualified graduates and could affect the competitiveness of American businesses in the global economy.

4. Effectiveness and Proportionality of the Proposed Fees

While preventing immigration fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate government objectives, the Department should demonstrate how the proposed fee amounts would effectively achieve these objectives.

A fee of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT is a substantial financial requirement. The Department should provide clear evidence demonstrating how these specific amounts were calculated, why they are necessary, and how they relate to the actual administrative and enforcement costs associated with OPT.

The Department should also explain how the proposed fees would distinguish between legitimate students and institutions that comply with all applicable regulations and those involved in

5. Request for Further Analysis

Before proceeding with this rule, I respectfully request that DHS provide additional analysis of:

The anticipated impact on public and private universities.
The financial consequences for small and medium-sized educational institutions.
The potential reduction in OPT and STEM OPT participation.
The impact on U.S. employers that recruit international graduates.
The consequences for students who have already enrolled in U.S. degree programs based on existing OPT regulations.
The legal and economic justification for the proposed fee amounts.
Conclusion

The OPT program plays an important role in connecting U.S. higher education with practical professional experience. Any changes to this program should carefully consider the interests of students, universities, employers, and the broader U.S. economy.

I respectfully request that DHS carefully evaluate the concerns raised in this comment, provide transparent evidence supporting the proposed fee structure, and consider less financially burdensome alternatives that address program integrity without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Thank you for the opportunity to participate in this rulemaking process and for considering my comments.

Respectfully,

A Concerned Member of the Public
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees place an extraordinary financial burden on universities and students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they are a tax that DHS has no power to impose. Agency fees are normally tied to the cost of a service or its value to the person who pays. This rule does not calculate any cost. DHS sets the amounts by comparing them to H-1B charges and to tuition. The money does not stay with ICE or pay for OPT oversight. It goes to the general fund of the Treasury under 31 U.S.C. 3302. The Supreme Court has drawn this line between fees and taxes since National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States (1974). The Constitution gives the power to tax to Congress.
DHS points to INA 214(a), which lets it set the time and conditions of a nonimmigrant's admission. That provision has never been read to allow a $70,000 charge on a school that goes to the Treasury. After Loper Bright v. Raimondo (2024), DHS gets no deference for this new reading. DHS expects the fees to raise billions of dollars a year and cut OPT use by more than half. A measure that large needs clear approval from Congress (West Virginia v. EPA, 2022). DHS should withdraw the fees.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are an unlawful tax and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alex Shin
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees because DHS has not shown a rational link between the fees and its stated goal, as the Administrative Procedure Act requires (Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm, 1983). DHS's main reason is fraud. Yet the fee is the same for every student and every school whether or not there is any sign of fraud. Being able to pay $70,000 says nothing about whether a job offer is real. The fraud schemes DHS describes are run for profit and can most easily absorb a flat charge. None of the money goes to investigation or enforcement. DHS never explains how one price for everyone separates honest students from fraud.

DHS also failed to consider obvious alternatives. It could act against the employers ICE has already flagged. It could decertify schools with high fraud rates or require fair wages for regular OPT. DHS also ignored the students who enrolled, paid tuition and took out loans because OPT was available. DHS v. Regents (2020) requires an agency to weigh that kind of reliance. This proposal does not, and it offers no protection for students already enrolled. DHS should withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees lack rational justification, ignore reliance interests, and asks DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alex Shin
comments.commentText: I oppose the alternative in Section V.A, which would charge the $70,000 fee again each time a student starts OPT at a new degree level. At least one comment on this docket (ICEB-2026-0100-2756) asks DHS to adopt it. Under this alternative a student who finishes a bachelor's degree here and goes on to a master's or PhD would pay at least $170,000 just for continuing to study in the United States. That student is the opposite of the fraud DHS describes, which is enrolling in a program with little educational value to get work authorization. The alternative would push the most committed students to graduate schools in other countries. DHS has not estimated how many students it would affect or what it would do to graduate enrollment. Adopting a much harsher measure in a final rule without that analysis would be arbitrary. DHS should reject the Section V.A alternative and withdraw the fees.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I understand DHS's goal of ending fraud in OPT. Fraudulent employers and sham programs hurt honest international students first.

But this rule does not target fraud. ICE says it found more than 10,000 STEM OPT students tied to employers it considers highly suspect. That means DHS already has the data to find these employers and the schools that send students to them. Those cases are about 3% of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. The other 97% would pay the same $70,000.

DHS should go after the employers ICE has already flagged and end SEVIS records tied to jobs that do not exist. It should verify employers through E-Verify before they can be reported in SEVIS and pull certification from schools that keep sending students to flagged employers. If a fee is needed it should cover the cost of oversight and stay with SEVP to pay for enforcement. Even the most detailed comment supporting this rule (ICEB-2026-0100-4243) asks DHS to strengthen site visits and publish data on employers and wages. None of these tools depends on a $70,000 fee. The fee would not fund them either because the money goes to the Treasury. DHS should withdraw the rule and use these tools instead.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the $70,000 fee is unfair to the majority and asks DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: This is a draconian rule. International PhD, masters and bachelors students can’t even think of paying 70k USD (for example this is 2 years of salary for a PhD student and 7-10 years worth saving). There are thousands of international students currently giving their blood and sweat, sacrificing their relationships with family and friends who are back in their countries, just with one hope to secure a good respected job. This rule will kill that hope and probably will kill the soul of the student. Universities can’t also pay this sum of money for the students because they draw significant funds from the enrollment of international students. When international students stops coming to U.S for their studies, most of these universities have to cut budget by firing staffs. This will create a vicious cycle. I strongly condemn for even thinking about this proposed law unless U.S. wants to stop bright, hardworking, intelligent international students to come to U.S. for their studies who have done so much for this country. I am an international student, and I have dreams to stay here and I want a chance to payback U.S. by working here and by creating jobs. Don’t take my chance away, don’t kill my hopes.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Abigail Cooke
comments.commentText: I wish to register my opposition to the DHS Proposed Rule on Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026) | DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. As a professor at a large public research university, I teach undergraduate students and I also train masters and PhD students. My students are a mix of domestic and international students. I am certain that maintaining that mix in the program greatly augments the education of all students as they engage across difference and learn from each others' experiences. The experience of gaining training in the US is obviously valuable to the international students. But learning alongside these students is also valuable for the American students, increasing their understanding of the global context in which they will be operating after graduation and sharpening their own learning and positions through sustained engagement with students from very different backgrounds. This is threatened by the proposed rule on OPT fees since it will likely substantially reduce enrollment of international students at my university. This will not 'open' more spots for domestic students - my program is not at capacity at the moment - but it will diminish the quality of the education I can provide for those domestic students via the absence of their international classmates. There are a host of reasons to oppose this proposed rule that impact my entire university, which I understand have been outlined separately in comments by my university. But I hope to draw attention to this more personal reason I have for opposing the proposed OPT fees for how negatively it will impact all my students - international and domestic. I greatly hope the proposed rule will be withdrawn. Thank you for your serious attention to these comments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am an F-1 student at the University of Pittsburgh, currently employed as a Research Scientist under post-completion Optional Practical Training, and I intend to apply for the 24-month STEM OPT extension. I write to oppose the proposed $70,000 first-recommendation and $30,000 subsequent-recommendation fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, 91 FR 64566).

I have studied in the United States since 2014, earned two master's degrees at Pitt, and now work full-time in university research — lawful employment that pays taxes and contributes to federally relevant science. Under this proposal, my university would have to pay DHS $30,000 before its designated school official could even recommend my STEM OPT extension. DHS states openly that schools may pass these costs on to students or employers. I cannot pay $30,000, and no early-career employer will pay it on my behalf. The practical effect is to price me — a graduate of two U.S. master's programs with years of U.S. research experience — out of authorized employment.

These fees bear no relation to the cost of administering the program. DHS itself estimates the rule would extract $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year from schools, with proceeds deposited into the general Treasury. That is a revenue measure imposed on a population with no political voice, not cost recovery. The rule punishes precisely the rule-following students the United States should retain, while schools with the fewest resources — and the students they serve — would face the harshest pressure to limit OPT recommendations.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. At minimum, the 24-month STEM OPT extension — a program Congress-adjacent policy has long treated as central to U.S. innovation — should be exempt from any new fee.

Respectfully,
Anonymous — F-1 student, University of Pittsburgh
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessively burdensome and will price students out of authorized employment.

I am an F-1 student currently on STEM OPT, and I oppose the proposed OPT fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).

OPT allows U.S.-trained graduates to gain work experience in their field, filling STEM, healthcare, and research roles that employers struggle to fill, and it is a major reason international students choose to study in the United States. I chose to study here largely because OPT would allow me to apply what I learned in school; without it, I would not have come.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Vishal Prajapati
comments.commentText:
Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees, Docket ICEB-2026-0100

My name is Vishal. I am an F-1 student from India, currently finishing my Master of Science in Computer Science at Saint Leo University in Florida. I will graduate in December 2026, with a GPA of 3.90, and I have applied for post-completion OPT with a requested start date of February 11, 2027.

I came to the United States to study, and I have invested my family's savings and two years of my life in this degree. OPT is the reason that investment makes sense. It is the only practical way for a student like me to get a first job in my field, gain work experience in the United States, and pay taxes here while I do it.

A $70,000 fee for a school to recommend a student for OPT, and $30,000 more for a STEM OPT extension, would effectively end OPT for students like me. My university cannot pay $70,000 per student, and no employer will pay that fee for a new graduate who has not started working yet. Schools will stop recommending OPT, or they will pass the cost to students who cannot pay it.

I am not asking for a free benefit. I paid tuition, I paid the $470 fee to file my OPT application, and I am actively applying for jobs in data analysis and machine learning, with a start date after my OPT begins. If this fee takes effect, students who did everything right, studied, graduated, and applied on time, will lose the work opportunity they came here for.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposed fee. OPT helps American employers hire trained graduates, helps students use the education they paid for, and keeps the United States competitive for international students. A fee of this size does the opposite.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Vishal Sureshbhai Prajapati
Gainesville, Florida

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong concerns regarding the proposed fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT), particularly the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations. As a doctoral student currently pursuing advanced scientific training at a U.S. university, I am concerned about the significant consequences this proposal could have for international students, American universities, scientific research, and the development of highly specialized professionals in the United States.

International graduate students contribute substantially to the research, teaching, and innovation missions of American universities. Many doctoral students spend several years conducting research, publishing scientific findings, supporting undergraduate education, and contributing to projects that address important challenges in public health, agriculture, biomedical sciences, and engineering. These contributions strengthen the United States' scientific capacity and international competitiveness.

OPT provides an important bridge between academic training and professional development. For doctoral graduates pursuing specialized training, postdoctoral research, or academic careers, OPT can be essential for continuing their contributions to American institutions. Imposing a substantial financial burden at this critical transition could effectively prevent highly qualified graduates from pursuing opportunities for which they have spent years developing their scientific expertise and professional qualifications. Furthermore, substantial investments of American taxpayers' dollars, often through publicly funded research programs and university resources, have contributed to the education and scientific development of these individuals. Preventing them from continuing their professional training and research activities in the United States could undermine the return on these investments and limit their ability to contribute their scientific expertise back to American institutions through cutting-edge research, innovation, and specialized professional services.

The United States benefits when talented individuals trained at American universities can continue contributing their expertise to its research institutions, industries, and communities. Policies governing practical training should recognize these contributions and avoid creating unnecessary financial barriers that could weaken the country's scientific and professional workforce and diminish American competitiveness on the international stage. Thank you for considering these concerns and for providing the opportunity for public input.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed $70,000 OPT Fee

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT), as it would place an unreasonable and disproportionate financial burden on international students and their families.

International students already make enormous financial investments to pursue higher education in the United States. They often pay significantly higher tuition than domestic students, in addition to substantial expenses for housing, food, transportation, health insurance, books, and other living costs. Many parents dedicate their lifetime savings, take out loans, sell assets, or make significant financial sacrifices to provide their children with an American education.

More importantly, some international students are not newcomers to this country. They have lived in the United States since elementary school, sometimes as early as first grade. They have grown up in American communities, attended American schools, graduated from American universities, and consider the United States their home. Their parents may have lived and worked here for 10, 15, or even more years, consistently paying federal, state, and local taxes while contributing to the economy and their communities.

Despite these longstanding contributions, families can remain caught in immigration backlogs and prolonged processing delays, often through circumstances entirely beyond their control. It is unreasonable to impose an additional $70,000 fee on students who have already spent most of their lives here and whose families have contributed financially to this country for more than a decade.

International students and their families already contribute substantially to the U.S. economy through university tuition, living expenses, rent, consumer spending, and applicable income and payroll taxes. OPT also allows U.S. employers to benefit from the skills and education these graduates have acquired at American universities.

A $70,000 fee would make practical training inaccessible to many qualified graduates, particularly those from middle-income and lower-income families. It would effectively make employment opportunities dependent on family wealth rather than academic achievement, professional qualifications, and merit. It could also discourage talented graduates from contributing their skills to the American workforce.

How is it reasonable to expect families who have spent more than a decade raising, educating, supporting, and paying taxes in the United States to suddenly pay an additional $70,000 simply so their children can begin working after graduating from an American university?

I respectfully urge policymakers to reconsider this proposed fee and evaluate its disproportionate impact on international students, long-term residents, and hardworking families. At a minimum, reasonable exemptions or reduced fees should be considered for students and families facing prolonged immigration processing delays and those with longstanding ties and contributions to the United States.

Immigration fees should be fair, proportionate, and reasonable. Students should be given the opportunity to contribute to the country where they have invested years of their lives and education, rather than being prevented from doing so by an excessive financial barrier.

Thank you for considering the financial realities and human impact of this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fee, arguing it places an unreasonable financial burden on students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I'm an international student on an F-1 visa in a STEM field, and I'll graduate within the next year. OPT is how I would start working after graduation, so I wanted to share how this rule would actually affect students in my position.

The part I most want to respond to is the reliance interests section. DHS says that applying the fee to recommendations dated on or after the effective date "should address any potential reliance interests of students who have applied for OPT employment authorization before the effective date." I don't think it really does, because the students relying on OPT the most are the ones who can't apply yet. When I enrolled, the F-1 program included up to 12 months of practical training after graduation, and I made my plans for after graduation based on that. I can't get my OPT recommendation until a few months before my program end date, so whether the fee applies to me would come down to the week the final rule happens to be published, and not anything I did or planned. I'd ask DHS to apply the fee only to students who begin a program after the final rule takes effect, or at least to exempt students who were already enrolled when the proposal was published on October 8, 2026.

DHS also says schools "may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers," and that this would discourage misuse. I don't think a fee can really tell which students are misusing OPT, though. A student with a real job offer and a student gaming the system would owe the same $70,000, so it basically comes down to who can afford it. I really doubt most small schools could cover that for each of their students, so in practice it would fall on the student or the employer. A lot of international graduates are hired by small and mid-sized businesses, not large tech companies. Under this rule a small business would have to come up with $70,000 before a graduate's first day, while a large company with a big immigration budget could probably just pay it. I think that ends up deciding which employers get to hire international graduates at all, and smaller businesses would mostly lose out.

The size of the fee is the other thing I wanted to point out. Filing the I-765 costs a few hundred dollars today, and DHS's own analysis estimates these fees would bring in $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion a year. Students in STEM fields can also apply for the 24-month STEM extension, which adds the $30,000 fee and makes the real cost $100,000 for us (DHS uses that same total in its analysis). DHS says the rule would lead schools to recommend "only the most promising students," but at that price I think schools would end up recommending the students whose families or employers can pay, and I don't think that's the same group.

DHS says it considered exempting small institutions and decided against it because 56 percent of SEVP-certified schools are small entities. I read that the other way. If most certified schools are small, then most schools are the ones least able to pay. If the fraud DHS describes is coming from specific schools or employers, I think the tools DHS already has, like SEVP recertification reviews and employer site visits, would get at those directly, without charging every student at every school the same amount.

Practical training is a big part of why a lot of us chose to study in the US. I'd ask DHS to withdraw the fee. If it does go forward, I'd at least ask that students who are already enrolled be exempt, and that the STEM extension not carry a second fee on top of the first. Thank you so much for reading this.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the new OPT fee harms students who planned based on existing rules and asks for exemptions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

For me, studying in the United States was never simply about getting a degree or finding a better-paying job. It was a dream I had as a teenager. I worked incredibly hard to make it a reality. Coming here represents years of dedication, sacrifices, and opportunities I hoped I would one day have.

I chose the United States because I wanted to be somewhere I could grow, challenge myself, and contribute to fields shaping the future. In my home country, opportunities for research and innovation in my field are extremely limited. I wanted to be part of an environment where ambitious ideas become real technologies, research is encouraged, and I can learn from people working at the forefront of computer science.

Since coming here, I have discovered another passion: research. I am currently pursuing my Master's degree in Computer Science at Miami University and working on research related to AI-powered assistive technology and accessible navigation for wheelchair users. I hope to continue this path and eventually work in an industry research lab, developing technologies that solve real problems and improve people's lives. This is the career I have been working toward, and the United States is one of the best places in the world to pursue it.

This proposed rule threatens that future. A $70,000 fee could make employers think twice before hiring an international graduate, regardless of their qualifications, skills, or potential contributions. It could mean losing an opportunity not because I am not capable, but simply because hiring me comes with an additional financial burden.

I also believe it is fundamentally unfair to impose such enormous fees on all international students to address potential cases of fraud. Many of us follow every immigration requirement, invest in our education, contribute to research, and genuinely want to use our knowledge to contribute to this country. We should not be treated as a financial risk because of the actions of others. Fraud should be addressed directly through targeted enforcement, not by creating barriers for every international student.

International students are not simply people who come to the United States to receive an education. We become part of university research teams, contribute to innovation, collaborate with American students and professors, and bring different perspectives and expertise. The United States has become a global leader in science and technology partly because it attracts talented people from around the world. It should continue to recognize and support that contribution.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for a fair opportunity to contribute to the country where I chose to study, where I am developing my skills, and where I hope to make a meaningful impact. Opportunities should be determined by a person's abilities, dedication, and potential, not by an extraordinary financial burden that makes their employment unattractive.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. Please do not turn an opportunity that has allowed generations of international students to learn, contribute, and innovate into a privilege accessible only to those who can afford an extraordinary fee.

Behind every international student is a person who made difficult decisions, left their home and family, and worked hard to build a future. I am one of those people. I hope the government considers not only the financial and administrative aspects of this proposal, but also the real people and futures it could affect.
