comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
People in Washington writing rules about a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 extension fee clearly do not live or run businesses in an American college town. If this policy goes through, it won't just hurt universities—it will devastate the local Main Street economies, small landlords, and working-class service employees who depend on university communities to survive.

In college towns across the Midwest, the South, and upstate regions, the university is the economic heartbeat of the entire county. International students and recent graduates on OPT don't just pay tuition; they sign twelve-month apartment leases, buy cars from local dealerships, shop at neighborhood grocery stores, eat at local restaurants, and pay state and local sales taxes every single day. Nationwide, that adds up to over $40 billion a year flowing directly into local American communities and supporting hundreds of thousands of local jobs.

For most international students, the ability to gain one to three years of practical work experience through OPT is the main reason they choose to study in the United States instead of going to the UK, Canada, or Australia. When you slap a $70,000 to $100,000 penalty on that program, international enrollment will plummet immediately.

When those students disappear, the university isn't the only one taking a financial hit. Local apartment buildings sit empty, family-owned restaurants and coffee shops lose their customer base, and local retail stores have to cut shifts or lay off American workers. There is no backup industry in most college towns to replace that lost revenue.

This fee does nothing to help everyday Americans. Instead, it pulls billions of dollars out of local towns and punishes the waiters, store clerks, contractors, and small business owners who keep campus communities running. Please withdraw this short-sighted proposal before it hollow outs our local economies.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the high OPT fees will devastate local economies, harm universities, and cause international enrollment to plummet.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Optional Practical Training Fees, Docket ICEB-2026-0100

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT recommendation fee and $30,000 subsequent recommendation fee in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i). I ask DHS to withdraw these fee amounts and preserve an accessible pathway for legitimate practical training.

I am a graduate student studying biostatistics and data science, with academic and research experience in public health and artificial intelligence. Supervised practical experience offers a way to apply statistical methods to real health data, learn how research findings inform decisions, and develop skills that classroom instruction alone cannot provide. The proposed fees would create substantial uncertainty about whether students can pursue these educational opportunities after completing their studies.

The proposal acknowledges that institutions may pass the costs to students or employers. If students bear the costs, access to training could depend on financial resources rather than academic preparation or the educational quality of an opportunity. If employers bear them, smaller research organizations, nonprofit organizations, and public-health employers could find it harder to offer training. These are potential consequences that deserve careful analysis, rather than assumptions that every participant or institution can absorb the costs.

I support effective measures to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers. However, a large uniform fee does not directly establish whether a particular training opportunity is genuine or compliant. DHS should evaluate less burdensome alternatives, including risk-based reviews of suspect employers, verification of training relationships, and enforcement focused on documented violations. Any necessary administrative charges should be supported by a transparent analysis of relevant costs and their effects on access.

I also ask DHS to give meaningful weight to the reliance interests of students already enrolled in U.S. degree programs. A 60-day transition after publication of a final rule would provide limited time for students, universities, and prospective training providers to adjust academic and career plans. DHS should protect currently enrolled students and provide a substantially longer transition if it proceeds with any new fee structure.

Please preserve legitimate, supervised practical training while addressing specific compliance problems through proportionate, evidence-based measures. Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Strong Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. These excessive fees would undermine American higher education, economic competitiveness, innovation, and fairness without adequately addressing the stated concerns about program integrity.

1. Harm to American Universities and the Economy

International students contribute significantly to U.S. universities and local economies through tuition, housing, consumption, and research. Imposing enormous fees on educational institutions would create unsustainable financial burdens, discourage international enrollment, and weaken the competitiveness of American higher education.

2. Loss of Talent and Innovation

OPT allows international graduates to apply their education through practical training in the United States. These fees would discourage talented students from choosing American universities and push skilled graduates toward competing countries, harming American research, technological advancement, and economic growth.

3. Disproportionate Impact on Smaller Institutions

A $70,000 fee per student would disproportionately burden smaller universities, public institutions, and research programs with limited financial resources. This could effectively eliminate OPT opportunities at many institutions, regardless of students’ qualifications or compliance with immigration requirements.

4. Unfair and Ineffective Approach to Fraud Prevention

Excessive financial barriers do not directly address immigration fraud. Legitimate students and compliant institutions should not face extraordinary financial penalties because of misconduct by others. Targeted enforcement, improved verification, and stronger oversight would be more proportionate and effective alternatives.

5. Insufficient Economic Justification

DHS should demonstrate that the proposed fees are reasonably connected to actual administrative and enforcement costs and that their benefits outweigh the substantial economic consequences. The proposal risks causing far more economic harm than any anticipated regulatory benefit.

Conclusion

The proposed OPT fees are excessive, economically counterproductive, and inconsistent with America’s long-term interests in education, innovation, and global competitiveness.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal, preserve accessible OPT opportunities, and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures to address legitimate program integrity concerns.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the excessive OPT fees, arguing they harm universities, the economy, and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sherry M
comments.commentText:
I support the proposed $70,000 fee for the initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 fee for any subsequent recommendation (including STEM OPT). These fees, paid by SEVP-certified schools before a DSO can enter an OPT recommendation in SEVIS, are a necessary step to reduce fraud and prioritize American workers.
Recent Federal Reserve Bank of New York data show a 5.2% unemployment rate for recent college graduates (ages 22–27) and a 42.5% underemployment rate among those employed—the highest underemployment since October 2020. Hundreds of thousands of American graduates who earned degrees and took on debt are either unemployed or working in jobs that do not require a degree. Many of these fields overlap heavily with OPT participation.
In 2024, roughly 194,500 international students received OPT authorization and about 95,000 received STEM OPT. OPT is a regulatory program, not a statutory right, and often functions as an uncapped bridge to longer-term work authorization. It expands the supply of entry-level talent in computer science, engineering, and related fields without the recruitment or wage protections that apply to H-1B. This disadvantages American-born recent graduates competing for the same roles.
ICE has identified more than 10,000 F-1 students linked to highly suspect OPT employers—empty offices, residential addresses with no employees, shell companies, and “pay-to-stay” schemes. Earlier cases such as Findream involved thousands of false employment verifications. High fees create a strong incentive for schools to verify legitimate training relationships and discourage high-volume, low-scrutiny recommendations.
The fees will not end legitimate OPT. They will reduce routine use of the program as a low-cost labor pipeline and pressure employers to recruit qualified Americans first. Universities that value continued OPT access can absorb or pass on the cost; those that cannot will become more selective. Exceptional international students will still find pathways when the economic case is strong. Any reduction in international enrollment or OPT volume is an acceptable trade-off given documented fraud and the employment challenges facing American graduates.
American-born citizens deserve priority in the domestic labor market. These fees advance that priority while addressing fraud at scale. I urge DHS to finalize the rule as proposed.
Respectfully submitted,
Sherry M
Houston, Texas
U.S. Citizen, mother of 3 Gen Z in college or just out of college, taxpayer

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation, and use targeted measures to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers.

DHS has a legitimate responsibility to enforce immigration law and address abuse, including fictitious worksites and “pay-to-stay” arrangements. Enforcement should nevertheless be proportionate and avoid needlessly burdening legitimate students, schools, employers, and research institutions.

The fees must be paid by SEVP-certified schools before a designated school official can recommend a student for OPT. The $70,000 fee applies to the student’s first OPT recommendation, whether pre-completion or post-completion. A $30,000 fee applies to each subsequent OPT recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. The fee is not tied to a specific employer or proven violation. A student using post-completion OPT followed by a STEM extension could therefore trigger $100,000 in school payments.

This risks deterring legitimate participation along with abuse. Schools with limited budgets may be unable or unwilling to absorb these costs. A qualified graduate with a genuine, degree-related job offer could lose OPT—not because of misconduct, but because the school cannot justify the expense.

DHS cites an investigation involving more than 10,000 F-1 students working for highly suspect employers. These concerns warrant action, but association with a suspect employer is not proof that each student committed fraud. DHS should disclose how many cases resulted in substantiated violations, who was responsible, and what proportion of OPT participation involved confirmed misconduct. Policy should rest on verified outcomes, not suspicion.

OPT participants may compete with U.S. graduates for some jobs, and effects on wages and hiring deserve evaluation. But every OPT position lost will not necessarily become a job for an American; employers might leave positions vacant, reduce projects, or move work and investment elsewhere. DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how much participation the fees would reduce. It should assess effects on U.S. hiring, wages, vacancies, and investment before concluding that these fees protect American workers.

The impact on doctoral researchers and innovation also deserves attention. Eligible F-1 doctoral graduates contribute to scientific discovery, medical research, engineering, artificial intelligence, and other fields with long-term value. Their work strengthens research teams, advances technology, and trains future scientists and engineers. DHS should assess how these fees could affect universities, laboratories, hospitals, and research programs that may lack resources to pay them. Discouraging legitimate early-career researchers could weaken U.S. research capacity and push projects or talent abroad.

The public value of technical work extends beyond research output or immediate job creation. In my work on health-related technology, I have seen U.S. users describe how features helped them recognize potentially serious health conditions or seek timely medical attention. Some described these experiences as life-changing or even life-saving. No single feature deserves sole credit for a health outcome, but this shows how engineering can benefit Americans. These contributions cannot be measured only by counting jobs filled.

DHS estimates about $12.4 billion in annual fee transfers under its primary scenario; collections would go to the U.S. Treasury, not be earmarked for OPT oversight or enforcement. DHS argues fees would deter abuse and encourage school scrutiny. It should explain why these amounts are necessary, how they relate to oversight costs or demonstrated risks, and how success will be measured. A fee that sharply reduces participation is not necessarily effective enforcement.

DHS should evaluate alternatives: risk-based audits and worksite verification; stronger employment and training-record checks; scrutiny of high-risk employers and schools; and meaningful penalties for proven misconduct. A pilot or phased approach could test these measures before imposing a uniform fee.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the fees in their current form; publish data distinguishing suspected from substantiated fraud; assess labor-market and research impacts; and compare targeted alternatives using transparent measures of cost and effectiveness. Protecting U.S. workers and program integrity is essential, but should not undermine legitimate education, research, and innovation without evidence these extraordinary fees are necessary and effective.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees, arguing they burden legitimate students and schools.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees
Dear DHS and ICE Officials:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw these fees. In my view, they would undermine America’s ability to attract outstanding international students, weaken the economic benefits of international education, and impose disproportionate burdens on legitimate students, universities, and employers.
Regarding Sections IV.C and V.A, the proposed fees would make access to practical training depend heavily on financial resources. A student’s ability to finance an extraordinary fee—or a university’s willingness to absorb it—is a poor measure of academic achievement, professional potential, or compliance with immigration rules. Talented students from modest financial backgrounds could lose access to valuable training despite fully meeting program requirements. Charging universities does not eliminate this problem: institutions could pass costs to students, reduce educational spending, or stop recommending otherwise qualified students for OPT.
I am particularly concerned that these barriers would discourage talented students from choosing American universities in the first place. The opportunity to apply classroom learning through lawful, supervised practical experience is a legitimate educational consideration. Making that experience financially inaccessible could redirect students toward other countries. The United States would risk losing both their educational spending and the opportunity for American research teams and businesses to benefit from their skills.
Regarding Section VII.A, the economic analysis should fully account for these broader effects. NAFSA and JB International estimated that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. These figures describe existing economic contributions, not projected losses from this proposal, but they demonstrate the scale of the interests at stake. Reduced enrollment could affect universities and surrounding businesses through lower spending on tuition, housing, food, transportation, and other services. Source: NAFSA, November 17, 2025.
DHS should evaluate potential losses in enrollment, research output, entrepreneurship, and economic activity alongside any anticipated benefits. It should also assess how burdens would differ across public universities, smaller institutions, startups, and nonprofit employers. Fee collections alone do not establish a net economic benefit. Nor should the analysis assume that every reduction in OPT participation produces an equivalent employment opportunity for a U.S. worker; that outcome requires evidence accounting for differences in skills, business responses, and changes in economic activity.
Regarding Sections IV.A–IV.C, I support preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, the ability to pay a large fee does not establish that a training arrangement is legitimate, and inability to pay does not establish abuse. DHS should demonstrate why these particular amounts would effectively distinguish misconduct from lawful participation. Targeted audits, verification of genuine training arrangements, enforcement against fraudulent institutions and employers, and enforcement of applicable worker protections would address misconduct more directly. DHS should compare the effectiveness and costs of those alternatives before imposing a broad financial barrier.
Regarding Sections V.C and VI, DHS should give greater weight to students who have already committed substantial time and resources to U.S. education under the existing framework. Although OPT approval is not guaranteed, the opportunity to apply under reasonably predictable conditions can influence major educational decisions. If DHS proceeds with changes, it should protect already-enrolled students and existing OPT participants, including their otherwise eligible STEM extensions, through meaningful grandfathering provisions.
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, preserve affordable access to legitimate practical training, and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures against documented abuse. Protecting American workers and maintaining America’s attractiveness to global talent should be complementary policy objectives.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and requests that DHS withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by David Landau

Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is David Landau and I am an Emeritus Professor of Computational Physics at the University of Georgia.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

While I am a native born U.S. citizen, I have mentored dozens of foreign born M.S. and Ph.D. students who have remained in the U.S. and enriched our nation with their skills. This would have been impossible if OPT fees had been at the proposed, excessive levels.

I cannot emphasize strongly enough how much the U.S. has benefited fform the expertise of international students who have remained in the U.S. following completion of their degrees and played significant roles in research and/or teaching at American universities and corporations.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Dr. David Landau
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessive and asks DHS to withdraw the rule to protect the U.S. STEM talent pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 international student currently pursuing my master's degree in the United States, and I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, including for STEM OPT extensions. I believe these fees could have serious consequences not only for international students but also for American universities, research institutions, employers, and the broader U.S. economy.

International students make enormous financial and personal sacrifices to pursue higher education in the United States. Many of us depend on educational loans, family savings, and years of financial planning. We already pay substantial tuition, living expenses, health insurance, and immigration-related fees. OPT provides a valuable opportunity to apply our education, develop professional skills, and gain practical experience in our fields.

Although the proposed fees would be imposed on educational institutions, their consequences could extend far beyond university budgets. Institutions may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial costs, potentially limiting OPT recommendations or passing costs on to students. This could make practical training inaccessible to many qualified international graduates, regardless of their academic achievements or professional abilities.

I am also concerned about the impact on American higher education. International students contribute tuition revenue, diverse perspectives, research assistance, and academic expertise to universities across the country. If studying in the United States becomes significantly less attractive because of reduced post-graduation opportunities, universities could experience declining international enrollment and associated financial losses. Research laboratories and academic programs could also lose access to talented students and graduates who support research, teaching, and innovation.

The consequences could extend to American businesses and the economy. International graduates contribute specialized knowledge and skills to fields such as technology, healthcare, engineering, science, and research. OPT allows employers to benefit from graduates educated at American institutions. If these opportunities become financially inaccessible, employers may lose access to qualified candidates, research projects may lose contributors, and the United States may lose valuable opportunities for innovation and economic activity.

Furthermore, international students have choices about where to pursue their education and build their careers. If the United States introduces financial barriers of this magnitude, prospective students may increasingly consider countries offering more accessible post-study work opportunities. Over time, this could weaken the global competitiveness of American universities and reduce the country's ability to attract and retain international talent.

As a master's student approaching graduation, this proposal is particularly concerning to me. After investing years of effort and substantial financial resources into my education, the possibility that practical training opportunities could become inaccessible creates uncertainty about my professional and financial future. Students who have followed immigration regulations in good faith should not face disproportionate barriers to applying the education they worked so hard to obtain.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud, protecting American workers, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, I believe targeted oversight, stronger verification procedures, and proportionate enforcement measures would address those concerns more effectively without creating financial barriers that could harm legitimate students, educational institutions, and employers.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw or substantially reconsider the proposed OPT fees and carefully evaluate their potential economic, educational, and workforce consequences. Policies intended to protect the United States should also consider the value that international students and graduates bring to its universities, research institutions, businesses, and communities.

Thank you for considering the concerns of international students whose educational investments, professional opportunities, and financial futures may be affected by this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm students, universities, and the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Edward Flagg
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am Edward Flagg, a professor of physics at West Virginia University.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Our department and the federal government spend a great deal of time and money educating and preparing students to contribute to the scientific endeavor of the U.S. Many of those students are international because for decades the U.S. has been the best place for smart people to come make the next step in their careers. After our University educates them, they often go on to a post-doctoral position, which sometimes requires an OPT visa. Furthermore, our department employs PhD graduates who use the OPT program. Increasing the OPT fees to the ludicrous amounts proposed will effectively shut down the OPT program except for the very richest corporations. No university will be able to pay a $100k fee for a single researcher. This will cut off the U.S. from the stream of scientists *that we have educated*. They will go to other countries. After we have spent our time and treasure educating them, we will not be able to reap the benefits. That will be the consequence of the vast increase in OPT fees.

The U.S. has held a dominant position in the world economy in large part because of our dominance in technology. That technology advantage comes from our educated people. Some of those people are from other countries, and the U.S. is stronger for their presence here. Instead of a "brain drain", where educated people leave an area because of a lack of opportunities, the U.S. has been a "brain magnet", attracting the best and brightest for almost a century. Policies like the increase in OPT fees threaten to immediately cause a brain drain in the U.S.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Edward Flagg

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
One potential consequence of the proposed OPT fees deserves more attention: the location where new intellectual property is developed and commercialized.

American universities produce research with applications in medicine, materials science, engineering, computing, and other fields. Turning a research finding into a commercial product often requires additional experimentation, technical validation, and collaboration with industry.

OPT can provide eligible international graduates with opportunities to participate in that process through degree-related practical training.

If substantial fees make those opportunities less accessible, some graduates may pursue professional development outside the United States. The research knowledge they acquired here may then contribute to commercial activities in other countries.

This does not mean that graduates take ownership of university intellectual property or that research results automatically leave the country. Patent ownership, confidentiality, and technology transfer are governed by separate legal and contractual arrangements.

The concern is about where future inventions, improvements, and commercial applications are developed.

The proposed fees under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) should be evaluated for their potential effects on domestic technology commercialization, patent-related activity, and research-to-industry transitions.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions pending an assessment of these longer-term economic consequences.

Targeted enforcement against fraudulent training arrangements would address compliance concerns more directly without imposing the same broad financial obstacles on legitimate graduates.

The United States has invested heavily in building a research environment that produces valuable knowledge. Regulatory decisions should consider whether they help retain the economic benefits of subsequent innovation within the country.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed substantial increase in fees associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT).

As an international student pursuing higher education in the United States, I am deeply concerned about the financial and professional consequences of making OPT prohibitively expensive.

International students already pay substantial tuition and living expenses, often without access to the same financial assistance or employment opportunities available to domestic students. OPT provides a critical opportunity to apply academic knowledge in professional settings and gain practical experience after graduation.

Imposing excessively high fees would effectively restrict OPT to students from exceptionally wealthy backgrounds. Access to professional development should not depend primarily on a student’s financial privilege.

Such a policy would also undermine the attractiveness of American higher education, discourage international talent from remaining in the United States, and weaken the connection between universities and the industries they support.

I urge the Department to reject any disproportionate fee increases and maintain OPT as an accessible pathway for eligible international graduates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public transportation systems do not improve on their own.

Cities need transportation planners, traffic engineers, geographic information specialists, and data analysts to understand congestion, improve bus routes, evaluate safety, and plan infrastructure investments.

Much of this work requires practical experience. A transportation planning graduate may understand modeling techniques in a classroom but still need professional training to work with actual ridership data, public budgets, and community needs.

OPT provides one pathway for eligible international graduates to gain that experience.

The proposed fees raise a concern for the organizations that depend on specialized planning skills, including transportation consultants, engineering firms, and research institutions.

Some public transportation projects already face staffing and budget constraints. If substantial OPT fees reduce access to qualified graduates, certain employers may experience additional recruitment difficulties.

I am not suggesting that international graduates are the only source of transportation expertise or that OPT restrictions would directly cause service reductions.

The question is whether DHS has adequately examined the potential effects on workforce development in transportation-related professions.

I request withdrawal of the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), together with a review of their potential impact on transportation planning and infrastructure development.

Compliance enforcement should focus on actual violations rather than using financial barriers that may affect legitimate practical training.

American communities need transportation systems that are safe, efficient, and accessible. Workforce policies should account for the technical expertise required to maintain and improve them.
comments.reason: The commenter requests withdrawal of the proposed fees due to potential negative workforce impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tobias Marriage
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security / U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

My name is Tobias Marriage. I am a professor of physics and astronomy at Johns Hopkins University, where I lead a lab that builds novel telescopes to study the early universe. Regarding DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, “Optional Practical Training Fees,” I am writing to oppose the new fees in Section V.A of the proposed rule: $70,000 for a school’s initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension.

Over the past eleven years, I have advised five international students who have used OPT. Their OPT followed clearly from their degree and advanced US science: developing multiplexed readout for quantum detectors, analyzing data for multiple astronomical surveys, and designing novel telescopes. Both during their degrees and during OPT, these talented young international scientists worked side by side with strong US students and scholars, a collaboration that elevated their collective research, benefitting the whole team and US science more broadly. All five of them remain in the United States, where they help train and inspire the next generation of American STEM innovators.

Because the proposed rule places the fee on the school, the decision about whether a student can pursue OPT would move from the student and employer to the university’s budget office. At $100,000 per STEM student, I expect that institutions like mine would be unable to absorb the cost for most of the excellent international students completing our programs. In practice the rule would close this pathway for most international students regardless of merit. The strongest of them would go to countries that offer post-study work routes, such as the UK’s Graduate Route or Canada’s Post-Graduation Work Permit, and they would take their expertise and future contributions with them.

In Section IV.C, DHS states that the fees are intended to combat fraud, strengthen program integrity, and protect U.S. workers. I share the goal of a program free of abuse. However, a flat fee falls equally on legitimate research training and on any fraudulent arrangements. Furthermore, in my experience, OPT participants, far from displacing US workers, raise the level of research for everyone involved, US-born and foreign-born alike. If DHS has identified patterns of fraud, I encourage it to address them through targeted measures, such as strengthened employer verification, audits of training plans, or enforcement against noncompliant employers, rather than a flat fee that uniformly chokes off the remarkable creativity and productivity of collaborations that stem from OPT.

In summary, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, which would deal a blow to American innovation. Instead, DHS should pursue more targeted measures to combat any observed patterns of fraud. U.S.–international collaboration is a central reason American science and technology leads the world, and OPT is a primary pathway that sustains it.

Sincerely,
Tobias Marriage
Professor of Physics and Astronomy, Johns Hopkins University
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm university budgets and international STEM collaboration.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,
I am an international graduate student who has invested years of time, money, and hard work in pursuing an education in the United States. I am concerned that the proposed OPT fees, combined with restrictions on Curricular Practical Training (CPT), could make it increasingly difficult for international students to gain experience and build careers in the fields they studied.

Internships are essential to professional development, particularly for students in STEM-designated programs. They allow us to apply classroom knowledge, build skills, and demonstrate our abilities to employers. When CPT opportunities become harder to access, students may graduate without the experience employers expect, making it more difficult to compete for jobs during OPT. Adding substantial OPT fees creates another barrier for students and institutions that already face significant costs.

What is the purpose of investing years in an American education if opportunities to apply that education become increasingly inaccessible?

I recognize the importance of enforcing immigration rules and protecting American workers. However, violations by some individuals should not justify broad barriers for students who comply with the rules. Targeted oversight and enforcement can address abuses without unnecessarily limiting legitimate educational and training opportunities.

These decisions could also affect universities and local communities. International students pay tuition, rent housing, spend money in local businesses, contribute to research, and participate in campus life. The Institute of International Education reported declines in new international student enrollment in fall 2025. Although multiple factors affect enrollment, uncertainty about practical training can influence whether prospective students choose the United States or another country.

Employers may also face consequences. Some industries struggle to recruit people with specialized skills, language abilities, and international experience. Limiting the pool of qualified candidates can increase hiring difficulties and workloads for existing employees. In fields such as hospitality, staffing challenges can affect turnover, stress, and service quality. Businesses may also consider expanding recruitment or operations elsewhere if access to talent becomes more difficult.

International students have options. Other countries offer strong academic programs and pathways to professional experience. If studying and training in the United States becomes too costly or uncertain, students may choose to take their tuition, skills, and future contributions elsewhere.

After years of sacrifices, I am now questioning whether I will have a fair opportunity to use the education I worked so hard to earn. I am not asking for guaranteed employment or special treatment. I am asking for the chance to gain experience, compete fairly, and contribute.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed OPT fees, examine their effects on students and educational institutions, and consider how CPT restrictions compound these barriers. Immigration compliance and workforce protections matter, but so do the long-term interests of American universities, employers, communities, and students who have followed the rules.

Thank you for considering this perspective.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees create financial barriers and limit legitimate training opportunities for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed imposition of additional fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). This proposal risks undermining one of the United States’ greatest competitive advantages: its ability to attract, educate, and retain talented individuals from around the world.

International students already make substantial financial contributions to the American economy. They frequently pay higher tuition rates, face significant restrictions on employment while studying, and must navigate an expensive and complicated immigration system. Imposing additional fees simply for the opportunity to gain practical experience in their fields would create yet another financial obstacle for individuals who have already invested considerable resources in American education.

More importantly, OPT is not a privilege that benefits international students alone. It is a program that benefits the United States. International graduates contribute their knowledge, skills, innovation, and productivity to American businesses. They help fill specialized positions, support research institutions, and strengthen the country’s position in an increasingly competitive global economy.

The United States should be encouraging talented graduates to contribute to its workforce, not making that opportunity progressively more expensive.

There is also a fundamental issue of fairness. International students pursue their education under a system that offers limited opportunities for authorized practical training. Introducing additional financial burdens on access to that training risks disproportionately affecting students from lower-income backgrounds. A student’s ability to gain professional experience should not depend on their financial capacity to absorb an ever-growing series of administrative fees.

Furthermore, the agency should demonstrate that any proposed fee is necessary, proportionate, and supported by a transparent accounting of actual administrative costs. Regulatory fees should reflect legitimate administrative expenses, not function as financial barriers to lawful participation in an established immigration program. Without a convincing justification, additional fees risk appearing arbitrary and unnecessarily burdensome.

The long-term consequences deserve serious consideration. International students have choices about where to pursue their education and begin their careers. Countries around the world are competing to attract highly educated individuals. If the United States continues increasing the financial and administrative obstacles facing international graduates, it risks pushing talent, investment, and innovation toward competing economies.

This is not simply an immigration issue. It is an issue of economic competitiveness, educational opportunity, and the future of American leadership.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reconsider this proposal, provide a rigorous justification for any additional costs, and fully evaluate its potential economic and educational consequences.

The United States should not invest in educating the world’s brightest minds only to create unnecessary financial barriers when they are ready to contribute to the American economy.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the agency to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yiming Chen
comments.commentText:
I’m an international student here on an F-1 visa, and I came to the U.S. to study. Between tuition, rent, daily living and travel, I spend about $200,000 a year, and most of that money goes to my school and to small local businesses.

I agree that OPT fraud is a real problem and that the government should stop it. I’m also fine with OPT users paying a reasonable fee to cover the cost of enforcement.

This proposal doesn’t do that. Nowhere does it say what enforcement actually costs or how that cost turns into $70,000 per student, plus $30,000 for each OPT after that. The problem is real, but this fix doesn’t match it. Please withdraw this proposal and replace it with a fee based on real enforcement costs, along with stronger checks on the employers who are actually committing fraud.

**Subject: Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees (Docket ICEB-2026-0100)**

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) - Oppose. The $70,000 initial fee is not a fee for a service. There is currently no school fee for an OPT recommendation, and a student already pays the USCIS Form I-765 filing fee ($470 online / $520 paper). DHS does not tie $70,000 or $30,000 to the actual cost of entering a recommendation in SEVIS, reviewing a file, or administering OPT. The NPRM itself says the money would be deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt under 31 U.S.C. 3302, that ICE would not retain or use it for SEVP or enforcement, and that deterrence is the point regardless of whether Congress later appropriates it. DHS estimates $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion a year, $12.4 billion as its primary estimate. A charge of that scale, untethered to cost and paid into general revenue, is a tax and a deterrent penalty, not a user fee. DHS should withdraw it and, if any fee is proposed, justify it with actual program costs.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is an unjustified deterrent tax and should be withdrawn by DHS.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) and the Legal Authority discussion - Oppose for lack of statutory authority. DHS relies principally on INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), the power to prescribe the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission. Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld DHS authority to create OPT; it did not hold that DHS may impose a $70,000 charge on a third party, a school, as a condition of a recommendation, or levy billions of dollars for the general Treasury. Congress has set specific immigration fees elsewhere in the INA. It has never authorized this charge, on this payer, at anything near this magnitude. A decision of this economic and political significance - effectively pricing a national training program out of existence - requires clear congressional authorization, which INA 214(a) does not supply.
comments.reason: Argues DHS lacks statutory authority to impose such massive fees, effectively pricing out the OPT program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i) - Oppose because this is a de facto elimination of OPT, not regulation of it. DHS acknowledges schools may stop paying, reduce pre-completion OPT, and become selective about which students they recommend, and that DSOs will become financial gatekeepers who may deny a recommendation to a student who is not judged a strong candidate. A qualified student would lose practical training - training directly related to the degree the F-1 program contemplates - not because the student is ineligible, not because the job is unrelated, and not because of any misconduct, but because the institution will not pay $70,000. If the government wishes to end OPT, that choice belongs to Congress after open debate. It should not be achieved indirectly by pricing every recommendation beyond what schools can rationally pay.
comments.reason: Argues the proposed fees are a de facto elimination of OPT that unfairly prices students out of practical training.

DHS estimates 1,389 small affected institutions, of which 841 (60.5 percent) would face impacts greater than 1 percent of annual revenue in the transition year. In that year 116 small institutions (8.4 percent) would face impacts greater than 20 percent of revenue, 85 would face 10 to 20 percent, and 135 would face 5 to 10 percent. Those are existential figures for small colleges, language schools, and specialized programs. A rule that its own author calculates could consume more than a fifth of a small school's revenue cannot be cured by telling the school to find outside funding or to stop recommending students. At minimum the impact on small entities alone requires withdrawal.

Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am Antonio Redondo, a scientist at Los Alamos National Laboratory and former head of its Theoretical Division.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international PhD student in engineering who has dedicated years to pursuing advanced education, conducting research, and gaining professional experience in the United States. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2).
1. Disproportionate Financial Burden on Universities and Students (Sections IV.C and VII.A.4)
In Section IV.C (91 FR 64575), DHS explicitly acknowledges that educational institutions may pass the financial burden of these fees onto international students, other students, or employers. This raises a serious concern: even though universities are officially responsible for paying the fees, students could ultimately bear the costs.
Furthermore, DHS estimates in Section VII.A.4 (91 FR 64583, Table 3) that the proposed fees could generate between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion annually, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. These figures demonstrate the extraordinary financial scale of the proposal.
Many universities, particularly smaller institutions and publicly funded research universities, may be unable to absorb these costs. As a result, qualified students could lose access to practical training simply because their institutions cannot afford the fees.
2. Financial Ability Does Not Establish Academic Merit or Prevent Fraud (Sections IV.A and IV.C)
In Section IV.A (91 FR 64570–64571), DHS describes fraudulent employment arrangements, including shell companies and nonexistent workplaces. I recognize the seriousness of these concerns and support stronger enforcement against such activities.
However, Section IV.C (91 FR 64574) suggests that requiring substantial fees would encourage institutions to recommend only highly qualified students. Financial capacity is not an appropriate measure of academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration regulations.
A student who has maintained lawful status, successfully completed an advanced degree, and secured legitimate training should not be denied an opportunity solely because their university cannot pay $70,000.
DHS should instead prioritize targeted employer verification, compliance investigations, and enforcement against fraudulent entities rather than imposing financial barriers on all students.
3. Negative Consequences for Research and STEM Education (Sections VI and VII.A.5)
In Section VI (91 FR 64578), DHS recognizes that the proposed fees could affect institutions' existing budgets and suggests that universities could mitigate those impacts by transferring the costs to students or employers.
This approach does not eliminate the financial burden; it simply transfers it to another party.
For international graduate students in engineering and other STEM fields, practical training provides an opportunity to apply years of specialized education and research to real-world challenges. These experiences can benefit American businesses, infrastructure development, and technological innovation.
The proposed fees could discourage universities from supporting OPT participation, limit access to professional training, and make the United States less attractive to talented international researchers.
4. Opposition to Repeated Fees at Higher Educational Levels (Section V.A)
In Section V.A (91 FR 64577), DHS specifically requests public comments on an alternative that would impose an additional $70,000 initial OPT fee whenever a student advances to a higher educational level.
I strongly oppose this alternative. Students who continue from bachelor's to master's or doctoral programs are investing additional years in education and developing specialized expertise. Repeatedly imposing such substantial fees would create an additional financial barrier to advanced education and professional development.
Requested Action
I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), reject the alternative of repeating the $70,000 fee at higher educational levels, and consider more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing OPT fraud.
Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs are legitimate and important objectives. However, these goals should be achieved through effective enforcement and oversight, not by imposing disproportionate financial barriers on legitimate international students, educational institutions, and employers.
Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to submit my formal comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to implement a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extensions. While the stated intent of this rule is to protect domestic workers and prevent program reliance, an empirical, data-driven analysis of the international student ecosystem demonstrates that this astronomical fee structure will severely damage U.S. higher education, stifle critical talent pipelines, and cause net harm to local and national economies.

1. The Financial Stabilization of U.S. Higher Education
International students act as a critical financial pillar for American universities. The vast majority of international undergraduates and master's students pay full, out-of-state tuition entirely out-of-pocket, with virtually no access to federal financial aid or state subsidies. According to data from NAFSA: Association of International Educators, during the 2022-2023 academic year alone, international students contributed $40.1 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 368,000 jobs. This massive influx of out-of-state tuition directly subsidizes institutional infrastructure, research facilities, and financial aid budgets that make higher education more affordable for domestic, in-state American students. Imposing a massive financial barrier at the post-completion stage will cause a sharp decline in international enrollment, leaving universities with severe budget shortfalls.

2. Direct Contributions to Local Businesses and Consumer Markets
International students do not live in an economic vacuum. During their years of study and subsequent operational training, they spend billions of dollars directly supporting local economies. This includes housing rentals, grocery stores, automotive purchases, utilities, consumer electronics, and local services. By discouraging international students from choosing the United States, DHS is effectively draining consumer capital out of college towns and metropolitan areas across the country, directly harming small businesses that rely on student populations to sustain their operations.

3. Fiscal Contributions Through Taxation and Work-Authorized Spending
When international graduates transition to OPT and STEM OPT, they become highly productive, tax-paying contributors to the U.S. labor force. Individuals working on OPT are subject to federal, state, and local income taxes. The wages earned by these specialized professionals are immediately recycled back into the U.S. economy through local rent, consumer spending, and tax revenues, creating a robust fiscal multiplier effect. A $70,000 baseline fee transforms the OPT program from an earned opportunity into an unviable financial liability, cutting off these vital tax streams.

4. Destruction of Critical STEM and Technology Talent Pipelines
The United States is currently facing severe domestic skill shortages in highly specialized technical fields, including critical infrastructure areas such as Mainframe systems, software engineering, and Artificial Intelligence (AI). American corporations rely on the OPT and STEM OPT programs to bridge these operational gaps with U.S.-educated talent. Forcing universities or employers to absorb a combined $100,000 in regulatory fees to authorize a single graduate completely blocks the entry-level talent pipeline. Instead of protecting domestic jobs, this policy will compel multinational corporations to outsource critical technology operations, engineering hubs, and high-value projects overseas to countries with more competitive talent pipelines, such as India, China, Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia.

Conclusion
The proposed fee structure is economically prohibitive and legally counterproductive. It fails to account for the profound economic benefits that international students provide through out-of-state tuition, local consumer spending, and critical technical labor. I strongly urge the Department to withdraw this proposal and maintain the standard, accessible infrastructure of the OPT program to ensure the United States remains the global leader in innovation and economic growth.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they will harm the U.S. economy and higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01), Comment in Opposition to the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT recommendation. I am an F-1 master's student in Computer Science. I moved across the world to pursue this degree, and this rule would change the terms of that decision after I have already made it. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The fee would effectively eliminate OPT for most students.
This is not a nominal administrative charge. It is more than a year of tuition and living costs for many international students, and it applies to every student seeking OPT. Schools must pay it before a DSO can enter an OPT recommendation, and it is not refundable once an EAD is issued. DHS acknowledges schools may pass the cost on to students. Very few schools can absorb $70,000 per student, so students must pay it themselves or lose OPT. Most cannot, having already spent their savings or taken on debt for their degrees.

2. Current students are being punished for decisions made under different rules.
I and thousands of other students enrolled in good faith under the rules as they stood. We paid application, SEVIS, and visa fees, tuition, relocation costs, and a year or more of living expenses, tens of thousands of dollars in total, understanding that OPT was part of the path. DHS says applying the rule only to recommendations dated after the effective date addresses reliance interests. It does not. A student who has not yet received a recommendation has already spent the money and moved their life. DHS itself concedes in a footnote that current students are in a different position, then dismisses their reliance anyway. At minimum, every student enrolled before this proposal was published on October 8, 2026 should be fully exempt.

3. The timing makes the harm worse.
Technology graduates face one of the hardest entry-level job markets in years, and DHS's own proposal cites high unemployment among recent computer science graduates. A $70,000 charge attached to the work authorization we need to get that first job makes us less hireable. Many employers will simply skip us. The rule would close the main door through which international graduates, who have invested heavily in U.S. education, can start their careers.

4. The rule will drive away future students and hurt U.S. universities.
DHS notes that only about 20 percent of F-1 students used OPT in 2024 and treats OPT as incidental to the decision to study here. That reasoning is flawed. OPT use is concentrated among graduate students in STEM and other high-demand fields, the students U.S. universities and employers most want. For them, practical training is a central reason to choose the United States over Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, or Germany. DHS's own regulatory analysis recognizes that institutions could see enrollment declines and lost tuition revenue, yet says these cannot be precisely quantified. Prospective students will see a six-figure penalty on top of tuition and choose another country. Universities, local economies, research programs, and employers would all bear the cost.

5. The fraud concerns do not justify a fee this broad.
Fraud by shell companies and visa mills deserves enforcement. But a blanket fee punishes the honest majority, treating students at reputable universities with legitimate employers the same as the schemes DHS describes. DHS rejected targeted alternatives such as expanded site visits, reporting, and stricter procedures in a single paragraph. Those would address fraud directly without destroying legitimate OPT.

6. I oppose charging the initial fee again at each degree level.
This alternative, on which DHS invites comment, would make it nearly impossible to pursue advanced degrees in the United States.

Requests: I respectfully ask that DHS (1) withdraw the proposed rule; (2) if not withdrawn, exempt all students enrolled on or before October 8, 2026, including post-completion and STEM OPT; (3) sharply reduce the fee and tie it to demonstrated risk, such as schools or employers with documented compliance problems; (4) reject the per-degree-level alternative; and (5) publish a full analysis of the effect on international enrollment and university revenue before any final rule.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they are prohibitive and unfairly punish current students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my concerns about DHS's proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations under 8 CFR 214.13.

While I recognize the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers, the proposed fee structure could create significant unintended economic consequences for American businesses, universities, and the broader U.S. economy.

1. Negative Impact on American Businesses and Workforce Development

OPT provides American employers with access to graduates who have received education and training in the United States. Many of these individuals develop specialized skills, gain familiarity with American industries, and are prepared to contribute immediately to the workforce.

If schools become unwilling or unable to pay the proposed fees, businesses could lose access to qualified candidates who are already educated and available in the United States. Recruiting replacements takes time and money, and suitable domestic candidates may not always be readily available for specialized positions.

This could increase hiring costs, delay projects, reduce productivity, and make it more difficult for American businesses, particularly small and medium-sized companies, to compete and innovate.

Restricting access to OPT does not automatically create an equivalent supply of qualified American workers. It could instead leave businesses with fewer qualified candidates and greater operational challenges.

2. Negative Impact on American Universities and the Education Sector

International students contribute significantly to American universities through tuition, research, academic collaboration, and innovation.

The availability of practical training opportunities is also an important consideration for many students choosing where to pursue higher education.

If universities face a $70,000 financial obligation for each initial OPT recommendation, they may become reluctant to support otherwise qualified students. This could discourage prospective international students from choosing American institutions, reducing university enrollment and revenue.

Over time, the United States could lose not only international tuition revenue but also valuable research talent and the economic contributions associated with international education.

3. The Proposed Fees Are Not a Targeted Approach to Preventing Fraud

I understand DHS's concerns about fraudulent OPT employment and abuse of the program. However, imposing the same extraordinary fee on every student does not distinguish between legitimate employment and fraudulent activity.

A student with a genuine job offer from a reputable American company should not face the same financial barrier as someone involved in a fraudulent arrangement.

DHS should prioritize targeted audits of high-risk institutions, investigations of fraudulent employers, and stronger verification of actual employment and training activities.

These measures would address the underlying problems more directly without unnecessarily restricting legitimate employment opportunities or imposing disproportionate costs on compliant universities and businesses.

4. The Economic Costs Deserve Greater Consideration

DHS's own regulatory analysis acknowledges that reduced OPT participation could result in productivity losses for employers, lower international student enrollment, and lost economic opportunities.

It also estimates annual fee collections ranging from $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion. However, the analysis acknowledges that there is insufficient data to precisely quantify the broader economic value lost when students cannot participate in OPT.

Government revenue should not be treated as an adequate measure of economic benefit. The long-term contributions of skilled workers, productive businesses, university research, and innovation must also be considered.

A policy that generates substantial fee revenue while reducing access to qualified talent may ultimately impose costs on the American economy that outweigh its intended benefits.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure.

If the objective is to strengthen OPT program integrity and protect American workers, DHS should pursue targeted enforcement, improved oversight, and risk-based compliance measures rather than imposing extraordinary financial barriers on every OPT recommendation.

The United States benefits when its universities educate talented individuals and its businesses have the opportunity to employ qualified graduates. OPT serves as an important connection between American higher education and the domestic workforce.

Protecting program integrity and maintaining America's ability to attract talent should be complementary goals, not competing ones.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will negatively impact American businesses, universities, and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01), Comment in Opposition to the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. I am an F-1 master's student in Computer Science. I moved across the world to pursue this degree, and this rule would change the terms of that decision after I have made it. The rule contradicts its own rationale in several ways. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The fee cannot fund the oversight DHS says it needs. DHS says it cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on fraud without the fees. Yet the rule states the fees would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, that ICE would not keep or use them, and that they are not earmarked for SEVP or enforcement. The fee raises no resources for oversight. DHS also designs the rule to shrink OPT, expecting a smaller pool of participants and treating unpaid fees as lost participation. A fee that succeeds by deterring use produces less revenue, and a fee that produces revenue has failed to deter. DHS does not say which it expects.

2. The remedy does not match the fraud described. DHS's examples involve shell employers, fake worksites, and visa mills, such as 15 students arrested in 2020. DHS's largest figure, more than 10,000 students working for highly suspect employers, is about 5 percent of the 194,554 students who received OPT in 2024, and those cases are suspected, not confirmed. The fee is paid by schools and, in practice, students. Employers pay nothing, even though DHS's worker-protection concerns, including wages and the FICA exemption, are employer-side. The rule does not address FICA. It also states it does not address CPT. A blanket fee on every honest student is not tailored to the conduct DHS describes.

3. DHS points students to the H-1B while pricing that path out. The rule says F-1 students may pursue employment through the H-1B, yet sets the OPT fee to align with H-1B fees and cites the $100,000 H-1B proclamation. Raising both fees leaves international graduates with no workable route to employment.

4. The rule creates the foreign-funding risk it warns about. DHS says large foreign payments toward OPT fees could be red flags for adversaries seeking to subsidize schools. But it sets six-figure per-student costs, allows schools to pass them to students, and imposes no limits on how fees are funded. That increases the incentive for outside funding.

5. Pre-completion OPT is penalized. DHS's own example has a school paying $70,000 for a student's pre-completion OPT and $30,000 for post-completion OPT with the same employer, $100,000 in total. That discourages the hands-on training directly related to a student's major that DHS says OPT exists to provide. Refunds are discretionary and not appealable.

6. Current students bear costs they could not foresee. We enrolled in good faith, paying application, SEVIS, and visa fees, tuition, relocation, and living costs, tens of thousands of dollars in total, understanding OPT was part of the path. DHS applies the rule to any recommendation dated after the effective date and admits current students are differently situated than prospective ones, then dismisses their reliance. At minimum, all students enrolled before October 8, 2026 should be exempt.

7. The harms are acknowledged but not measured. DHS concedes enrollment declines and lost tuition revenue are possible but cannot quantify them. It rejected exempting small schools because 56 percent are small entities, while admitting it cannot predict how many would be affected. It dismisses OPT's role in enrollment by noting only 20 percent of F-1 students used it in 2024, ignoring that use is concentrated among STEM graduate students. In a weak entry-level technology job market, the fee makes international graduates harder to hire, and prospective students will study in Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia instead.

8. I oppose charging the initial fee again at each degree level, which would make advanced degrees nearly impossible.

I respectfully ask that DHS (1) withdraw the rule; (2) if not, exempt students enrolled before October 8, 2026, including STEM OPT; (3) replace the blanket fee with targeted measures against documented bad actors; (4) reject the per-degree alternative; and (5) publish expected participation, revenue, and enrollment estimates before any final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.commentText:
Subject: Protecting America’s Global Competitiveness by Retaining International Talent

The United States has long been a global leader in innovation, technology, and economic growth because of its ability to attract and retain talented individuals from around the world. International students and skilled foreign professionals contribute not only their technical expertise, but also diverse perspectives, new ideas, and entrepreneurial ambition that strengthen American industries.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) plays a critical role in connecting highly educated international graduates with the American workforce. It allows U.S. companies to benefit from talent trained at American universities, particularly in high-demand fields such as artificial intelligence, software engineering, and advanced technology.

Imposing additional financial burdens or restricting employment opportunities for international graduates would risk driving highly skilled talent to competing countries. After investing years in educating these individuals, the United States should not create unnecessary barriers that prevent American companies from benefiting from their knowledge and skills.

Such restrictions could ultimately slow technological innovation, weaken American businesses, discourage international talent from choosing American universities, and undermine the nation’s long-term economic competitiveness.

Countries around the world are competing to attract the brightest minds. If the United States makes it increasingly difficult for talented graduates to contribute to its economy, other nations will gladly welcome them.

America’s greatest strength has always been its ability to attract talent, foster innovation, and turn ideas into progress. Protecting that advantage is not simply about supporting international students. It is about protecting America’s economic future.

I strongly encourage policymakers to consider these long-term consequences and preserve accessible pathways for highly skilled international graduates to contribute to the American workforce.

I respectfully request reconsideration of the proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee on educational institutions seeking to recommend students for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT recommendations.

The F-1 student program allows international students, who have lawfully entered the United States after a rigorous screening and admission process, to pursue higher education and contribute to our academic institutions. Upon completion of their degree programs, OPT and STEM OPT provide these students with the opportunity to apply the knowledge and skills they have gained through authorized employment, benefiting both the students and the U.S. workforce.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gaurav chavan
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 student studying Engineering at Drexel University. I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT.

OPT is a core part of my F-1 program's practical training. I came to the United States to study engineering, paying a lot in tuition and living costs, far from home, with very limited options to work while I study. OPT is the main chance I have to get the industry experience I need as an engineer. I have paid a lot for my education, and it is only fair that I have the chance to apply what I have learned in a real workplace. Without OPT, that investment and years of study would not lead to the practical experience employers expect.

A $70,000 fee, charged to my school before it can recommend OPT, would make OPT effectively unavailable to students like me. Schools cannot reasonably absorb that cost for every student, and many would have to limit or stop OPT recommendations. That would leave F-1 graduates without the practical training their programs were designed to include, and leave U.S. employers without a lawful, short-term way to hire them.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. If a fee is needed, it should be proportionate to the cost of administering OPT, not set at a level that ends the program in practice.
